# gclone — final implementation spec (v1.2, 2026-11-11, review round 2 + auth redesign + review round 3 applied; errata of WP0 and of integration waves 1 (WP1, WP2, WP8), 2 (WP3, WP4, WP5), 3 (WP6) and 4 (WP7), and of the final pass: §17; review round 4 — worker security: §17.7, crypto and formats: §17.8, auth client: §17.9, Drive API: §17.10, index and local state: §17.11, sync engine: §17.12, transfer: §17.13, command line and setup: §17.14; download durability in batches: §17.15, and its review — a barrier for every writer of base state, sync through the writing descriptor: §17.16; Linux builds, releases and the installer: §17.17; **0.2.0 — the login is Google's device authorization grant, proxied by the Worker: §0.6, §2, §16, §17.18; its review: §17.19; 0.3.0 — `gclone web`, the vault in a browser: §7.4, §17.20; its review: §17.21; 0.4.0 — the hosted viewer, a read-only page served by the auth Worker that decrypts in the browser: §1.3, §2.3, §7.5, §16.8, §17.22; its review: §17.23; 0.5.0 — `gclone serve restic`, a restic repository on Drive beside the vault: §3.4, §7.6, §17.24; its review: §17.25; the cryptography audit of 0.4.0, the CLI and core part — gc on an incomplete index, presence by content, removal times, keyfile selection, a 130-bit generated passphrase, `passwd --purge-old`, what the ciphertext shows, attested binaries: §1.3, §2.6, §2.7, §5.2.2, §5.3, §5.9, §15, §17.26; its hosted-viewer part — tickets sealed to the Service Worker, a Service Worker that a hostile host left behind, what the attestation does not cover: §1.3, §2.3, §7.5, §15, §16.8, §17.27; where a device keeps its secrets — a key store sealed by the Mac's Secure Enclave, chosen with `gclone keystore use`, a trial that risks nothing, the state root left out of backups — and releases that are drafts until signed on the owner's Mac: §2.5, §7.1, §7.3, §8, §9, §13, §14, §15, §17.28; the review of all of the above before the release — a passphrase is set to what 0.4.0 makes of it, versions ordered causally, `passwd` asks before it writes, sealed keys never replaced by a keyless login, a bounded trial, a lock no script can skip, a release script that fails closed and can verify again: §1.3, §2.6, §2.7, §5.2.2, §5.3, §7.5, §8.2, §17.29; 0.5.1 — the sealed store is a Mac's default: a login seals from the start, a device on the plain file is tested and then moved without a command, the passphrase is the way back: §1.3, §2.5, §7.1, §7.3, §8, §13, §14, §15, §17.30; the README became a product page and its sections moved to `docs/USAGE.md`, `docs/SETUP.md`, `docs/SECURITY.md` and `DEVELOPMENT.md`: §17.31**)

Single-binary Rust CLI that stores files on Google Drive with client-side authenticated encryption, for ONE user with several devices — an rsync-style sync tool (no mount) — plus one small Cloudflare Worker (`worker/`, TypeScript) that is the user's single OAuth client. This document is the contract for parallel implementation. Companion: `RESEARCH.md` (verified facts; every `[U]` there is still unverified; its §6 covers the auth redesign).

Conventions: all integers big-endian unless stated; `‖` is concatenation; KiB/MiB are binary; "MUST/NEVER" are normative. Section numbers are referenced from the work packages (§12).

Build note for this machine: plain `cargo` is a rustup shim without a toolchain. Use `nix-shell -p cargo rustc --run 'cargo …'`. The Worker's tests need Node ≥ 20: `nix-shell -p nodejs --run 'cd worker && npm ci && npm test'`. Nothing in this spec is deployed by the implementation work — deploying the Worker is the user's one-time setup (§2.1).

---

## 0. Architecture in one page

- **Drive is a dumb, ID-addressed store of immutable, put-once ciphertext objects.** No mirrored tree, no encrypted file names, no `appProperties`, no Changes API, no object is ever overwritten.
- **The directory tree lives in an encrypted, append-only, per-device journal** (`index/`): small immutable *segments* plus periodic *snapshots*. Every device keeps a full replica in SQLite. Listing `index/` (normally one API call) is the only remote listing a normal command performs.
- **Small files (< 1 MiB) are packed** into ~16 MiB blobs; larger files are one blob each. An index entry is `(blob, offset, length, salt)`.
- **Merge = version heads with base pointers** (§5.2): causal successors replace, concurrent writes produce deterministic conflict copies, a put beats a concurrent delete. **Planner = three-way** over a per-device base table (§5.5): a stale device can neither overwrite nor delete what it has not seen.
- **Crypto**: one container format (HKDF-SHA-256 per-object key + ChaCha20-Poly1305 STREAM with age's nonce layout + key-commitment tag). Sealed bytes are only ever replayed, never regenerated: a new salt always means a new object ID.
- **Auth**: ONE Google OAuth client of type *TVs and Limited Input devices*, scopes `openid email drive.file`, "In production". Its ID and secret live only in a small stateless Cloudflare Worker (§16); no device ever holds them. `gclone login` — the same command for the first and for every later device, with or without a browser on the machine — is Google's **device authorization grant** (RFC 8628) proxied by the Worker: the device asks the Worker for a code, shows it, the user enters it at `https://www.google.com/device`, and the device polls the Worker until Google hands out **its own** refresh token (§2.3, §2.4). Access tokens are refreshed through the Worker; file data flows device ↔ Google directly, never through the Worker.
- **Key distribution**: a random master key, wrapped under a user **passphrase** (Argon2id, 256 MiB) and stored as a small keyfile object in the vault (§2.6). A new device logs in, finds the vault, asks for the passphrase once and caches the unwrapped key in a 0600 file. No secret is ever copied between devices: there is no kit and no `link`/`join`.
- **Beside the vault (0.5.0, §17.24)**: `gclone serve restic` speaks restic's REST backend protocol and keeps restic's own files — already encrypted, deduplicated and packed by restic — as plain Drive files in a tree of their own (`gclone-restic/<repo>/`, §3.4). It uses the sign-in and the Drive client and nothing else of the above: no index, no keys, no passphrase, no local state (§7.6).

### 0.1 Where this spec takes each idea from
| Area | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Journal with inner identity, `prev` chain, `seen` refs, coverage sets, rollback marks | security design | made fork-tolerant, with repair paths, auto-compaction, process lock; marks are trust-on-first-use on a new device since v1.2 |
| Merge rule + 3-way planner + conflict copies | security design | reformulated as order-independent "heads" (§5.2) |
| SQLite state, kernel lock, durable pending ops, md5 verify, upload ledger, quota-unit pacer, per-device data folders, pre-generated IDs for everything | perf design | cross-restart resume, inode cache and blob manifest trailer cut |
| Zero daily prompts, `:path` syntax, `--vault-dir`, targeted error messages, excluded-never-deleted, path-ordered packs | UX design | the kit / `link` / `join` of that design are replaced by `login` + passphrase keyfile (§0.4) |
| One OAuth client behind a stateless Worker, per-device refresh tokens, passphrase-wrapped keyfile on Drive | user decision (v1.2) | §2, §16 |

### 0.2 Decision log for the critiques' MUST-FIX items
Applied: never re-seal under an existing salt (replay buffers, §6.2); new ID whenever the salt changes + size/md5 check on 409 (§6.2); secrets (passphrase, tokens, keys) never in argv/env (§2.6, §7.1); inner identity + hash chain + exact coverage sets for every index object (§4.6, §5.3); index objects fully buffered and authenticated before parsing (§4.6); KDF parameter floors/ceilings + constant-time compares (§4.3); `key_epoch` in the v1 header (§4.2); three-way planning + causal merge + conflict copies (§5); ctime in the stat signature + racy-timestamp rule, no inode-keyed hash cache (§5.4); scan errors suppress deletes (§5.4); re-stat before every destructive local op (§5.7); explicit case/NFC handling with exact name bytes stored (§5.1); file-vs-directory conflict rule (§5.2.3); blobs verified before pending ops are published, GC two-phase with 30-day grace (§5.8, §5.9); process lock (§8.3); recovery paths for Rollback/Gap, fork tolerance (§5.3, §5.10); automatic compaction, snapshots carry all heads and removed versions (§5.6); durable intent transactions (`synchronous=FULL`); delete guard trips on either threshold (§5.5.2); filters applied to both sides; deletes after uploads; GC scoped to this vault's own data folders (§5.9); unit-aware pacing (§6.5); multipart only ≤ 4 MiB (§6.2); 308 without `Range` = offset 0, status query 200/201 = done (§6.2); `trashed = false` + `nextPageToken` loop + trashed-vault detection (§3.3); setup covers homepage/privacy URL (served by the Worker) and the show-once client secret (§2.1); orphan grace 14 days, server-time ages (§5.9); undelete (`restore`), index republish (`repair`).

Consciously **not** applied (with reason):
1. *Seal local secrets + index cache under a device key (keychain default).* Rejected for the MVP: the user requirement is zero prompts after the one-time unlock, on macOS and headless Linux alike; a device key stored next to the sealed file is theatre; SQLite cannot be sealed cheaply. Secrets are a 0600 file in a 0700 directory, same trust level as an SSH key; at-rest protection is disk encryption (documented, §1.3). `config::SecretStore` is a trait so a keychain store can be added without touching callers (§11).
2. *Rendezvous object / split enrollment.* Cut (two of three critiques): it needs both devices online within minutes and rests on unverified list consistency. (v1.2: nothing is handed from device to device any more; the master key reaches a new device through the passphrase keyfile, §2.6.)
3. *`rotate` / re-key.* Cut (deferred, §14); the header carries `key_epoch` so rotation needs no format break. Grant-wide revocation ships as `gclone logout --revoke` (§2.7).
4. *Argon2 `p=4`.* Not adopted: the `argon2` crate computes lanes sequentially without its `parallel` feature, so `p > 1` would cost the defender time and the attacker nothing; `p = 1` with 256 MiB is used. Passphrase normalisation (NFC) **is** specified now that a human passphrase exists (§2.6).
5. *64 MiB packs / 8 MiB members.* Not adopted until pack compaction exists (1 MiB / 16 MiB instead).
6. *Blob manifest trailer written from day one.* Cut in review round 2: its only reader (`repair --from-blobs`) is deferred, it put a second, under-specified format on the hot path of every upload, and a blob without the `GCBLOB01` footer simply has no manifest, so adding it later is backward compatible. Stream type 0x04 and the footer magic stay reserved (§4.5).

### 0.3 Review round 2 — what changed (details in the sections named; its kit / shared-token / `init` items are superseded by §0.4)
- **Index** (§4.6, §5.2, §5.3, §5.6): snapshot coverage is an exact set of segment identities (`covered`), not a per-device sequence number; rollback marks are statements about the local replica, plus a separate remote-presence check; no collapse in `apply` (identical heads are deduplicated by `resolve_conflicts`); listed snapshots are adopted instead of re-written; cleanup trashes only what every retained snapshot covers; clone detection by own-segment history and a machine fingerprint; a stuck outbox no longer blocks reads.
- **Sync** (§5.1, §5.4, §5.5, §5.7): leftover staged ops are committed before planning; full case folding; one spelling per key; base rows are refreshed after a matching re-hash and after downloads; filters match parents on both sides; file↔directory type changes are ordered groups; the pair identity is `(st_ino, birth time)` and is never dropped silently.
- **Drive / auth** (§2.4, §6.2–§6.5): `refresh_token_expires_in` stops a Testing-mode login; pinned wire shapes; `fields=` on upload initiation; 401 handling inside sessions; `gc --purge`.
- **Formats** (§4.2–§4.5): `Loc` carries `suite`/`flags`; decoder error precedence fixed; the blob manifest trailer is cut.
- **Architecture** (§9, §12): `ui.rs`, time helpers and the conformance suite moved so that WP1–WP6 need no later package; the transfer layer no longer depends on `Vault`; one upload entry point (`upload_batch`); `Vault::finish_mutation`; fallible `HeadStore`; `open_ctx(OpenOpts)`.

### 0.4 v1.2 — auth and key-distribution redesign (user decision: "I never want to set up OAuth clients again, so that Worker is my one OAuth client")
What changed, and what it reverses:
- **One Web-application OAuth client behind a stateless Cloudflare Worker** replaces the Desktop client whose JSON every first device needed. The Worker is specified in §16 and built by WP8 (`worker/**`). No device holds `client_id` or `client_secret`.
- **Every device has its own refresh token**, obtained by `gclone login` through the Worker (§2.3, §2.4). The shared refresh token and its concurrency probe are gone.
- **`login` / `logout` / `passwd` replace `init` / `auth` / `link` / `join`** (§7.1). `login` detects whether a vault exists: none → it creates one; one → it attaches this device (§2.6).
- **A passphrase-wrapped master key is stored on Drive** (keyfile, §2.6). This reverses the earlier MUST-FIX "nothing passphrase-derived on Drive": the user accepted that Google — and Cloudflare, which can obtain a token (§1.3) — can attack a weak passphrase offline; Argon2id at 256 MiB, a 12-character minimum and a generated 100-bit default are the mitigation.
- **The kit format, the pairing code and `format/kit.rs` are removed.** Recovery = Google account + passphrase (or a downloaded vault folder + passphrase, `--vault-dir`). `gclone key export` is deferred (§14).
- **Rollback marks no longer travel**: a new device trusts the first state it is served (trust on first use, §1.3, §5.3); `hw.inherited` and `index::seed_marks` are gone.
- **`gclone logout` does not revoke at Google by default**: Google documents revocation as grant-wide — it "removes all OAuth 2.0 scopes previously granted to a project, invalidating any issued access or refresh tokens for all clients" (RESEARCH §6.3) — so revoking one device's token would sign out every device. `logout` discards the local token; `logout --revoke` is the deliberate "sign out everywhere" (§2.7). *This deviates from the wording of the decision ("logout revokes this device's token"); manual probe 3 (§2.9) decides whether the default can be flipped.*
- Sections touched: §0, §1, §2 (rewritten), §3.1, §3.3, §4.1–§4.3, §4.7, §5.3, §6.4.1, §7, §8, §9.1–§9.4, §9.6, §9.7, §9.10, §10–§15, new §16.

### 0.5 Review round 3 — what changed in the auth and login parts (details in the sections named)
- **Worker** (§2.3, §16): the check-code confirmation page is shown in **both** login modes (no direct redirect to Google); Google's authorization code is bound to the device's challenge by an OIDC `nonce` that `/token` verifies itself; a per-address rate limit (`429 rate_limited`) and syntactic pre-filters stand in front of every call to Google; `/refresh` re-checks the allowlist when Google returns an ID token; no `login_hint`; `ALLOWED_EMAILS` is a secret; invocation logs are off; `defaultDeps` is pinned and tested in the Workers runtime.
- **Contract fixture** (§16.5): `worker/test/contract.json` is checked by the Worker's tests and by WP3's `tests/auth.rs` — WP3 now needs WP8's fixture (§12).
- **Keyfile** (§2.6, §2.7, §9.4): tighter accepted KDF bounds, at most 4 keyfiles tried, overflow-checked generation; the Rust field is `generation` (`gen` is a reserved word in edition 2024), the JSON name stays `"gen"`.
- **Device** (§2.4–§2.8, §8, §9.10, §10): `secrets.json` and `token.json` live under the state root and are refused when their permissions are too open; `auth_url` is also kept in `config.json`; the login fields of `Secrets` are optional; `NotLoggedIn` / `Locked` and the backend choice of `login` are defined for both backends; ATTACH saves the key only after the device registered itself; `login` never writes `token.json`; a **head fingerprint** gives a new device a value to compare (§2.6).
- **Packages** (§9.2, §12): `tests/live.rs` (WP7), `worker/package-lock.json` and `worker/scripts/check-config.mjs` (WP8), `Cargo.lock` and the root `.gitignore` (WP0).

### 0.6 v1.3 (gclone 0.2.0) — the login is the device authorization grant (user decision: "can we do polling oauth instead of the localhost thing?")
What changed, and what it reverses (errata and transition: §17.18):
- **`gclone login` uses only Google's device authorization grant** (RFC 8628, client type *TVs and Limited Input devices*): `POST /device/start` → the user enters a code at `https://www.google.com/device` → `POST /device/poll` until the tokens arrive (§2.3, §2.4). One flow for every machine; `--no-browser` only means "do not try to open a browser".
- **The browser-redirect flow is removed**: the Worker's `/login`, `/callback` and `/token` routes and its confirmation pages, the sealed state / pending / grant blobs and `SEAL_KEY`, the OIDC nonce and the check code; on the device the loopback listener, the paste flow and the verifier / challenge. The items of §0.5 that describe them are history.
- **The Worker stays stateless** — now without any blob of its own: Google holds the pending login, the device carries the device code.
- **Two OAuth clients for a while**: refresh tokens issued before 0.2.0 belong to the old *Web application* client. `/refresh` serves them through optional legacy secrets; the device names its client in every `/refresh` and in `secrets.json` (`"client": "device"`; absent = legacy) (§2.3, §8.2). **Closed in 0.4.0 (§17.22)**: the Web application client became the hosted viewer's, `/refresh` serves the device client only, and a device that has not run `gclone login` since 0.2.0 has to run it once.
- **New residual risk: device-code phishing** (§1.3, §2.3.2) in place of the hand-over phishing of the redirect flow.
- Sections touched: §0, §1.1, §1.3, §2.1–§2.6, §2.8, §2.9, §7, §8.2, §9.2, §9.3, §9.6, §9.10, §10–§16; new §17.18.

## 1. Goals, non-goals, threat model

### 1.1 Goals
1. One-time setup for the user's lifetime: one Google OAuth client plus one small Cloudflare Worker (§2.1). Every device — the first or the tenth — is connected with one command (`gclone login`), one code entered at Google and, once, the passphrase. No device ever holds OAuth client credentials and no secret is copied between devices.
2. No recurring re-authentication on a device that runs gclone at least once per ~5 months (an idle device needs one `gclone login`, i.e. one code entered at Google).
3. All content, names, tree shape, mtimes and hashes are encrypted and authenticated client-side.
4. Fast: no remote tree walks; small files packed; rename/move/delete/dedup are index-only; parallel transfers; adaptive pacing without tuning flags.
5. Safe multi-device use by default: no silent overwrite, no lockout states, crash-safe, trash instead of delete (permanent deletion only by the explicit `gc --purge`, and of retired keyfiles by the explicit `passwd --purge-old`, §2.7), 25-day undelete.
6. Testable end to end without Google credentials.

### 1.2 Non-goals (MVP)
FUSE mount; two-way `bisync` as one command; multi-user sharing; shared drives; Windows; hiding file sizes (of large **or small** files: packing is for speed and hides nothing, §1.3, §15), file and object counts or activity timing; re-keying (§14.5, §15); snapshots/dedup at chunk level; migrating an existing rclone crypt remote (invisible under `drive.file`).

### 1.3 Threat model
| Adversary | Capability | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Curious Google | reads everything stored + request metadata | Learns **the exact plaintext length of every non-empty file and the number of files** (§17.26): a blob's length inverts exactly to its content's (`ciphertext_len` is a bijection — the "0.03 %" this row used to name is the container's overhead, not an uncertainty), and a pack does not hide its members — each begins with its own 60-byte cleartext header whose first 12 bytes are the same in every stream of the vault, so a pack splits into its members without any key, in the order they were packed (sorted path order within an upload). Also: write timing; which device uploaded what (device IDs are in index object names and data-folder names); per-device journal activity and the number of commits (sequence numbers and lamport values in index object names); how often the passphrase was changed (the generation in keyfile names); the length of index objects, which grows byte for byte with the lengths of the paths in them and with the number of entries (index objects are not padded); IPs; the account e-mail. A size sequence can confirm that a known set of files — a public repository's checkout, a published album — is in the vault. Learns no names, tree, mtimes, hashes, contents — **as long as the passphrase resists guessing**: the keyfile (§2.6) lets Google test passphrase guesses offline at Argon2id cost (256 MiB, t = 3 per guess), for as long as it likes and on every keyfile version it ever held. The generated passphrase (130 bits; 100 bits when generated before 0.5.0) is out of reach; a weak typed one is not, and the only rule enforced on a typed one is its length. Accepted by the user (§0.4). The same is learned by **anyone who can read the vault folder** without being Google: a phished device grant, a token obtained through the Worker, a browser signed in to the hosted viewer. **With the hosted viewer (§7.5)** Google additionally learns that and when it is used and from which origin (the `Origin` header of the browser's Drive requests), and which blobs and byte ranges are read — hence the approximate size and the viewing pattern of what is opened. No names: the viewer's addresses, title and session history carry none, so a history sync has nothing to upload. Still no content — **unless the passphrase is saved where Google can read it** (the password-manager row). |
| Malicious Google — and, except where stated, anyone who can **write** to the vault folder without the key (a phished device grant, a token obtained through the Worker, a signed-in viewer browser) | modify, swap, truncate, reorder, duplicate, delete, withhold, roll back objects; overwrite an object in place or delete it and create another under its name; choose the creation time of what it creates | Any byte change, swap, slice, truncation: detected (AEAD + final flag + salt/size/BLAKE3 in the authenticated index). Journal rollback: index objects that a device has **applied** and that are then deleted, trashed, renamed, overwritten in place or re-created under the same name are detected by that device (`Rollback`, exit 3) — presence is the object the replica accepted (its size and md5), not a listed name (§5.3, §17.26). A withheld segment that an accepted one refers to: `Gap`. **Not detected in-protocol**: the *newest* objects withheld from a device before anything it is shown refers to them (the device stays on the older state for as long as that is kept up; two devices can be held on different states; only Google can do this per device — a token holder cannot show two devices different listings, but he can replace an object for every device that has not applied it yet, which those devices report as an object that failed verification, on every command, and for which `gc` refuses, §5.9). A **fresh** device has no marks: it trusts the first state it is served (trust on first use) and detects rollbacks only relative to that; `login` prints a **head fingerprint** to compare with `gclone status` on the device that wrote last — the one check that exposes a stale or truncated journal, and what it does and does not prove is in §2.6. **Creation times** are whatever the creator of an object asks for — Drive accepts a `createdTime` on create, from any token holder, not only from Google itself: the time a removal counts from is therefore the later of the listed creation time and the `created_ms` the writer sealed into the segment, so the store can lengthen the restore window and the gc grace and never shorten them (§5.2.2); `gc` additionally refuses while the store's clock is more than a day from the device's (§5.9). Deletion is DoS: detected, not prevented. A substituted or old keyfile gains nothing: it either fails to open (leaking nothing — nothing derived from the passphrase is ever sent) or wraps the same master key. Drive-reported md5 is used only against accidental corruption, never as tamper evidence. **The hosted viewer (§7.5) is a fresh device on every visit**: it keeps no marks, trusts the state it is served and cannot detect a rollback between visits; it shows the head fingerprint to compare with `gclone status`. An old index shows an older vault; it cannot forge an entry or a byte. Planted objects cost at most a question: an oversized index object or an expensive keyfile is announced with its size and can be skipped; **in the hosted viewer and, since 0.5.0, in the CLI** a planted keyfile cannot hide the real one behind "wrong passphrase" — objects that are no keyfile take no place among the candidates, and while well-formed keyfiles remain untried the answer is "N were not tried", never "wrong passphrase" (§2.6 ATTACH; what remains is the bound on how many are looked at, §15); unreadable snapshots stop the load instead of showing a partial tree; a newer format anywhere stops it. |
| Cloudflare / whoever controls the Worker, its secrets or its domain (**changed in 0.4.0**) | sees the OAuth client secrets, `SEAL_KEY`, and every refresh and access token passing through `/device/poll`, `/refresh`, `/web/token` and `/web/refresh`; can mint access tokens for the account's gclone files; **serves the page of the hosted viewer (§7.5), into which the passphrase is typed** | **For anyone who uses the hosted viewer: full compromise** — a modified page takes the passphrase and, with the access token, every file. Accepted with the decision to offer the hosted viewer (§17.22). No header, hash or integrity attribute changes this, because the same party serves them. What limits it: the deployed static bytes can be compared with the attested release bundle (`verify-deployed`, §7.5), from any machine and at any time — which finds an accident or a changed asset, not a Worker that answers selectively; and a device that never opens the hosted viewer is exposed exactly as before 0.4.0, which is the rest of this cell. **The compromise does not end when the release is deployed again** (§17.27): a browser that loaded the page while someone else served it can keep what they left there — a Service Worker registered for the origin, which answers `/` out of the browser without asking the host, or a long-lived cache entry for the page — and goes on showing *their* page under the real address, across restarts and ordinary reloads; `verify-deployed` has no browser profile, cannot see any of it and reports the host clean. The remedy is in the browser: **in every browser that had the viewer open in that time, clear this site's data before the passphrase is typed there again** (`docs/SECURITY.md`, "After a change of hands"; `docs/AUTH.md`). Two aids, neither a substitute for that: the Worker answers a request for the script of any Service Worker other than `/sw.js` with `Clear-Site-Data` (§16.8 — Chrome then drops the registration at its next update check, which is after a visit that still showed the other page; Firefox ignores the header on that request and WebKit kept the registration, as measured; a script planted under `/a/` is never asked of the Worker at all), and the viewer's page removes Service Worker registrations that are not its own whenever it gets to run (§7.5) — which a foreign worker for the whole origin prevents. `SEAL_KEY` adds nothing to this party's reach. **Without the hosted viewer**: same reach as Google and no more: ciphertext, metadata, the keyfile (offline passphrase guessing), deletion (DoS; detected as above). Never sees the passphrase, the master key or any file data (data flows device ↔ Google). What the Worker makes the device **show** is bounded too: the sign-in address of `/device/start` is opened in a browser only when it is a `google.com` address, and anything the device prints from the Worker's answers is checked plain text (§2.4) — a Worker controller cannot put a page of his own, or terminal control sequences, in front of the user through `gclone login`. Remedy after a suspected leak: rotate the client secret in the Google console, `gclone logout --revoke`, `gclone login` on each device. |
| Someone else using the Worker | calls its public endpoints (the URL is not a secret) | `/device/start` hands anyone a device code and a user code for a login of their own — which is worth something only if the **owner** then enters that user code at Google (the Phisher row); `/device/poll` hands a refresh token only to an account in `ALLOWED_EMAILS` (others are refused and their grant revoked — and the refusal shows that account's address only masked, so the route is no way to learn who entered a code) and only for a grant that carries nothing beyond the Worker's own scopes; `/refresh` only relays to Google: a string that is not a live refresh token of one of the Worker's clients gets nothing back. Abuse of the relay is limited by a rate limit per client address — per /64 prefix for IPv6, where one host owns a whole /64 — and syntactic pre-filters (§2.3); the limit is approximate and does not stop a sender with many networks — and every request, refused or not, counts against the Worker plan's daily request quota, so on the `workers.dev` host a flood can stop logins and token refreshes until the quota resets (DoS only; mitigation: a custom-domain route with a zone rate-limiting rule, §15, §16.6). Google additionally limits device-code requests per client ID; someone who exhausts that quota through `/device/start` delays logins, nothing else. The Worker's only redirect is `http` → `https` (§2.3). **The viewer's routes (0.4.0)**: `/web/start` only formats a URL; `/web/token` needs a code that Google issued to the web client after a consent, the matching verifier, and an allowlisted account; `/web/refresh` asks Google only after a cookie opened under `SEAL_KEY`; `/refresh` does not serve the web client at all, so a refresh token of that client is worth nothing outside its sealed cookie. Cross-site use is refused three ways (`SameSite=Strict`, JSON-only bodies, the `Origin` check) and could not read the answers. Requests for the viewer's static files do not run the Worker and cost no quota. |
| Network attacker | MITM | TLS everywhere (rustls + platform verifier); the device talks to the Worker over HTTPS only (`http://` is accepted for loopback hosts, for tests). Login: the device code — the only thing that can collect the tokens — travels only inside TLS, in the answer of `/device/start` and the bodies of `/device/poll`; the user code is typed by the user into Google's own page; the refresh token never appears in a URL (§2.3.2). **Hosted viewer (0.4.0)**: plain `http` is never served — the Worker answers `308` to `https` (and the zone's "Always Use HTTPS" before it, which is also what covers the static files, §16.8); HSTS for two years, subdomains included, after the first `https` visit. **The first visit from a new browser is protected only if the `https` address is used** (bookmark, typed with `https://`): a browser that is handed the `http` address can be given a fake viewer by an active attacker — then the Phisher row (b) applies, without the cookie (`Secure`, `__Host-`) and without the redirect flow. Preloading the apex domain closes it and is the owner's choice (`worker/README.md`). The authorization code crosses the browser's address bar once; it is single-use and useless without the verifier in the tab's `sessionStorage`. |
| Phisher | (a) **device-code phishing**: calls `/device/start` himself (it is unauthenticated — a device that logs in has no credentials yet), receives a user code, and talks the owner into entering **that** code at `https://www.google.com/device` and approving ("gclone needs re-authorising, please enter WXYZ-ABCD") | Needs the owner to type a code they did not get from their own terminal into Google's page and to approve the consent — within the code's lifetime (30 min), and a new code per attempt. If they do, the phisher's `/device/poll` receives a refresh token for the vault's files: the keyfile (offline passphrase guessing) and the ability to trash or overwrite every vault object — not the file contents, and **nothing outside the vault**: the Worker asks Google for `SCOPES` only and hands out no token for a grant that carries anything else (§2.3). **The e-mail allowlist does not help**: the account that consents is the owner's, the allowed one. Mitigations: the terminal says with every code *"enter only a code shown in this terminal"*, and the Worker's home page says the same; Google's consent screen names the app; `/device/start` and `/device/poll` are rate-limited, take no input that reaches Google except a pre-filtered device code, and log neither codes nor tokens. Residual risk, **accepted**: a known weakness of the grant itself (RFC 8628 §5.4). A phished grant reaches only ciphertext but could trash it — trashed objects are restorable for 30 days and every modification is detected; the remedy is removing the app at https://myaccount.google.com/permissions (or `gclone logout --revoke`) and `gclone login` on each device. **(b) A look-alike of the hosted viewer (0.4.0; worse than (a))**: until the hosted viewer existed, no web page had a reason to ask for the vault passphrase. A page that imitates it does not need the Worker's redirect flow: it calls the open `/device/start` from its own server, shows the user code with "to sign in, enter this code at google.com/device" (Google's real page, naming the real app), polls `/device/poll`, receives a refresh token for the vault's files, and then asks for the passphrase in its own form — **tokens plus passphrase: full compromise**, without any control over Cloudflare. (Sending the owner an authorization URL with the phisher's own challenge achieves nothing: the code lands in the owner's browser at `/callback`, where no matching `state` exists, and is never sent on.) What stands against it: (1) the unlock field is a credential field (§7.5), so a password manager offers the passphrase on the real origin and **not** on a look-alike — an owner who never types the passphrase into a web page by hand has nothing to give away; WebAuthn PRF unlock (deferred, §14) is its stronger successor; (2) static sentences on the real sign-in and unlock screens, in `docs/SECURITY.md` and in `worker/README.md`: the viewer signs in by redirect only and never shows or asks for a device code — a web page that shows a code is not gclone; (3) the owner reaches the viewer by bookmark or home-screen icon only. The signed-in address and the vault's folder on the unlock screen help the habit and prove nothing (a phisher holding a token can show them). **Accepted residual risk** (§15, §17.22), like (a) and with a higher price. |
| Thief of an unlocked device / malware as the user | reads `secrets.json` — or, on a Mac, whose secrets are sealed by default (0.5.1, §8.2, §17.30), asks the Secure Enclave as gclone does, or runs gclone: the sealed store protects **copies of the file** (a backup, a synced folder, a disk image, the disk taken out of the Mac), not against code running as the user — the enclave key has no user-presence condition, by the owner's choice: gclone runs unattended | Full compromise (cached master key + this device's refresh token). Remedy for the login: `gclone logout --revoke` on any other device (or remove the app at https://myaccount.google.com/permissions ) — this ends the login of **every** device — then `gclone login` on each device you keep. **There is no remedy for the key**: it is unchanged, and whoever holds it decrypts whatever ciphertext of the vault they can obtain — what they copied, and, if they can still fetch (the Google account, the Worker), everything uploaded later. Re-keying is deferred (§14.5); the only full remedy in v1 is a new vault (`logout --forget` on every device, `login --new-vault` with a new passphrase, upload again, delete the old folder — `docs/SECURITY.md`, "If a passphrase or a device's key file leaked"), which protects what is uploaded from then on and nothing that the old vault held. |
| Another user of the machine, or any local process that is not the user's | connects to the port of a running `gclone web` (§7.4); can read process lists; can run servers of their own on loopback | Gets `403` on every route: the session secret is 256 random bits, handed out only for the key of a one-time link. The link is printed on the user's terminal or, when gclone opens the browser itself, written into a `0600` page in the `0700` state directory whose **path** is what the launcher gets — the key is in no argument list. The cookie is scoped to a random path (`/s-<128 bits>/`), so the browser does not attach it to requests for that user's server on another loopback port. Whoever gets hold of a link first all the same (a shoulder, a screenshot of the terminal) makes the user's own link fail with a text that says so and what to do: a new link (Enter) starts a new session and ends every session before it, downloads included. |
| A web page in the user's browser | makes the browser send requests to `127.0.0.1:<port>` (cross-site requests, DNS rebinding) | Nothing: the cookie is `SameSite=Strict`; a request whose `Host` is not one of the three loopback authorities of the listening port, whose `Origin` is not the viewer's, or whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not `same-origin` / `none` is refused before the session is looked at; no response carries a CORS header, every response carries `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`. |
| Content of the vault | a file that someone got into the vault (a downloaded HTML page, an SVG, a PDF) is opened in the viewer | It never becomes a document of the viewer's origin with script: HTML, XHTML, XML and JavaScript are served as `text/plain`, SVG as an image under `CSP: sandbox`, everything unknown as an attachment; types come from the file name, `nosniff` everywhere; the page builds its DOM from text nodes only and runs under a CSP without inline script (§7.4). A PDF is shown by the browser's own viewer, whose script sandbox is the browser's business. **In the hosted viewer (§7.5)** the same holds by another mechanism: file bytes reach a browser context only as a Service Worker response whose type, policy and disposition come from the file name through the same table (`src/web/mime.rs`, compiled into the wasm); there is no `blob:` URL, and the page has no HTML sink. |
| Script in the hosted viewer's origin (0.4.0): an injected script, a malicious browser extension with access to the page | runs with the page's rights while the vault is unlocked | Reads every file through the vault worker and the Service Worker, gets access tokens (`/web/refresh`), and can trash or overwrite ciphertext (`drive.file` has no read-only form: read-only is a property of the viewer's code, not of its token). **What it cannot take is a key — enforced since 0.5.0 (§17.27); until then this row claimed it and nothing held a script to it**: it cannot read the refresh token (sealed, `HttpOnly`); no call exports a master key; and a ticket — the key of one file's stream — leaves the vault worker only **sealed to the Service Worker** (§7.5, the ticket port), so the port that the page hands out, and that such a script can keep, replace or sit in the middle of, carries ciphertext which only the Service Worker instance of that moment can open, and nothing can after a Lock that took place. What a script that is **gone before the passphrase is entered again in that tab** takes away is therefore what it read while it ran — plaintext, pulled through the browser file by file — and at most one hour of access token; not, as before, some 350 bytes per file that open the whole vault later, offline, in seconds (the audit's L2). **What this does not cover, said plainly**: (a) a script that is in the page when the passphrase is typed **or filled in by a password manager** has the passphrase, and the page also hands the vault worker the port the key bundle arrives on — that is the vault. That includes a script that arrived *after* the unlock and is still there the next time: it can keep the tab from ever locking (below) and answer a click on Lock with the page's own unlock screen, and what is typed into it is the passphrase (§17.29). So: **after anything suspicious, close the tab or the browser — do not press Lock and type the passphrase into the same tab again**; (b) while the vault is unlocked the script reads the plaintext of **every** file and every name, through the same `/v/<id>` addresses the page uses — that is what the page is for, and no design that shows files in a page changes it; (c) **a script in the unlocked page can keep that tab from locking or signing out at all**, and then keeps the open vault — the vault worker with the master keys, which goes on issuing tickets — **for as long as the tab lives**: not "until the browser stops the Service Worker", as this row said before §17.29. It can swallow the click, override the clock the idle lock reads, or (until §17.29) make one statement of `lock()` throw, after which every later Lock, the lock by the clock, another tab's lock and Sign out returned at once. The page's lock now does its irreversible steps first, each on its own, with functions taken before any later script ran (§7.5), which closes the cheap ways; it cannot close this in principle — the lock is code of the page the script is in. Plaintext still, not keys; (d) the boundary is the browser's separation of a page from its workers and from the Service Worker, together with a policy under which the origin serves no script but the build's: whatever can change what the origin serves, or reach into another context — the serving party (the Cloudflare row), an extension that rewrites responses or attaches a debugger — is not held by it. Mitigations: a CSP without inline or foreign script, Trusted Types, no third-party resource, no HTML sink, the same static bytes for every request, no reflected input (§7.5). |
| Someone with the browser profile (0.4.0): a borrowed, shared or stolen phone or laptop that is signed in to the hosted viewer | uses the session cookie; reads what the browser kept | With the vault locked: ciphertext, the keyfile (offline passphrase guessing at Argon2id cost) and the ability to trash, until the sealed end of the session (12 h, or 30 days if chosen). Not the vault key: it is never stored. No names: the address, the title and every session-history entry are free of them, and nothing else is stored. The vault **is** locked when the device was put away: the lock goes by wall clock (15 minutes without input, 5 minutes in the background, any restore from the back/forward cache), so a phone picked up hours later shows the passphrase screen, not the listing. Exposed: a vault left open and visible is open for up to 15 minutes; a passphrase saved in the browser's password manager is one device unlock away (next row). **Sign out does not sign the browser out of Google**: on a computer that is not the owner's, the next person passes Google with one click and gets a fresh viewer session (ciphertext, keyfile, trash) and the Google account itself; the signed-out screen says so and links to Google's sign-out, and the 30-day option is labelled "only on your own device". Remedies: Sign out; a new `SEAL_KEY` (ends every browser session and no device login — no other route accepts a web-client refresh token); removing the app at Google (ends every login). A **copy** of the cookie stays valid until its sealed end — the price of a stateless Worker. |
| The browser's password manager and its sync provider (0.4.0) | stores the passphrase if the owner accepts the browser's offer; syncs it | If the manager is one that the Drive account's provider can read — Google Password Manager with standard encryption, in a Chrome that is signed in to the same Google account — then **Google holds ciphertext, keyfile and passphrase**: the "Curious Google" row no longer holds. One click on a prompt does it. The viewer cannot see or reliably suppress that prompt (browsers offer to save login fields whatever `autocomplete` says). Managers Google cannot read are fine and **wanted** (Phisher row (b)): Google Password Manager with on-device encryption turned on, iCloud Keychain, a separate manager. Mitigation: one sentence on the unlock screen, in `docs/SECURITY.md` and in `worker/README.md`. |
| The supply chain of a deployment of the hosted viewer (0.4.0) | changes what `wrangler deploy` uploads: a release asset, a step of the release workflow, an npm package of the deploy toolchain | Same outcome as the Cloudflare row. Mitigations (§7.5): no npm dependency in the page; the bundle is built on the tag in a job that runs no npm code, with the pinned toolchain and lockfiles, and is signed by a build-provenance attestation that names the workflow and the tag; the owner's machine verifies that attestation before unpacking, again immediately before `wrangler deploy` (with a byte comparison of `dist/`), and again when comparing the deployed host — never trusting `SHA256SUMS` or the working `dist/`. The attestation names the *tag*, so the scripts also verify that the release is **immutable** (`gh release verify-asset`, which passes only for a file of an immutable release and binds tag, commit and file digests) and, where they deploy from a checkout, that the bundle was built from the commit that is checked out (`--source-digest`, §7.5, §17.26); a release published before the repository made releases immutable is used only when named (`GCLONE_MUTABLE_RELEASE=<tag>`). Left: **anyone who can push a tag or publish a release in the repository** (they can publish a new, correctly attested release of their own — and, for a release that is not immutable, move its tag and have other bytes attested under the same name, which is what the immutability check is for); the Rust crates in the lockfile (watched for advisories: `.github/workflows/audit.yml`, Dependabot, §17.26), the pinned actions, GitHub's attestation service, and wrangler itself as the uploader (caught afterwards by `verify-deployed`, for the static files). **And the Worker script itself, which is outside the attestation altogether** (§17.27, the audit's I3): the attestation, `check-release` and `verify-deployed` cover the viewer's *static files*; the code that answers `/`, `/callback` and the sign-in routes (`worker/src/`) — which puts the status line into the bundle's `index.html`, sets every header of that answer and so has the last word on the page the passphrase is typed into — is bundled by wrangler and esbuild on the owner's machine, after `npm ci` of 186 npm packages (three with install scripts), from the working tree. The deploy scripts hold that tree to the release's commit and list its local changes without refusing them; nothing builds the Worker script in the release workflow, signs it, or compares what was uploaded with the tag, and `verify-deployed` sees only what the deployed Worker answers to `verify-deployed`'s own requests. |
| The supply chain of the CLI (0.5.0, §17.26) | changes what `install.sh` installs: a release asset, a step of the release workflow, `install.sh` itself, a crate | The CLI is typed the passphrase and caches the master key: a malicious binary is full compromise of every vault its device attaches to. Mitigations: lockfiles and `--locked` everywhere; each archive carries a build-provenance attestation made in the job that built it (`release.yml`), which the release job verifies again before it creates the draft release, which the owner's `scripts/release-sign-macos.sh` verifies once more before it publishes (§17.28), and which `install.sh` verifies with `gh attestation verify` (repository, signer workflow, `refs/tags/<tag>`) **when the GitHub CLI is installed and signed in** — then a release whose files were replaced is refused; without `gh` only `SHA256SUMS` is checked, which comes from the same release as the archive and shows a damaged download only, and the script says so in one line. Left: anyone who controls the repository (a new malicious release is attested correctly; `install.sh` on `main` is what the README pipes into `sh`); installs without `gh`; the crates, the pinned actions and GitHub's attestation service as above. |
| Thief of a powered-off device | offline disk access | Protected only by disk encryption (FileVault/LUKS). Explicitly accepted; see §0.2 item 1. |
| Someone who learns the passphrase | — | Passphrase alone: nothing without access to the Google account (or a copy of the vault folder). Passphrase + a keyfile it opens (any generation, retired or not: a copy of the vault folder, the Google login, Google itself): full compromise — the master key, hence every object the holder can obtain, **including what is uploaded later**. `gclone passwd` does not undo a leak for anyone who already copied an old keyfile (same master key), and by default the retired keyfile stays in Drive's trash for 30 more days, where the old passphrase still opens it; `gclone passwd --purge-old` deletes the retired keyfiles from the account, trash included (§2.7) — which helps only against a party that had not yet copied one, and not against Google's own retention. Re-keying is deferred; the full remedy is a new vault (the row "Thief of an unlocked device"). |

Local `state.db` and the index cache contain plaintext paths/hashes resp. ciphertext; same sensitivity as the synced files themselves.

---

## 2. Auth, enrollment and key distribution

**Roles.** *Google*: authorization server and Drive. *Auth Worker* (§16): a stateless Cloudflare Worker and the only holder of the OAuth client's ID and secret; it turns one consent at Google into a refresh token for one device and turns refresh tokens into access tokens. It has no storage (no KV, no D1, no Durable Object) and never sees file data. *Device*: the gclone CLI; it holds the Worker's URL, its **own** refresh token and — after the one-time unlock — the master key. All Drive calls go device ↔ Google directly. The login is Google's **device authorization grant** (RFC 8628): there is no redirect, so neither the Worker nor the device has to be reachable from a browser. *Browser* (0.4.0, optional): the hosted viewer of §7.5, a page served by the same Worker. It signs in with a redirect through a second OAuth client ("the web client"), keeps its refresh token in a cookie that only the Worker can open, and holds — in memory only — an access token and, after the passphrase, the master key; its Drive calls go browser ↔ Google directly as well. Everything in §2.1–§2.9 is about devices unless it says otherwise; the browser's routes are in §2.3.

```
 device (gclone login)                    auth Worker                                 Google                      the user, any browser
   POST /device/start {} ───────────────►  POST device/code (client_id, SCOPES) ───►
   ◄── {device_code, user_code,           ◄── {device_code, user_code, verification_url,
        verification_url, expires_in,          expires_in: 1800, interval: 5}
        interval}
   print: "To sign in, open  <verification_url>" / "and enter the code  <user_code>"
   every `interval` s:
   POST /device/poll {device_code} ─────►  POST token (grant_type=device_code,
                                            device_code, client_id, client_secret) ─►  428 authorization_pending
   ◄── 400 authorization_pending ────────
                                                                                        ◄── opens google.com/device, enters the code,
                                                                                            chooses the account, consents
   POST /device/poll {device_code} ─────►  POST token (…) ─────────────────────────►  200 {refresh_token, access_token, id_token, scope}
   ◄── {refresh_token, access_token,       check id_token: e-mail verified ∈ ALLOWED_EMAILS (else revoke);
        expires_in, scope, email}          scope ⊆ ALLOWED_SCOPES and ∋ drive.file
   …later:  POST /refresh {refresh_token, client: "device"} ──►  + client_id, client_secret ──► token endpoint
   ◄── {access_token, expires_in, scope}
```

### 2.1 One-time setup (once per user — never per device; the authoritative step list is `worker/README.md`, WP8; URLs are [K] and may drift)
1. **Deploy the Worker**: `cd worker && npm install && npx wrangler login && node scripts/stub-dist.mjs && npx wrangler deploy` (the third command writes the placeholder for the viewer's static files, without which wrangler refuses to deploy; §16.8). Note the printed URL `https://gclone-auth.<acct>.workers.dev` — this is `AUTH_URL`; `<host>` below is its host name. Until step 3 the Worker answers `500 server_misconfigured`. **The host is chosen before this step** (§17.14): the URL goes into the Google app's branding and into every device's login, so a user who wants the custom domain of step 5 puts its `routes` entry into `wrangler.jsonc` first (`node scripts/custom-domain.mjs <host>`, §16.1) and uses `https://<host>` from the start — `<host>` is then the custom host and the Authorized domain of step 2.3 its registrable domain. Moving later means a second round in the Google console and a new `gclone login` on every device.
2. **Google Cloud console**:
   1. Create a project: https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate (any name). Enable the Drive API: https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/drive.googleapis.com → **Enable**.
   2. Google Auth Platform → **Get started** (https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview): app name `gclone`, your e-mail as support and contact address, Audience **External**. Do **not** upload a logo (a logo triggers brand verification).
   3. Branding: Authorized domain `<acct>.workers.dev`; Application home page `https://<host>/`; Privacy policy `https://<host>/privacy` (the Worker serves both pages — Google requires the two links for every external production app, RESEARCH §6.1).
   4. Audience → **Publish app** → status must read **In production**. Do **not** click "Submit for verification": `openid`, `email` and `drive.file` are non-sensitive. *(If you skip this step, Google ends every login after 7 days; `gclone login` detects it, §2.4.)*
   5. Clients → **Create client** → Application type **TVs and Limited Input devices** (any name; this client type has no redirect URI and no JavaScript origin). Copy the client ID and the client secret now — the secret is shown only once.
3. **Worker secrets** (three; each `wrangler secret put` deploys a new version at once, no further `wrangler deploy` is needed): `npx wrangler secret put GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `npx wrangler secret put GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `npx wrangler secret put ALLOWED_EMAILS` (comma-separated Google account addresses). `ALLOWED_EMAILS` is a secret, not a `vars` entry: the address never sits in a tracked file, and a later `wrangler deploy` cannot reset it (§16.2). (Three more, optional, switch on the hosted viewer of §7.5: `GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_ID` / `GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_SECRET` — the ID and secret of a second client, of type *Web application*, whose only Authorized redirect URI is `https://<host>/callback` — and `SEAL_KEY`, 32 fresh random bytes in base64 (`openssl rand -base64 32 | npx wrangler secret put SEAL_KEY`). The two names date from 0.2.0–0.3.x, when that client refreshed logins made before 0.2.0; it no longer does: §2.3 `/refresh`, §17.22. The viewer's whole setup — the console, the zone settings, the deploy from a release — is `worker/README.md`, "The hosted viewer: setup".)
4. **Check**: `curl https://<host>/` answers 200 and contains `Status: ready`.
5. *Recommended*: put the Worker on a custom domain with a zone rate-limiting rule over all of its paths (§16.6) — on the `workers.dev` host anyone can use up the plan's daily request quota. With the host chosen in step 1 only the rule is left.

`worker/setup.sh` walks through steps 1, 3 and 4 interactively: it asks first whether the Worker is served on its `workers.dev` host or on a host name of the user's own (then it writes the `routes` entry before the first deploy and uses that host everywhere), and it prints the console checklist of step 2 at the right moment. Google console changes can take "5 minutes to a few hours" to apply. Workspace users may choose Audience **Internal** instead of External/Publish.

After that, on every device: `gclone login https://<host>` (the URL is needed once per device — it is remembered in `config.json` and survives `logout`; §2.2).

### 2.2 Constants
```
GOOGLE_DEVICE_CODE_URL = https://oauth2.googleapis.com/device/code      (used by the Worker only)
GOOGLE_TOKEN_URL   = https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token                (used by the Worker only)
GOOGLE_REVOKE_URL  = https://oauth2.googleapis.com/revoke               (Worker: refused logins; device: `logout --revoke`)
SCOPES             = "openid email https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file"      what the Worker asks Google for; fixed, never taken from a request
SCOPE_DRIVE_FILE   = https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file
ALLOWED_SCOPES     = { openid, email, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email, SCOPE_DRIVE_FILE }
                     everything a grant of the Worker's clients may carry: SCOPES plus Google's spelling of the granted `email` scope (Worker, §2.3)
DEVICE_GRANT       = urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code       (the grant_type of a poll, Worker → Google)
AUTH_TIMEOUT       = 1800 s    the longest a device waits for a sign-in: the lifetime Google gives a device code, and the cap on `expires_in`
AUTH_POLL_SLOW_DOWN = 5 s      `slow_down`: the device's poll interval grows by this much (RFC 8628 §3.5)
AUTH_POLL_INTERVAL_DEFAULT = 5 s   the poll interval when none is named (RFC 8628 §3.5) — by Google to the Worker, by the Worker to the device
AUTH_RETRY_AFTER_MAX = 60 s    cap on a `Retry-After` the device honours, on the `interval` it accepts from /device/start,
                               and on the pause between two polls that failed (§2.4 step 3)
AUTH_REFRESH_ATTEMPTS = 5      tries of /refresh and of /device/start on 5xx / network errors
ACCESS_TOKEN_SKEW  = 60 s      (refresh when < 60 s to expiry)
IDLE_WARN_DAYS     = 150
AUTH_BODY_MAX      = 8 KiB     largest request body the Worker reads
AUTH_RATE_LIMIT    = 30 requests per 60 s per client address (IPv6: per /64 prefix), over /device/start, /device/poll, /refresh and /web/* together (Worker, §2.3)
GOOGLE_AUTH_URL    = https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth       (0.4.0: the address /web/start formats; the Worker never fetches it)
WEB_COOKIE         = __Host-gclone-web                                  (0.4.0: the hosted viewer's session cookie, §2.3)
WEB_SESSION_TTL    = 12 h; WEB_SESSION_REMEMBER_TTL = 30 d              (0.4.0: the absolute lifetime of a browser session, sealed inside the cookie)
PASSPHRASE_MIN_CHARS = 12      Unicode scalar values, for a typed passphrase
PASSPHRASE_GENERATED_SYMBOLS = 26       Crockford symbols of a generated passphrase: 130 bits (0.5.0, §17.26)
PASSPHRASE_GENERATED_SYMBOLS_OLD = 20   what gclone before 0.5.0 generated (100 bits); still recognised by the normalisation (§2.6)
PASSPHRASE_WARN_CHARS = 20     a typed passphrase shorter than this gets a warning and a question (§2.6)
KEYFILE_MAX        = 64 KiB
KEYFILE_TRY_MAX    = 4         one passphrase attempt asks at most 4 keyfiles — 4 key derivations — unless the person asks for the rest (§2.6 ATTACH)
KEYFILE_LOOK_MAX   = 32        objects with a keyfile's name that a new device fetches and looks at (64 KiB each); what is no keyfile is refused
                               there and takes none of the KEYFILE_TRY_MAX places (0.5.0, §17.26; the hosted viewer's number, §7.5)
KEYFILE_LOOK_ALL_MAX = 1024    the same with `gclone login --all-keyfiles`
KEYFILE KDF        = Argon2id v1.3, m = 262144 KiB (256 MiB), t = 3, p = 1, 16-byte salt      (accepted on decode: §2.6)
```
Device-side URLs are injectable for tests (`AuthEndpoints { base, revoke_url }`, `DriveEndpoints`); the Worker's Google URLs are injectable through its `deps` (§16.3). A poll every 5 s is 12 requests per minute: inside `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT` for two devices behind one address signing in at once.

**Auth URL** (`AUTH_URL`, the Worker's base URL). `gclone login [AUTH_URL]` resolves it as: the argument, else env `GCLONE_AUTH_URL`, else the value stored in `secrets.json` by an earlier login, else the one in `config.json` (it is not a secret and is written there when the device is attached, so it survives `gclone logout`), else the compile-time default `option_env!("GCLONE_DEFAULT_AUTH_URL")` (set when building one's own binary), else an error that names the three ways. Every other command uses the value in `secrets.json` only. Validation (`auth::validate_auth_url`; a stored value is validated when it is **used** — `Secrets::endpoints()`, §9.10 — never when a file is merely loaded, so the secrets of a directory vault, which have no `auth_url`, load fine): it parses as a URL with scheme `https`, a host, no userinfo, no query, no fragment; scheme `http` is accepted **only** for the hosts `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `[::1]` (tests); a trailing `/` is removed. Routes are appended to it (`<AUTH_URL>/device/start`, `/device/poll`, `/refresh`). The HTTP client used for the Worker is built with `redirect(Policy::none())`: a 3xx answer is an error, so a device code or a refresh token is never re-sent to another host.

### 2.3 Auth Worker HTTP API (normative for `worker/` — WP8 — and for the fake auth endpoints of `FakeDrive` — WP3)

General rules:
- JSON answers: `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. **Every** error answer, on every path and method, is `{ "error": "<code>", "message": "<one English sentence>" }`.
- **`https` only** (0.4.0; before routing, on every path): a request whose URL is not `https` — on a host other than `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` — is not served. `GET` and `HEAD` → `308` with `Location:` the same URL under `https:` (path, query and port unchanged), no body, `Cache-Control: no-store`; every other method → `400 https_required`, without looking at its body or cookie.
- The Worker's own two HTML pages — `/privacy` always, and the home page for `/` and `/callback` **in a deployment without the viewer's files** (the placeholder of §16.8 has a page of its own; this one is the fallback when the assets binding or its `index.html` is missing): `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, and since 0.4.0 `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains`. They are static: no script, no form, and nothing taken from a request. **With the viewer's files deployed, `/` and `/callback` are the viewer's page** (below).
- No CORS headers on any route, no storage. **One cookie** (0.4.0), set and read by the `/web/*` routes only; the device routes set and read none. **One redirect**: `http` → `https`, above.
- `POST` routes require `Content-Type: application/json` (else `415 unsupported_media_type`), a body of at most `AUTH_BODY_MAX` (else `413 payload_too_large`) that is a JSON object whose required fields are strings within the stated bounds (else `400 invalid_request`). Unknown fields are ignored. (`/device/start` uses nothing of its body and still requires the JSON object: a request that needs `Content-Type: application/json` cannot be made by a cross-site form, and without CORS headers not by a cross-site script either.)
- Unknown path → `404 not_found` (this includes every file name of the assets directory — `/index.html`, `/_headers` — and the viewer's own `/v/…` addresses and `/seal-key`, which only its Service Worker answers); **a request for the script of a Service Worker other than `/sw.js`** — `Service-Worker: script`, with `Sec-Fetch-Dest` absent or `serviceworker` — is answered as its path is answered, plus `Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "storage"` (0.5.0, §16.8); known path with another method → `405 method_not_allowed` + `Allow` (`GET` for the pages `/`, `/callback`, `/privacy` — `HEAD` is not accepted — `POST` for the JSON routes).
- An unexpected exception inside the Worker answers `500 internal_error` without detail. The code is outside the mapped list below on purpose: a device treats it as "other 5xx" (§2.4).
- **Rate limit** (`AUTH_RATE_LIMIT`, §2.2): `/device/start`, `/device/poll`, `/refresh` and the four `/web/*` routes — after the path/method check and before anything else — ask the Worker's rate-limit binding (§16.2) with a key made from the `cf-connecting-ip` header: an IPv4 address as it is; an IPv6 address as its /64 prefix, written as the first four groups in lower-case hexadecimal without leading zeros followed by `::/64` (`2001:db8::1` → `2001:db8:0:0::/64`) — one IPv6 host owns at least a /64, so a key per address would give it 2^64 budgets; an IPv4-mapped address (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`) as that IPv4 address; `"unknown"` when the header is absent or empty; any other text as it is. Over the limit → `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After: 60`; Google is not contacted. Without the binding (unit tests) the check is skipped. The limit is per Cloudflare location and approximate; it bounds what one sender can relay to Google through the OAuth client — a sender with addresses in many networks (many IPv4 addresses, an IPv6 allocation larger than a /64) has one budget per network, which only a zone rule in front of the Worker can stop (§16.6) — and it does **not** keep refused requests from counting against the Worker plan's daily quota (§16.6).
- Configuration is checked on every request: `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` non-empty; otherwise every JSON route but `/web/logout` answers `500 server_misconfigured` and the page says `Status: not configured`. **The hosted viewer is configured** (0.4.0) when `GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_ID` **and** `GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_SECRET` are non-empty (the web client) **and** `SEAL_KEY` decodes — as base64 or base64url — to exactly 32 bytes. While one of the three is missing — every Worker passes through that state, because each `wrangler secret` command is deployed at once — that is not a reason to stop: the device routes work as always, the page says `Status: ready. The web viewer is not configured: it needs GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_LEGACY_CLIENT_SECRET and SEAL_KEY.`, and only `/web/start`, `/web/token` and `/web/refresh` answer `500 server_misconfigured`. (The half-set-pair rule of §17.19 for `/refresh` is gone with the legacy branch, §17.22.) An empty or missing `ALLOWED_EMAILS` is not a misconfiguration: it allows nobody (fail closed).
- Nothing secret is ever logged or echoed: no request bodies, device codes, user codes, tokens, client secrets. Log lines carry route, status and error code only; `route` is one of `/`, `/callback`, `/privacy`, `/device/start`, `/device/poll`, `/refresh`, `/web/start`, `/web/token`, `/web/refresh`, `/web/logout`, or `other`. No cookie, authorization code, verifier or e-mail address either. **One URL carries a secret** since 0.4.0: Google's redirect to `/callback` has the authorization code of a browser sign-in in its query — single-use, and worth nothing without the verifier in the browser tab. The platform is configured so that no request is stored beyond that log line: invocation logs off, query-string redaction on, traces off, no log export (security requirements of `wrangler.jsonc`, §16.2) — until 0.4.0 a second line of defence, now the first for that query. `wrangler tail` shows it while it runs. Requests for the viewer's static files do not run the Worker and write no line.

| Route | Called by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /`, `GET /callback` | browser, Google reviewers | the page (0.4.0): the bytes of `dist/index.html` — the hosted viewer's page, or the placeholder's — with the first `<!--gclone-status-->` replaced by the status line (`Status: ready`, `Status: ready. The web viewer is not configured: …`, `Status: not configured`). The same bytes for both paths and every query: nothing of the request is read. `/callback` is the redirect URI of the browser sign-in. Without viewer files: the Worker's own home page (what this is, a warning never to enter a code that someone sent, link to `/privacy`, the status line) |
| `GET /a/<build>/<file>`, `GET /sw.js` | the viewer's page | **answered by the asset layer; the Worker does not run** (0.4.0, §16.8): the viewer's static files, with the header set of §7.5 |
| `GET /privacy` | browser | static privacy statement (stores nothing; uses `drive.file` + e-mail only to sign the owner in) |
| `POST /device/start` | device | start a login at Google; pass Google's device code, user code and verification URL on |
| `POST /device/poll` | device, every `interval` seconds | ask Google whether the code was entered; on success check the grant and hand out this device's refresh token |
| `POST /refresh` | device | refresh token → access token, for the device client only |
| `POST /web/start`, `/web/token`, `/web/refresh`, `/web/logout` | the viewer's page | the browser sign-in of the hosted viewer (0.4.0; below) |

**`POST /device/start`** — body: a JSON object; nothing in it is used. The Worker sends `POST GOOGLE_DEVICE_CODE_URL`, form-encoded: `client_id=<GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID>`, `scope=<SCOPES>` (no secret; timeout 10 s). On `200` it requires `device_code` (16..=512 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_/.~+=-]`), `user_code` (2..=64 printable ASCII characters, no leading or trailing space), `verification_url` (`https://` followed by 1..=200 printable non-space ASCII characters), `expires_in` (a number > 0) and — when present — `interval` (a number > 0; RFC 8628 §3.2 makes the field optional, and an absent one is `AUTH_POLL_INTERVAL_DEFAULT`, 5) — else `502 upstream_error` — and answers `200`: `{ "device_code": "…", "user_code": "GQVQ-JKEC", "verification_url": "https://www.google.com/device", "expires_in": 1800, "interval": 5 }` — those five fields exactly as Google sent them (`interval`: 5 when Google sent none). The Worker does not judge the host of `verification_url`: its upstream is Google's own endpoint, and a host rule here would only break every login on the day Google moves its page. The party that has reason to distrust the address is the device, which opens it only when it is a `google.com` address (§2.4). Error answers of Google are mapped by the table below (a client that is not of the device type → `500 client_invalid`; Google's own limit on device-code requests, `403 {"error_code": "rate_limit_exceeded"}` → `502 upstream_error`).

**`POST /device/poll`** — body `{ "device_code": "<16..=512 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_/.~+=-]>" }`; anything else → `400 invalid_request` without contacting Google (a pre-filter against malformed input; it does not assume Google's current code format).
1. `POST GOOGLE_TOKEN_URL`, form-encoded: `grant_type=<DEVICE_GRANT>`, `device_code`, `client_id`, `client_secret`. Timeout 10 s.
2. The states of a device code are passed on under Google's own error names, whatever HTTP status Google used for them (it answers `428` for `authorization_pending` and `403` for `slow_down`; the Worker goes by the `error` field): `authorization_pending` → `400 authorization_pending`; `slow_down` → `400 slow_down`; `expired_token` → `400 expired_token`; `access_denied` → `403 access_denied`; `invalid_grant` (unknown or already redeemed code) → `400 invalid_grant`. Other errors: the table below.
3. On `200` without an `error` field (an answer that names an error is that error under any status) — Google has now consumed the device code, so **nothing from here on is answered with a 5xx**: a device repeats a poll that got one (§2.4), and repeating can only bring `invalid_grant` and hide the reason. The Worker requires, in this order:
   - `refresh_token` and `access_token` present, `expires_in` a number, and an `id_token` whose payload (the middle `.`-separated part, base64url JSON) decodes with `aud == GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `iss ∈ {"https://accounts.google.com", "accounts.google.com"}` — else `403 grant_unusable` with a message that says which part was missing (*"Google approved the sign-in, but its answer carried no ID token (the account cannot be checked without one), so nothing was handed out and the code is used up. …"*; at most 300 characters). Nothing is revoked: without a readable ID token the Worker does not know whose grant it is, and a revoke is grant-wide. The signature is **not** verified: the token was received directly from Google's token endpoint over TLS, authenticated with the client secret (Google's own guidance, RESEARCH §6.2). An ID token from any other source is never accepted. (That Google's device-grant answer carries an ID token when `openid email` was requested follows its "Sign-In on TVs" guide; first confirmed by probe 5, §2.9.)
   - `email_verified === true` and `email` is an entry of `ALLOWED_EMAILS` (comma-separated; entries trimmed). **The comparison is byte for byte, except that the 26 ASCII letters match in either case** — no Unicode case mapping, which would turn other code points into ASCII letters (U+212A KELVIN SIGN lower-cases to `k`). An `email` claim, or an entry, that is not 3..=254 characters of printable ASCII (`0x21..=0x7e`) matches nothing. Else: best-effort `POST GOOGLE_REVOKE_URL` with `token=<refresh_token>` (so no grant for a stranger's account stays behind; revocation is grant-wide, which is exactly right here), then `403 email_not_allowed`. Its message shows the address **masked** — the first character, `***`, and everything from the last `@` on: *"The Google account s\*\*\*@example.net is not allowed to sign in here."* — or *"This Google account …"* when the claim is absent or not such printable ASCII. The caller of `/device/poll` is anonymous, and whoever entered its user code at Google agreed to show the address to the app, not to that caller; the masked form still tells the owner which account was picked by mistake.
   - every entry of `scope` (space-separated; empty entries ignored) is a member of `ALLOWED_SCOPES` (§2.2; compared exactly) — else `403 scope_not_allowed`: the tokens are discarded, nothing is handed out, and nothing is revoked (a revoke is grant-wide and would sign out the owner's other devices). The message tells the user to remove the app at https://myaccount.google.com/permissions if this was unexpected and then names up to three of the excess scopes (only entries of at most 100 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9:/._-]`; they come last so that a client that shortens the message keeps the remedy). The Worker itself asks for `SCOPES` only and no request can change that, so this check is defence in depth: the client's secret never turns into a refresh token for more than gclone's own files, whatever Google reports for the grant.
   - `scope` contains `SCOPE_DRIVE_FILE` — else `403 scope_missing` (no revoke, for the same reason; the user unticked the permission on the consent screen).
4. `200`: `{ "refresh_token": "1//…", "access_token": "ya29.…", "expires_in": 3599, "scope": "openid https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file", "email": "me@example.com" }`, plus `"refresh_token_expires_in": <seconds>` exactly when Google sent that field (time-limited grant, §2.4).

A refusal in step 3 ends that login for good: the device code is spent, and a further poll gets `400 invalid_grant`. All four refusals are `403` and final for the device.

**`POST /refresh`** — body `{ "refresh_token": "<20..=512 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_/.~+=-]>", "client": "device" }`; a malformed `refresh_token`, or a `client` that is present and not the string `"device"` → `400 invalid_request` without contacting Google (the token filter is a pre-filter against malformed input; it does not assume Google's current `1//…` prefix). **Which client**: Google refreshes a token only for the OAuth client that issued it, and the Worker cannot tell from a token which one that was — the device says so. `"client": "device"` → the client of `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, **the only client this route serves**. No `client` field — a login made before 0.2.0, through the *Web application* client (§17.18) — → `400 invalid_grant`, message: *"This login was made with gclone's earlier browser sign-in, which this sign-in helper no longer serves. Run `gclone login` again."*, **in every configuration** and **without** contacting Google (a device maps it to `Expired`, exit 4). **Changed in 0.4.0 (§17.22)**: from 0.2.0 to 0.3.x a request without `client` was refreshed through that client when its two secrets were set (and a half-set pair answered `500 server_misconfigured`). The client is the hosted viewer's now, and its refresh tokens are honoured in the sealed cookie only (`/web/refresh`): there they have an end, the allowlist is applied on every use, and a new `SEAL_KEY` cuts them all off — a route that accepted such a token bare would undo all three. For `"client": "device"` the Worker sends `POST GOOGLE_TOKEN_URL`, form-encoded: `grant_type=refresh_token`, `refresh_token`, `client_id`, `client_secret` of that client (timeout 10 s), maps errors by the table, and answers `200`: `{ "access_token": "ya29.…", "expires_in": 3599, "scope": "…" }`. **Allowlist re-check**: when Google's answer carries an `id_token` (it may, for a grant with `openid`; [U]) whose payload has `aud` = the ID of the client that was used and Google's `iss`, and whose e-mail is not verified or not in `ALLOWED_EMAILS`, the Worker revokes the refresh token (best effort) and answers `403 email_not_allowed` (the address masked, as on `/device/poll`) — so removing an address from the allowlist cuts that account off at its next refresh. Without an `id_token` there is nothing to check: the access token is returned (a refresh token of these clients can only have come out of a login, which checked the allowlist as it was then). **Scope re-check** (after the allowlist re-check): when the `scope` of Google's answer has an entry outside `ALLOWED_SCOPES`, the access token is discarded and the answer is `403 scope_not_allowed` (same message, no revoke) — a refresh token with wider access than gclone's, however it came to exist, gets nothing through the Worker. Only excess is refused here: a missing or empty `scope` field passes.

**The hosted viewer's sign-in (0.4.0)** — Google's authorization-code flow with PKCE (S256) through the web client; the tab that starts is the tab that finishes, and the Worker keeps nothing in between. The page makes `verifier` (32 random bytes, base64url), `challenge = base64url(SHA-256(verifier))` and `state` (16 random bytes, base64url) and keeps them in the tab's `sessionStorage`; `/web/start` formats Google's address; Google redirects to `/callback?code=…&state=…`; the page compares `state`, removes the query from the address bar and sends `code` and `verifier` to `/web/token`.
