Rules of all four `POST /web/*` routes, **checked in this order**: (1) method, else `405 method_not_allowed` + `Allow: POST`; (2) the request comes from the viewer's own page — `Origin` equals the request URL's origin, and `Sec-Fetch-Site`, when present, is `same-origin` — else `403 cross_origin` (a missing `Origin` is refused); (3) the rate limit, else `429 rate_limited` + `Retry-After: 60` — **not for `/web/logout`**, which is never limited; (4) the web client pair and a 32-byte `SEAL_KEY` are set, else `500 server_misconfigured` — not required by `/web/logout`; (5) `Content-Type: application/json`, else `415`; (6) a body of at most `AUTH_BODY_MAX`, else `413`; (7) a JSON object, else `400 invalid_request`. Unknown body keys are ignored. No answer carries a CORS header; every answer is `no-store`. **Why the origin comes before the limit, and why sign-out has none** (§17.23): a request of another site is refused without work — no secret, no call to Google — and a page anywhere can send one without a preflight (`fetch(url, {method: "POST", mode: "no-cors"})`); counted, any page open in the owner's browser could keep the 30-per-minute budget of the owner's address used up, so that the viewer gets no access token, the devices behind that address no refresh, and "Sign out" answers `429` without clearing the cookie. `/web/logout` uses no secret, asks nobody and answers a constant; a sign-out that is turned away would leave the session in a browser its owner believes signed out. **The device routes** (`/device/start`, `/device/poll`, `/refresh`) refuse, for the same reason and at the same place — after the method, before the limit — every request that carries an `Origin` or a `Sec-Fetch-Site` header: `403 cross_origin`. A browser puts them on what a page sends; the gclone command sends neither. (A client that is not a browser can still forge headers and spend the budget of its own address; that is what an address-keyed limiter is.) **The session cookie is found however the cookies arrive**: `Cookie` values are split at `;` **and at `,`** — a browser sends one `Cookie` field per cookie over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and the runtime's `Headers.get` joins several fields with `, `; the blob is base64url and holds neither character.

- **`POST /web/start`** — `{ "challenge": "<43 characters: the canonical base64url of 32 bytes>", "state": "<22..=128 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_-]>" }` → `200 { "authorization_url": "<GOOGLE_AUTH_URL>?…" }` with exactly these query parameters, in this order: `client_id` (the web client), `redirect_uri=<origin>/callback`, `response_type=code`, `scope=<SCOPES>`, `access_type=offline`, `prompt=consent`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `state`, `nonce` = base64url(SHA-256(`"gclone-auth/v2/nonce"` ‖ the challenge text)). Nothing else of the request gets into it; Google is not contacted. Malformed → `400 invalid_request`.
- **`POST /web/token`** — `{ "code": "<8..=512 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_/.~+=-]>", "verifier": "<43..=128 characters of [A-Za-z0-9._~-]>", "remember": true|false }` (`remember` optional; a non-boolean is `400`). The Worker redeems the code at `GOOGLE_TOKEN_URL` (`grant_type=authorization_code`, `code`, `code_verifier`, `redirect_uri`, the web client's ID and secret) and applies the checks of `/device/poll` step 3 with one more — after the ID token was recognised as Google's for the web client and before the allowlist: the ID token's `nonce` equals the nonce of `base64url(SHA-256(verifier))`, i.e. the code was issued for an address that `/web/start` built for **this** verifier; else `400 invalid_grant`, nothing revoked (the grant belongs to whoever consented, and that may be the owner). `200`: `{ "access_token", "expires_in", "scope", "email", "session_expires_in": 43200|2592000 }` and `Set-Cookie: __Host-gclone-web=<blob>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, with `; Max-Age=2592000` appended only when `remember` is `true` (otherwise the cookie ends with the browser session; the sealed lifetime is 12 h). Errors, none of which sets a cookie: `400 invalid_request` (Google was not asked, the code is not spent); `400 invalid_grant`; `403 grant_unusable` (a missing refresh, access or ID token; an ID token that is not Google's for the web client; a refresh token longer than 512 characters or outside the token alphabet, which the seal cannot hold); `403 email_not_allowed` (the grant is revoked; the address masked); `403 scope_not_allowed`, `403 scope_missing`, `403 access_denied`; `500 client_invalid` (includes Google's `redirect_uri_mismatch`); `502 upstream_error`.
- **`POST /web/refresh`** — `{}` plus the cookie → `200` with the same five fields, `session_expires_in` being the seconds **left**; no `Set-Cookie` (the lifetime is absolute, not extended by use). The Worker opens the seal, checks its end and that the sealed address is still in `ALLOWED_EMAILS`, and only then asks Google (`grant_type=refresh_token` with the web client). Errors: `401 no_session` with no cookie → no `Set-Cookie`; `401 no_session` with a cookie that does not open or has run out → the clearing cookie (below), Google is not asked; `403 email_not_allowed` — the sealed address is no longer allowed, or an ID token in Google's answer says so → revoke plus the clearing cookie; `400 invalid_grant` → the clearing cookie; `403 scope_not_allowed`, `403 access_denied`, `500 client_invalid`, `502 upstream_error` → the cookie is kept (the session may work again).
- **`POST /web/logout`** — `{}` → `200 {}` with `Set-Cookie: __Host-gclone-web=; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=0` (the clearing cookie) and `Clear-Site-Data: "storage"` (not `"cookies"`, which would clear the whole registrable domain). Works with no cookie, a bad cookie and an unconfigured Worker. Nothing is revoked at Google — that would sign every device out. The Worker keeps no list of sessions: a **copy** of a cookie stays valid until its sealed end or a new `SEAL_KEY`.

**The cookie blob** — base64url of `0x02 ‖ 0x04 ‖ nonce(12) ‖ AES-256-GCM(key, nonce, aad = the first two bytes, iat u32 BE ‖ exp u32 BE ‖ len(email) u8 ‖ email ‖ refresh_token)`; key = HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = `SEAL_KEY`, salt = 32 zero bytes, info = `gclone-auth/v2/web-session`). `0x02` is the blob version (`0x01` were the three blob kinds of the browser sign-in before 0.2.0, which nothing opens any more), `0x04` the kind. At most 805 bytes / 1074 characters; with the cookie's name 1092. The refresh token appears in no response body and in no log line; the access token only in the bodies of `/web/token` and `/web/refresh`. Contract: `worker/test/contract.json` version 3 holds these routes as cases (§16.8).

Mapping of Google's answers (every route that asks Google; the device-code states of `/device/poll` are listed there):
| Google answers | Worker answers |
|---|---|
| `error: invalid_grant` | `400 invalid_grant` (for `/refresh`: the refresh token is revoked, expired or unused for six months; for `/device/poll`: the device code is unknown or was already redeemed) |
| `error: invalid_client`, `deleted_client`, `unauthorized_client`, `invalid_scope`; on `/web/token` also `redirect_uri_mismatch` | `500 client_invalid` (message carries Google's code) |
| `error: access_denied`, `admin_policy_enforced`, `org_internal` | `403 access_denied` (message carries Google's code) |
| any 5xx, network failure, timeout, a body that is not a JSON object, any other error | `502 upstream_error` — Google gave no usable answer, and nothing was consumed |
| `/device/poll` only: a `200` token answer that lacks a part the Worker needs (step 3) | `403 grant_unusable` — the code **was** consumed |

All error codes: `invalid_request` 400, `invalid_grant` 400, `authorization_pending` 400, `slow_down` 400, `expired_token` 400, `email_not_allowed` 403, `scope_missing` 403, `scope_not_allowed` 403, `grant_unusable` 403, `access_denied` 403, `not_found` 404, `method_not_allowed` 405, `payload_too_large` 413, `unsupported_media_type` 415, `rate_limited` 429 (+ `Retry-After`), `server_misconfigured` 500, `client_invalid` 500, `upstream_error` 502, `internal_error` 500; since 0.4.0 also `https_required` 400, `no_session` 401 and `cross_origin` 403.

#### 2.3.1 Statelessness
The Worker remembers nothing between two requests: a login in progress exists at Google, under the device code, and the device carries that code from `/device/start` to every `/device/poll`; **a browser session of the hosted viewer (0.4.0) exists in the browser**, as the sealed cookie of §2.3, which the Worker opens with `SEAL_KEY` on each `/web/refresh` and forgets again. From 0.2.0 to 0.3.x there was no `SEAL_KEY` and no blob format (both had existed for the browser-redirect flow before 0.2.0, §17.18); 0.4.0 has one blob kind again, for the browser only — the device routes still seal nothing. The Worker's bindings are the rate limiter and, since 0.4.0, the **read-only static assets** of the viewer (§16.8): files that are part of the deployment and change only with a deploy — no KV, D1, R2, Durable Object or queue. Consequences of having no session list: a copy of a cookie cannot be revoked singly — it ends at its sealed `exp`, or for all browsers at once with a new `SEAL_KEY`. A device code is single-use without any server state because Google's is: once a poll was answered with tokens — whether the Worker then handed them out or refused them — a further poll with the same code gets `invalid_grant`.

Consequence, accepted: a `/device/poll` answer that carries the tokens and is lost on its way to the device (or a Worker invocation that dies between Google's answer and its own) loses that login; the device's next poll gets `400 invalid_grant` and the user runs `gclone login` again. Nothing else is affected.

#### 2.3.2 Why this is safe — and where it is not
- **The client secret never leaves the Worker.** The device-code request needs none; every token request is made by the Worker. A device holds a device code for at most 30 minutes and its own refresh token afterwards.
- **Binding.** The tokens of a login go to whoever polls with its device code; only the party that called `/device/start` has it (TLS answer, never printed, never in a URL). The user code is useless to anyone but Google's page. There is no browser hop back to the device, so there is no state to forge, no code to inject and no redirect to bend: the CSRF, code-injection, open-redirect and mix-up questions of a redirect flow do not arise.
- **Token theft.** The refresh token never appears in a URL or a page; it exists only in the TLS response of the `/device/poll` that completes the login.
- **Scope.** The access a login yields is fixed by the Worker: `/device/start` sends the constant `SCOPES`, `/device/poll` hands out tokens only when every scope Google reports for the grant is in `ALLOWED_SCOPES` and `drive.file` is among them, and `/refresh` refuses a refresh token whose grant is wider. (Google restricts the device grant to a short list of scopes anyway; `drive.file` and the OpenID scopes are on it, full `drive` is not.)
- **Cross-site requests.** No CORS headers and JSON-only POST bodies: a web page cannot call the device routes through a visitor's browser — and what it could start with `/device/start` it could not read. Since 0.4.0 a request that names a page as its sender (`Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-Site`) is refused on the device routes before it is counted (above), so that a page cannot use up the rate limit of the address it is opened from either. The `/web/*` routes, which act on a cookie, add the `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site` check and `SameSite=Strict`.
- **The browser sign-in (0.4.0).** A redirect flow has the questions the device flow avoids, and answers them: *CSRF / code injection* — the page sends a code on only when the `state` in the address equals the one in the tab's `sessionStorage`, and the Worker accepts a code only with the verifier whose challenge it was issued for (PKCE) **and** whose nonce is in the ID token (so a code from an address the Worker did not build for this verifier fails even if the attacker supplies a matching verifier of his own to his own page — he cannot plant it in the owner's tab); *open redirect* — `redirect_uri` is the Worker's own origin plus `/callback`, nothing of a request; *token theft* — the refresh token leaves the Worker only inside the seal, in an `HttpOnly` cookie; the authorization code is in a URL once, single-use; *session fixation* — a cookie is only ever set by `/web/token` after Google's answer passed every check.
- **Strangers.** Anyone can start a login and reach Google's consent screen with their **own** account; `/device/poll` refuses (and revokes) any account outside `ALLOWED_EMAILS`: nobody else obtains tokens. Anyone can also send junk to the three routes; the pre-filters and the rate limit per client address (per /64 for IPv6, §2.3) bound what one sender can relay toward Google, but they do not stop a sender with many networks, and they do not keep anyone from using up the Worker's own request quota or Google's per-client quota of device-code requests (§1.3, §16.6) — a denial of logins, nothing more.
- **Device-code phishing** (residual, **accepted**): see the Phisher row of §1.3. `/device/start` is unauthenticated by nature, so a phisher can start a login and try to make the **owner** enter the phisher's user code at Google. The allowlist cannot notice it — the consenting account is the allowed one — and the Worker, being stateless and never seeing the user's browser, has no place to put a confirmation step: Google's page is the only page there is. What is done: (1) the device prints, with every code, *"(enter only a code shown in this terminal; waiting…)"*, and the Worker's home page carries the same warning; (2) the routes are rate-limited and pre-filtered, and nothing in a `/device/start` request can change what Google is asked for; (3) device codes, user codes and tokens are never logged, and every answer is `no-store`. What a phished grant yields is bounded as for every gclone login: ciphertext and the keyfile, the ability to trash or overwrite vault objects (trash is recoverable for 30 days; modifications are detected), nothing outside the vault.

### 2.4 Login on the device, token handling

`auth::login_interactive` has **one** flow, the same on every machine.

1. **Start** (`auth::device_start`): `POST <AUTH_URL>/device/start` with `{}` → `DeviceCode { device_code, user_code, verification_url, expires_in, interval }`. The route is repeatable (it only leaves an unused code behind): 5 tries on 5xx / network errors, one more after a `429` (mapping table below). The answer is checked before any of it is shown, because the user code and the URL end up in a terminal and the URL in a browser: `device_code` non-empty; `user_code` 1..=64 bytes of printable ASCII (`0x20..=0x7e`) without leading or trailing space; `verification_url` at most 256 bytes of printable ASCII without a space that parses as an `https` URL with a host and **without a user name or password** (`https://www.google.com@other.example/` reads like a host it is not); `expires_in` a number > 0; `interval` a number > 0, or absent — then `AUTH_POLL_INTERVAL_DEFAULT` (fractions count; `expires_in` is capped at `AUTH_TIMEOUT`, `interval` at `AUTH_RETRY_AFTER_MAX`). Anything else → `Network("unexpected answer from the auth Worker")`, with nothing printed.
2. **Show** (`InteractiveOpts.print`; stderr in production, also with `-q` and `--json` — the lines are needed to get through the sign-in at all). Exactly these three lines ▸:
   ```
   To sign in, open  https://www.google.com/device
   and enter the code  GQVQ-JKEC
   (enter only a code shown in this terminal; waiting…)
   ```
   The URL and the code are the Worker's answer verbatim. Then, unless the CLI decided against it, `InteractiveOpts.open(verification_url)` opens the page in the local browser (the `open` crate in production) — a convenience whose failure changes nothing; the code still has to be typed there. **Only a Google page is opened** (`auth::is_google_page`: scheme `https`, host `google.com` or a host ending in `.google.com`). For any other address — the Worker's word is all the device has for it — a fourth line is printed after the code ▸ `(warning: that is not a google.com address, and it was not opened. Google's page for this is https://www.google.com/device; open another one only if you trust this auth Worker)` (`auth::NOT_GOOGLE_NOTE`), nothing is opened, and the login goes on: should Google ever move its page, the user can still follow the printed address. The CLI does not try to open a browser when `--no-browser` is given, when `SSH_CONNECTION` or `SSH_TTY` is set, or on Linux when neither `DISPLAY` nor `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` is set (`want_headless`, §9.10).
3. **Poll** (`auth::device_wait`): sleep `interval`, then `POST <AUTH_URL>/device/poll` with `{ "device_code": … }`, until an answer ends the login (table below): the tokens (`LoginGrant { refresh_token, access_token, expires_at_ms, scope, email, refresh_expires_in }`; the device also requires `scope` to contain `SCOPE_DRIVE_FILE`, else `AuthError::ScopeMissing`, and `email` — which it prints and stores — to be at most 254 bytes of printable ASCII without a space (`0x21..=0x7e`) containing an `@`, else `Network("unexpected answer from the auth Worker")`), a refusal, or the end of the code. `slow_down` adds `AUTH_POLL_SLOW_DOWN` to the interval for the rest of the login. **A poll that fails without an answer about the login** — a network error, `502 upstream_error` or another 5xx, `429` (then the device first waits `Retry-After`, capped) — is followed by the next one: the Worker answers 5xx only where Google has not consumed the device code (§2.3), so repeating is harmless. **The device backs off** (RFC 8628 §3.5: "clients MUST unilaterally reduce their polling frequency"): after `n` polls in a row that failed with a network error or a 5xx it waits `interval · 2ⁿ`, at most `AUTH_RETRY_AFTER_MAX` — but never less than `interval`, so `slow_down` increments are kept in full, and never so long that the last poll the plain interval would still have made is skipped (the wait is cut to `time left − interval`). A `429` is not counted: its `Retry-After` is the back-off. The first poll that is answered about the login (`authorization_pending`, `slow_down`) ends the streak, and the wait is `interval` again. The first failure of a streak is reported through `print` (*"(cannot reach the sign-in service right now: … — still trying)"*), the rest silently. The device stops by itself when the next poll would lie past `expires_in` after the start: `AuthError::Timeout` — or `AuthError::Network(<the last failure>)` when the polls were failing at that point.
4. **Ctrl-C** ends the process with exit 130 (§7.2); nothing was stored, and the abandoned device code simply expires.

**Expiring-grant check.** `refresh_token_expires_in` (seconds of refresh-token lifetime left; Google sends it only for time-limited grants — its Testing-mode value ≈ 604799 is [U], manual probe 1) arrives as `LoginGrant.refresh_expires_in`. If it is present, `gclone login` stops **before** storing the token or touching a vault: *"Google will expire this login in N days — the OAuth app is still in Testing (Google Auth Platform → Audience → Publish app), or time-limited access was chosen. Publish the app, then run `gclone login` again."* (exit 4). `--allow-expiring-login` overrides; then `refresh_expires_at_ms = now + n·1000` is stored in `secrets.json` (§8.2), shown by `status` and used by the Expired message (§2.8). Field absent → `refresh_expires_at_ms = null`.

**Token handling.**
- Refresh (`auth::refresh`): `POST <AUTH_URL>/refresh` with `{ "refresh_token": …, "client": "device" }` → `access_token`, `expires_in`. The `client` field is `Secrets.client` (§8.2): `"device"` for every login made by 0.2.0 or later; **omitted** for a login on file from before (`AuthClient::Legacy`), which a Worker of 0.2.0–0.3.x refreshed through its legacy client and the Worker of 0.4.0 answers `400 invalid_grant` (§2.3, §17.22).
- `TokenProvider` caches `{access_token, expires_at_ms, refreshed_at_ms}` in `<state root>/token.json` (0600, §8.1) so most commands make no request to the Worker at all; single-flight in-process. On a Drive API `401`: `force_refresh()` once, retry once, then `AuthError::Expired`. The cache file is written only after a **real** refresh; `prime()` (the access token that came with a fresh login) is memory-only. `gclone login` builds its providers **without** a cache file and deletes `token.json` after every interactive sign-in, whatever its outcome (§2.6): an access token obtained during a login — possibly for the wrong Google account — is never left on disk for later commands.
- Every *real* refresh stores `refreshed_at_ms`; `status` warns when the newest refresh is > `IDLE_WARN_DAYS` old. A refresh token dies after six months without use — per device. Recommended keep-alive for rarely used machines (documented, not installed): monthly cron `gclone status -q`.

Mapping of Worker answers to `AuthError` (`auth/login.rs`; identical for the fake):
| Worker answer | from `/device/start` | from `/device/poll` | from `/refresh` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `400 authorization_pending` | unexpected | poll again after `interval` | unexpected |
| `400 slow_down` | unexpected | `interval += 5 s`, poll again | unexpected |
| `400 expired_token` | unexpected | `Timeout` | unexpected |
| `400 invalid_grant` | unexpected | `LoginFailed("the code is no longer valid: it expired, or this sign-in was already completed")` | `Expired` |
| `403 grant_unusable` | unexpected | `LoginFailed(message)` — the Worker's own sentence; final, no further poll | unexpected |
| `403 email_not_allowed` | `NotAllowed(message)` | `NotAllowed(message)` | `NotAllowed(message)` |
| `403 scope_missing` | `ScopeMissing` | `ScopeMissing` | `ScopeMissing` |
| `403 access_denied`, `403 scope_not_allowed` | `Denied(message)` | `Denied(message)` | `Denied(message)` |
| `500 client_invalid`, `500 server_misconfigured` | `WorkerMisconfigured(message)` | `WorkerMisconfigured(message)` | `WorkerMisconfigured(message)` |
| `404 not_found` | `LoginFailed("the auth Worker at this URL is an older version without the code sign-in; deploy the current worker/ first (worker/README.md)")` | unexpected | unexpected |
| `429 rate_limited` | wait `Retry-After` (capped at 60 s), retry **once**, then `Network("the auth Worker is rate-limiting this address")` | wait `Retry-After` (capped), poll again | as `/device/start` |
| `502 upstream_error`, other 5xx, connect/read errors | retried 5× with backoff, then `Network(…)` | poll again, backing off (step 3) | retried 5× with backoff, then `Network(…)` |
| any 3xx, a non-JSON body, any other status | `Network("unexpected answer from the auth Worker")` — the "unexpected" of this table | same | same |

### 2.5 What is stored where
| Item | Location | Protection |
|---|---|---|
| OAuth `client_id`, `client_secret`, `ALLOWED_EMAILS`; for the hosted viewer (0.4.0) the web client's ID and secret and `SEAL_KEY` | the Worker's configuration at Cloudflare (§16.2) | Cloudflare account; never on a device, never in a browser, never in the repository |
| The hosted viewer's page, scripts and wasm (0.4.0) | the Worker's static assets, part of the deployment (§16.8) | public and the same for everyone; comparable with the attested release bundle (§7.5) |
| A browser's refresh token for the hosted viewer, the account `email`, the session's end (0.4.0) | the cookie `__Host-gclone-web` in that browser | sealed under `SEAL_KEY` (§2.3): the browser can neither read nor change it; `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, host-only |
| In a browser tab of the hosted viewer (0.4.0): access token; after the unlock the master key(s), the decrypted index, per-file stream keys | memory of the page's workers only (§7.5) | gone with Lock, reload or the tab; nothing derived from the passphrase is ever stored |
| `auth_url`, this device's `refresh_token` and the `client` it belongs to, account `email`, `refresh_expires_at_ms`, cached master key(s), `min_epoch` | `<state root>/secrets.json` — under `~/.local/state`, not `~/.config`, which is what dotfile repositories and synced home folders pick up. **Or**, on a Mac — by default since 0.5.1 (§8.2, §17.30): from the first save of a login, or once the Secure Enclave has passed gclone's trial on a device that was on the plain file; `gclone keystore use file` opts out — `<state root>/secrets.sealed`, the same document encrypted to a Secure Enclave key of that Mac | `secrets.json`: 0600, dir 0700, plaintext JSON (§8.2); refused when the file or its directory is owned by someone else or readable by group/others (§8.1). Never copy it to another machine. `secrets.sealed`: the same file rules; a copy is useless on any other machine — also on the owner's next Mac: **the passphrase is the way back** (`gclone login`) — and it stops nothing that runs as the user on this Mac (§8.2, §15). The state root is left out of Time Machine backups and carries a `CACHEDIR.TAG` (§8.1). |
| access token | `<state root>/token.json` | 0600 |
| vault id/name, Drive folder IDs, backend kind, `auth_url` (not a secret) | `<config>/config.json` | 0600 |
| index replica, base tables, pending ops, device id | `<state>/state.db` | 0600 |
| On Drive | vault folder | ciphertext under random 256-bit keys + one plaintext descriptor hint + the **keyfile**: the master key wrapped under the passphrase (§2.6) |
| Passphrase | the user's password manager | — ; gclone never stores it. The hosted viewer's unlock field is a credential field, so a browser offers to save it there: wanted when that manager is one Google cannot read, a full compromise against Google when it is not (§1.3) |

### 2.6 Passphrase, keyfile, and the vault part of `gclone login`

**Passphrase.**
- *Normalisation* (`Passphrase::from_input` when a passphrase is **entered**; for one that is **set** see "Setting and entering" below — the two differ for exactly one shape of input since §17.29): drop one trailing `\n` or `\r\n`; apply Unicode NFC; then, if the text with ASCII whitespace and `-` removed is exactly **26 or exactly 20** characters, each a Crockford symbol in either case or one of `I L O i l o`, it is rewritten to the canonical generated form of that length (upper case, `I`/`L` → `1`, `O` → `0`, regrouped: 26 symbols as `XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXXX` — groups of five, the last of six —, 20 symbols as `XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX`). Any other text is used as is (case-sensitive, inner spaces kept, nothing trimmed — a byte-order mark or a space at the start of a `--passphrase-file` line is part of the passphrase). The KDF input `P` is the UTF-8 encoding of the result.
  - The rule is about the *shape*, so it also applies to a **typed** passphrase that happens to have the 20-symbol one: `hello hello hello hello` is set, and entered, as `HE110-HE110-HE110-HE110` — by every gclone since the first. That costs the case of the letters and nothing else, and is the same on every device.
  - **Setting and entering (0.5.0, §17.29).** A passphrase is **set** (`Passphrase::for_setting`, behind `set_checked`: `login` creating a vault, `passwd`) to *exactly the text gclone 0.4.0 makes of the same input*: the normalisation above, except that an input of the **26-symbol** shape that is not written in the canonical form stays the text **as typed** — as every typed passphrase does. Only the canonical form itself (what `generate()` displays) is one text under both readings. A passphrase is **entered** with both readings of such an input: `Passphrase::readings()` is the canonical form first and the text as typed second, and `open_keyfile` tries them in that order. Consequences, all intended: (1) a keyfile sealed by 0.5.0 opens on gclone 0.4.0 and in a hosted viewer still on 0.4.0 with the passphrase exactly as it was set — the first cut of 0.5.0 sealed a typed passphrase such as `the new victim passphrase long` (26 letters, no `u`) under `THENE-WV1CT-1MPAS-SPHRA-SE10NG`, and 0.4.0 answered "Wrong passphrase" to the passphrase as typed; (2) a **generated** passphrase, set in the form it is displayed in, is entered in any case and grouping from 0.5.0 on (and in the displayed form on 0.4.0); (3) a **typed** passphrase of that shape is exact in case, spaces and hyphens, on every version — `login` and `passwd` say so once when it is set (a warning: *"This passphrase has the shape of a generated one (26 letters and digits) but is not written the way gclone displays one: it is kept exactly as entered. …"*, `Passphrase::looks_generated`), because the shape invites the opposite assumption. The repeat prompt compares the two entries as they are set.
  - **Compatibility (0.5.0, §17.26).** gclone before 0.5.0 generated 20 symbols and knew only that shape. A passphrase generated then is the same text now, however it is typed. A *typed* passphrase of the 26-symbol shape — five words without a `u`, 26 letters in all — was used as typed by those versions, and a keyfile sealed then opens with the typed text, not with its canonical form. `Passphrase::legacy()` is that older reading of the same input, present exactly when the 26-symbol rule changed the text; `open_keyfile` tries it second, after the canonical form answered `WrongKey`. A passphrase that opened a keyfile before 0.5.0 opens it now, byte for byte (frozen vectors: `tests/vectors/passphrase_v0_4_0.json`, keyfiles sealed by the v0.4.0 source); nothing but an input of that one shape ever costs a second derivation. A keyfile that 0.5.0 or later seals is sealed under the text of "Setting and entering" above — the canonical form for a generated passphrase, the text as typed for a typed one of that shape — which is what gclone 0.4.0 and the hosted viewer of 0.4.0 make of the same input when it is entered there in the spelling it was set in (§17.29; the first cut of 0.5.0 sealed every input of the shape under the canonical form). **The memo of refused passphrases is per reading** (`cli::login::unlock`): two spellings with one canonical form are two passphrases to a keyfile that was sealed as typed, so a candidate is skipped only when every reading of the current input has answered `WrongKey` there, and only the readings it has not refused yet are derived — the right spelling after a mis-cased attempt costs one derivation and opens (it was answered "Wrong passphrase" without a derivation while the memo was keyed by the canonical form alone).
- *Setting one* (vault creation, `passwd`). Prompt: *"New passphrase (leave empty to let gclone generate a strong one):"*.
  - empty → `Passphrase::generate()`: `PASSPHRASE_GENERATED_SYMBOLS` = 26 symbols drawn uniformly from the Crockford alphabet `0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ` with the OS CSPRNG (130 bits; 20 symbols and 100 bits before 0.5.0), shown once in the canonical form with *"Store it in your password manager. It is needed once on every new device and cannot be recovered."*
  - typed → at least `PASSPHRASE_MIN_CHARS` Unicode scalar values, else `FormatError::WeakPassphrase` and ask again; fewer than `PASSPHRASE_WARN_CHARS` = 20 → warning *"This passphrase is short. Anyone who can read the vault folder, Google included, can try guesses against it offline, for as long as they like — and changing the passphrase later does not take a weak one back (the old keyfile stays good for whoever copied it). Prefer five or more random words, or the generated passphrase (26 characters, 130 bits)."* and a confirmation; then typed a second time (must match). Length is all that is judged (§15): the threshold is a hint, not a strength estimate.
  - non-interactive: `--passphrase-file PATH` (first line of the file, e.g. `/dev/fd/3`; same minimum — so an empty line is refused; no warning, no confirmation). Neither a TTY nor the flag → error. A passphrase is never accepted in argv or the environment.
- *Entering one* (new device): no-echo TTY prompt, 3 attempts; or `--passphrase-file`.

**Keyfile** (byte-exact; stored in the vault root, §3.1):
```
keyfile     = KdfPreamble(36) ‖ Stream(type = 0x05 Bundle, key_epoch = 0, chunk_log2 = 16, key = K_pass)       (§4.2; one chunk in practice)
KdfPreamble = "GCK1"(4) ‖ alg = 0x01 (Argon2id) ‖ version = 0x13 ‖ 0x00 0x00 ‖ m_kib u32 BE ‖ t u32 BE ‖ p u32 BE ‖ salt(16)        (big-endian, like every other integer of the formats)
K_pass      = HKDF-SHA-256(salt = the 36 KdfPreamble bytes, ikm = Argon2id(P, salt = preamble.salt, m_kib, t, p, 32 bytes out),
                           info = "gclone/v1/passphrase/keyfile", L = 32)
plaintext   = UTF-8 JSON KeyfilePayload
name        = "gclone-key-" ‖ gen (8 lowercase hex digits) ‖ "-" ‖ h8          h8 = first 8 hex characters of BLAKE3(keyfile bytes)
```
- Written parameters: `m_kib = 262144` (256 MiB), `t = 3`, `p = 1`, fresh random salt per keyfile. Accepted on decode: `8192 ≤ m_kib ≤ 524288`, `1 ≤ t ≤ 4`, `p = 1`, `alg = 1`, `version = 0x13`; anything else → `FormatError::KdfParams` **before** running Argon2 or allocating its memory. The upper bounds cap the work a planted keyfile can demand — the parameters are read before anything is authenticated, and anyone who can write to the folder can plant one: at most 512 MiB and four passes per attempt (writers only ever emit 262144 / 3 / 1; raising a ceiling later is a reader-side change). The lower bounds are sanity limits only: a keyfile that opens was written by someone who knows the passphrase, and a substituted keyfile with cheap parameters merely fails to open — the device never sends anything derived from the passphrase anywhere.
- AEAD and binding: the body is the standard stream container — ChaCha20-Poly1305 STREAM with the key-commitment tag (§4.2). That construction uses an empty AEAD associated-data field; every context byte is bound through key derivation instead: the KDF parameters and salt are the HKDF salt of `K_pass`; suite, chunk size, stream type, flags and epoch are in the HKDF `info` of the stream key; the vault id and the generation are inside the authenticated plaintext and are compared after opening. A wrong passphrase fails at the commit tag and is reported as `CryptoError::WrongKey`, distinguishable from damage (`Corrupt`).
- Versioning: preamble magic `GCK1` + `alg` + `version`; stream magic `GCS1` + `suite`; payload `v`. Unknown anywhere → fail closed ("needs a newer gclone").

`KeyfilePayload` (JSON; unknown fields ignored; `v` must be 1):
```json
{ "v": 1, "vault_id": "<32 hex>", "gen": 1,
  "keys": [ { "epoch": 1, "key": "<base64url-nopad 32 bytes>" } ], "min_epoch": 1,
  "created_ms": 1794400000000, "by": "mbp" }
```
`gen` (the *generation*; the Rust field is `KeyfilePayload::generation`, serialized as `"gen"` — `gen` is a reserved word in edition 2024, §9.4) starts at 1 and grows by one per `passwd`. Keyfiles are put-once objects like everything else (§3.2): a new passphrase is a **new** object; older generations are trashed, or with `--purge-old` deleted (§2.7). The generation in an object's *name* is unauthenticated until the keyfile opens: it only orders candidates (ATTACH) and is never trusted as a number without overflow checks (§2.7).

Opening (`format::keyfile::open_keyfile(name, bytes, passphrase)`), in this order: `36 + 76 ≤ len ≤ KEYFILE_MAX` and the name parses, else `FormatError::KeyfileDamaged` → `BLAKE3(bytes)` matches the name's `h8` (`KeyfileDamaged`; an accidental-corruption check, not an authentication) → preamble bounds (`KdfParams`) → Argon2id → stream header, commit check (`CryptoError::WrongKey` = wrong passphrase; where the passphrase has an older reading, `Passphrase::legacy()` above, Argon2id and the commit check run a second time with that) → chunk authentication (`CryptoError::Corrupt`) → JSON with `v == 1` (`FormatError::KeyfileVersion`) → `gen` equals the name's, `keys` non-empty, every key 32 bytes, every epoch ≥ `min_epoch` (`KeyfileDamaged`). The caller then requires `payload.vault_id` to equal the vault id it is attaching to.

The checks before the key derivation are `format::keyfile::check_keyfile(name, bytes) -> (generation, KdfPreamble)` on their own: an object that passes is a **well-formed** keyfile — it can be tried, at the cost its preamble names — and anything else can never open, whatever the passphrase, and is refused without any work. ATTACH and the hosted viewer (`keyfile_cost`) pick their candidates with it. Well-formed is not authentic: anyone can make a well-formed keyfile — the keyfile of any other vault under a name of his choosing is one.

**`gclone login`, the whole command** (idempotent and resumable: run it again after any failure).
```
0. Backend  (cli::login_backend, §9.10)
      --vault-dir DIR                                           → directory backend at DIR; skip A
      no --vault-dir, no AUTH_URL argument, config.json says
        kind: dir                                               → directory backend at config.backend.path; skip A
      otherwise                                                 → Drive backend
      mixing kinds on an attached device (--vault-dir on a Drive-attached one; AUTH_URL, or another DIR, on a directory-attached
      one) is a usage error: "this device is attached to <…>; run `gclone logout --forget` first".

A. Sign in  (Drive backend only)
   1. auth_url = resolve (§2.2).
   2. If secrets.json holds a refresh token for the same auth_url AND its `client` is "device": force_refresh().
        Ok                       → "Already signed in as <email>."; go to B
        Expired / anything else  → continue with 3
      A login on file WITHOUT `client` (the legacy client, gclone before 0.2.0) is never kept, working or not: `gclone login`
      is how a device moves to the device client (§17.18). stderr: "This device's Google login was made with the browser
      sign-in of gclone before 0.2.0. Signing in again replaces it; until that has worked, nothing on this device changes."
   3. login_interactive (§2.4) → LoginGrant; expiring-grant check. The login it yields has client = "device".
   4. No config.json (a device that is not attached to a vault yet): save it now { auth_url, refresh_token, client, email,
      consent_ms, refresh_expires_at_ms, keys: [] } so the grant survives a later failure.
      EXCEPT when the sign-in replaces a login of the legacy client (step 2) — a device that signed in with gclone before
      0.2.0 and never finished the vault part: there the new token is saved only once B.2 found a vault (or `--new-vault`
      was given). A vault made through the legacy client may exist and be invisible to the new login (§17.18), and the
      legacy login cannot be issued again. If B.2 finds nothing: VaultNotVisible with the text of §2.8 for this case,
      secrets.json untouched, nothing created (§17.19).
      config.json exists: the new token is saved only once the attached vault was seen with it — after B.1 succeeded (cached
      key: re-login of a connected device) or as soon as B.2 found config.vault_id among the discovered vaults (no cached key:
      after `logout`, or an interrupted first login), with keys: [] and before the passphrase is asked. A login with the wrong
      Google account must neither replace the token on file nor become it: step 2 would find a login that works on every later
      run and never ask again (§17.9). The price: a failure between the sign-in and that point costs one more sign-in.
   Token cache: every TokenProvider `login` builds has NO cache file (drive_backend(.., cache = false)) and `prime` is
   memory-only, so `login` never writes token.json. After step 3 ran, token.json is deleted — on success and on failure of B.

B. Vault
   1. config.json exists and secrets.json has keys (a re-login):  Vault::verify_visible(backend, stored handles)
        Ok      → save the new token (if step A.3 ran); "Signed in again. Vault unchanged."
        failure → VaultNotVisible / VaultTrashed (§2.8); secrets.json is untouched: the old token stays in use
   2. Otherwise discover: found = Vault::discover(backend)     — every vault this login can see (§3.3)
        config.json exists (keys were removed by `logout`)  → the entry with config.vault_id (found: save the token of step
                                                               A.3 now, A.4), else VaultNotVisible with secrets.json untouched; → ATTACH
      VaultNotVisible in B.1 or B.2 while step A.2 kept the login on file (nobody was asked to sign in): the message adds that
      this device is signed in as <email> and that `gclone logout`, then `gclone login`, signs in with another account (§2.8).
      VaultNotVisible in B.1 or B.2 after step A.3 ran (a sign-in was just made and does not see the attached vault): the
      message of §2.8 for a fresh login — what was (not) changed, and the two causes: another Google account, or a vault that
      was created through another OAuth client (the legacy client of §17.18). Never CREATE on a device with a config.json.
                                                               (on an attached device — with or without cached keys — `--new-vault`, or
                                                               a `--vault-id` other than the attached vault, is a usage error naming
                                                               `gclone logout --forget`, checked before step 0; §17.5)
        --new-vault                                          → CREATE
        --vault-id HEX                                       → that entry, else a usage error listing what was found — also when
                                                               nothing was found: a vault asked for by id is never created; → ATTACH
        found is empty                                       → CREATE — except after a sign-in that replaced a legacy login
                                                               on this unattached device (A.4): VaultNotVisible, §2.8
        exactly one entry                                    → ATTACH
        several entries                                      → on a TTY ask which (name, creation date, id prefix); otherwise an
                                                               error listing them and asking for --vault-id; → ATTACH

CREATE (first device)
   passphrase (set, above) → vault_id = 16 random bytes; MK = MasterKey::generate(); Keyring(epoch 1)
   → keyfile generation 1 = seal_keyfile(payload, passphrase, KdfParams::default()), then open_keyfile on the result as a self-test
   → lock → Db::open → Vault::create(…, keyfile)      objects are written in this order: root folder, index/, data/, README.txt,
                                                        the keyfile, the first segment [VaultInit, Device], and the descriptor LAST —
                                                        a vault exists for discovery only once it is complete
   → save config.json (handles, auth_url), then secrets.json (keys)       in this order (§17.5): a cached key never exists
                                                        without the config it belongs to; a kill in between leaves `Locked` (Drive)
                                                        or `NotLoggedIn` (directory), which the next `login` repairs through ATTACH
   → race check (below) → print "Vault created" (§7.3)
   (killed between Vault::create and the save: the next `login` discovers the finished vault and takes ATTACH with the passphrase
    just chosen; the state directory still holds the device id.)

ATTACH (every later device)                                                             (keyfile selection: 0.5.0, §17.26)
   candidates = the WELL-FORMED keyfiles among the root's objects with a keyfile's name (FoundVault.keyfiles: highest
     generation first — the generation is a number from an unauthenticated name and only orders them):
       an object listed larger than KEYFILE_MAX is refused without a download;
       at most KEYFILE_LOOK_MAX = 32 objects are fetched (get_all, at most KEYFILE_MAX + 1 bytes each; `--all-keyfiles`:
       KEYFILE_LOOK_ALL_MAX = 1024); names beyond that are counted as `unseen`;
       a fetched object that fails `check_keyfile` (junk, another name's content, KDF parameters out of bounds, too large)
       is refused — before any key derivation — and takes no place among the candidates.
     Objects under keyfile names can be planted by anyone who can write to the vault folder; planted names of higher
     generations therefore do not push the real keyfile out.
   no candidate → exit 3: "The vault's keyfile is missing or damaged …" — or, when `unseen` > 0, "None of the N object(s)
     with keyfile names that this login looked at is a keyfile. M more … were not looked at (`gclone login --all-keyfiles`
     looks at up to 1024; `gclone passwd` on a connected device writes a keyfile ahead of them all)."
   → ask for the passphrase (candidates were downloaded before: nothing is fetched between the prompt and the answer)
   → try the candidates in order with it: the first that opens wins. Work is bounded:
       one attempt asks at most KEYFILE_TRY_MAX = 4 candidates — one key derivation each (two for a passphrase with an
       older reading, above) — unless the person asked for all (`--all-keyfiles`, or a yes to the question below);
       each (keyfile, passphrase) pair runs at most once: a candidate remembers the passphrases that answered WrongKey and
       is neither asked nor counted again for them, and a candidate that fails with anything other than WrongKey (bad KDF
       parameters met only now, unknown payload version, another vault's keyfile) is dropped for the rest of the command.
     Outcomes of one attempt:
       opened                                                  → continue below
       every remaining candidate has answered WrongKey         → "Wrong passphrase." and ask again (3 attempts; with
                                                                  `--passphrase-file` one); at the end
                                                                  ConfigError::WrongPassphrase, exit 4
       KEYFILE_TRY_MAX answered WrongKey and n were not asked   → NEVER "wrong passphrase" — the passphrase may be right:
                                                                  on a terminal (no `--passphrase-file`): "That passphrase
                                                                  does not open the K newest keyfiles of this vault. Try it
                                                                  on the n older one(s) too (a key derivation each)? [y/N]";
                                                                  yes → the same passphrase on all remaining candidates;
                                                                  no → "…; n older keyfiles were not tried." and ask again.
                                                                  At the end (exit 4, the error is still WrongPassphrase,
                                                                  the text is not): "The passphrase does not open the K
                                                                  newest keyfiles of this vault, and n older keyfiles were
                                                                  not tried. … If the passphrase is right, run `gclone login
                                                                  --all-keyfiles`: it tries every keyfile, one key
                                                                  derivation each."
       all candidates answered WrongKey but `unseen` > 0       → exit 4 with "The passphrase opens none of the N keyfiles
                                                                  this login looked at. M more object(s) … were not looked at"
       no candidate left                                       → exit 3
     The same passphrase entered again goes on where the last attempt stopped (the candidates it was tried on are skipped
     and do not count), so three attempts never cost more than 12 derivations unasked.
   → payload.vault_id must equal the descriptor's → Keyring, held in memory only
   → lock → Db::open → Vault::open → refresh()        the authoritative identity check: every index object's inner vault_id (§4.6)
        refresh ends with Gap or Rollback (§5.3)      → nothing is published from this device (as for every mutating command);
                                                         continue at the save, and print the verdict as a warning instead of the head
                                                         line: "… This device is connected, but nothing can be changed in the vault
                                                         until the index is repaired: run `gclone repair` …" (exit 0). See below.
        any other refresh error                       → the login fails, nothing is saved
   → commit_ops([Device{id, name}])                   skipped when the replica already lists this device id under this name
   → finish_mutation()
   → ONLY NOW save config.json (handles, auth_url), then secrets.json (keys, min_epoch)      (the same order as in CREATE)
   → print: vault name, file count, device name, and
     "Compare with `gclone status` on a device you trust (run it there now): head XXXX-XXXX, N files.
      A new device trusts the vault as Google serves it; equal head values mean both devices see the same history."
   A failure or kill anywhere before the save leaves the device unconnected (no cached key): the next `gclone login` runs ATTACH
   again — the passphrase is asked again, the state directory keeps the device id, an already published Device op is not
   repeated. A device therefore never counts as connected before the other devices can see it — with one exception:
   A Gap / Rollback verdict does not stop ATTACH (§17.11). The verdict is computed at the end of the refresh, after every
   accepted object was checked against the vault id, so the identity check has passed; what is wrong is the index, and the
   cure is `gclone repair` — which needs the cached key, and for which this device's index cache may hold the only copy of
   the missing objects. A device that had run `gclone logout` could otherwise never log in again while its replica (which
   keeps its marks and `blocked` rows across a logout, §2.7) has such a verdict, and its only way out, `logout --forget`,
   deletes that cache. The device's `Device` op is then not published by `login`; `commit()` announces a device id the
   vault does not list by itself (§5.6) once the index is repaired.
```
**Trust on first use, and the head fingerprint.** A new device has no rollback marks: whatever consistent state it is served first becomes its baseline (§5.3); from then on it detects rollbacks and gaps like any other device. (v1.1 carried marks inside the kit; v1.2 has no channel between devices.) A file count cannot expose a stale baseline — any rollback that keeps the count passes — so the user gets a real comparison value instead:
```
head = Crockford32( BLAKE3( "gclone/v1/head" ‖ for every row of `hw` (§5.3) in ascending device order:
                                                 device (8) ‖ seq (u64 BE) ‖ segment hash (32) ) [0..5] )        40 bits, shown XXXX-XXXX
```
`hw` holds, per device, the greatest `(seq, hash)` this replica has applied or adopted; because every segment names its predecessor and what it has seen by hash (§4.6), two replicas with equal tips have applied the same journal. `Vault::head_fingerprint()` computes it; `gclone status` prints it on every device (after its refresh), and ATTACH prints it at the end. The values are equal on any two devices that are up to date with each other — the trusted device must run `gclone status` *after* the new device attached, so that it has applied the new device's first segment. A new device that was served a rolled-back or truncated journal shows a different value. This needs no channel between devices and no format change; the e-mail shown after login remains the check for "the right account".

**What the fingerprint is, and what it does and does not prove (§17.26).** It is 40 bits of an **unkeyed** BLAKE3 over public inputs: device ids and sequence numbers are in object names, and the segment hash is the hash of the stored ciphertext. The store can therefore compute the value of any state it holds — every `gclone status` line can be reproduced from a listing and the object bytes — and it is no secret and no authenticator. What makes the comparison worth something is that the store cannot *make* states: every state it can show is a causally closed set of authentic segments, so to pass a stale state off as the reference device's it needs a stale state and a state it can hold the reference device at whose values collide in 40 bits — about (number of such states) / 2^40, of the order of 10^-8 for a vault of tens of thousands of segments — and it knows beforehand whether such a pair exists. For the value a **new CLI device** prints at the end of `login` the store cannot even compute it in advance: it includes the hash of the segment the device has just written. For the hosted viewer (which writes nothing) and for later status-to-status comparisons it can. So:
- equal values on two devices mean both have applied **the same journal**; they do not mean that journal is the **current** one. A reference device that is itself held back — possible for any established device, without any signal, by withholding the newest objects (§15) — agrees with a new device that is shown the same old state. The reference must be **the device that wrote last**;
- the comparison is made by a person, and only where it is asked for (`login`); nothing compares two established devices automatically, which is the only way a fork of views would be noticed;
- only tips are hashed: a fork twin below a device's tip (a cloned state directory) is not covered; that is not something the store can produce.
A keyed value (HKDF label under the master key) and more bits would take the store's ability to compute it away; every device and the viewer would have to change together, so it is deferred (§14).

**Two first devices at the same time.** Two devices that both find no vault each create one. Handling:
1. The descriptor is written last, so a half-created vault is never discovered; an interrupted creation leaves an orphan folder without descriptor that `login` ignores (the user may delete it in drive.google.com) and the next `login` starts over. **Directory backend**: the orphan keeps the path `DIR/<vault_name>`, and a directory cannot hold a second folder of that name (§9.5) — the next `login --vault-dir DIR` gets `BackendError::Fatal{409, "nameConflict"}` from `Vault::create`, which `cli/login.rs` reports as *"`DIR/<vault_name>` exists but holds no complete vault (an interrupted `gclone login`?). Delete that folder, or choose another name with `--vault-name`."* (exit 1); the same applies to `--new-vault` with a name already present in `DIR`.
2. Right after CREATE (unless `--new-vault`): `found = Vault::discover(backend)`; this device's own vault always counts, listed or not. If another vault is visible, the **winner** is the one with the smallest `(descriptor createdTime, vault_id)` — server clock first, id as the tie-break; both devices evaluate the same rule.
   - This device won: print a warning naming the other vault; nothing else. (The other device discards its vault when it sees this one.)
   - This device lost: trash its own root folder (`backend.trash(root)` — the vault holds nothing but this run's first segment), delete its `config.json`, state directory and cached key, and continue with ATTACH on the winner: *"Another device created the vault a moment earlier; using that one. The passphrase you just set here is NOT in use — enter the passphrase chosen on the other device."*
3. List lag can hide the other vault from this check. Therefore `gclone status` (Drive backend) runs one `find_by_name(DESCRIPTOR_NAME)` and warns when a descriptor whose parent is not the configured root is listed (no download needed): *"Another gclone vault exists in this Drive. If it was created by accident on another device, run `gclone logout --forget` there and `gclone login` again."* A later `login` on a third device sees both and asks (step B.2).

**Recovery.** Google account + passphrase are sufficient on any machine: `gclone login <AUTH_URL>`. Without OAuth at all: download the vault folder from drive.google.com (or Takeout), unzip, `gclone login --vault-dir DIR`, enter the passphrase. A forgotten passphrase is repaired from any still-connected device with `gclone passwd` (it needs no old passphrase). All devices lost **and** passphrase lost = data lost; a printable master-key export (`gclone key export`) is deferred (§14).

### 2.7 `gclone passwd` and `gclone logout`

**`gclone passwd [--passphrase-file PATH] [--purge-old]`** (on any connected device; the old passphrase is not asked for — the device already holds the master key):
1. `open_ctx{Exclusive, Required, no settle}`.
2. New passphrase by the setting rules of §2.6.
2a. **The purge question, before anything is written** (§17.29). `purge` is `--purge-old`, or — at a terminal, to a person who typed the passphrase (no `--passphrase-file`: as in `login`, a file gets no question) — a yes to: *"Delete the old keyfiles for good — also the ones in the Drive trash — instead of leaving the retired one in the trash for 30 days? Yes if the old passphrase may have leaked; no keeps a way back if the new one is lost."* Otherwise: trash. From step 4 to the end of step 5 the command waits for nobody. (The question used to come after step 4 and after "Passphrase changed.": Ctrl-C there, or the end of the ssh session, left the old keyfile in the vault folder — not even in the trash — and the old passphrase attaching new devices for good.)
3. `generation = 1 + max(generation in the names of the keyfiles in the vault folder **and in its trash**)` (`vault.keyfiles_and_trashed()`; 1 if there is none; the trash counts since §17.29, so that a number is never used twice — also after the current keyfile was moved to the trash by hand), computed with `checked_add`. The device cannot open the listed keyfiles (it has no passphrase), so these numbers are unauthenticated names: an overflow — a stray or planted `gclone-key-ffffffff-…` — is a plain error (exit 1) that names the object: *"keyfile generation exhausted by <name>; remove that object in drive.google.com and run `gclone passwd` again"* (for one in the trash: *"… remove that object from the trash in drive.google.com (delete it forever) and run …"*); it never panics or wraps. payload = `KeyfilePayload::from_keyring(vault.keys(), generation, device name, now)`; `seal_keyfile(…, KdfParams::default())`; `open_keyfile` on the result as a self-test.
4. `vault.put_keyfile(&kf)`: `put` into the vault root under a pre-generated ID; the returned size and md5 must match (else trash it and fail); then the object is **read back from the store and compared byte for byte** with what was sealed (a difference: trash it and fail). Nothing is retired before this: the store verifiably holds a keyfile that step 3 opened with the new passphrase.
5. Retire the old keyfiles, in the same breath — `vault.retire_keyfiles(&new, purge)` (0.5.0, §17.26, §17.29) — and only then print (stdout): *"Passphrase changed. New devices need the new passphrase; connected devices are unaffected."* If the retirement fails, the error says what is true instead: *"The new keyfile <name> is in the vault folder and opens with the new passphrase, but retiring the old keyfiles failed: an old keyfile is STILL in the vault folder and still attaches new devices with the OLD passphrase. Run `gclone passwd` again … until it reports "Passphrase changed.""* Every listed keyfile of the vault root with a lower generation (junk planted under a lower number goes with them; a keyfile of the same generation — a concurrent `passwd` — stays) is
   - **trashed** (the default): Drive keeps it for 30 days, and for those 30 days the old passphrase still opens it for whoever can reach the account. That window is also the way back when the new passphrase is lost together with the last connected device, which is why trashing stays the default;
   - **deleted for good** with `purge`: `backend.delete` on each, and on **every object under a keyfile's name that is in the trash already, whatever its generation** (§17.29) — what earlier `passwd` runs left there, and what was trashed by hand — found with `Backend::list_trashed(root)` (Drive: `files.list` with `'<root>' in parents and trashed = true`, which `drive.file` answers for the files the app created; §9.5). Nothing in the trash is a keyfile in use, and each opens with an old passphrase; the generation rule holds for the objects that are **not** in the trash only (the new keyfile itself is never touched, in the trash or out of it). Until §17.29 the trash was purged below the new generation only, and the generation was counted from the listed keyfiles alone: after the current keyfile had been moved to the trash by hand — the obvious reaction to a leak — the new keyfile got generation 1 again, every trashed keyfile survived the purge, and the command still said "gone … trash included". With `purge`, print (stdout): *"Deleted for good: N old keyfile(s) in the vault folder, M in the Drive trash."*
6. Print the caveat as a **warning** (`ui.warn`: stderr, shown with `-q` too — it was an info line, which `-q` hid): what is left of the old keyfiles — trashed: *"The old keyfile stays in the Drive trash for 30 days and opens with the old passphrase, like every copy made of it before (Google's backups, a download of the vault folder). `gclone passwd --purge-old` deletes it from the account now."*; purged: *"The old keyfiles are gone from this Google account, trash included. Copies outside its reach stay what they were — Google's own backups, a download or Takeout of the vault folder, a keyfile somebody copied earlier — and each still opens with its old passphrase."* — **said only when a listing made after the retirement shows it** (§17.29: `keyfiles_and_trashed()` again; no object under a keyfile's name is left in the trash); otherwise *"The old keyfiles this run found were deleted for good, but it is not shown that every keyfile of an earlier passphrase is gone from this Google account. Still in the Drive trash: <names>. …"* (or, when the listing itself failed, that the folder could not be listed again and where to look). Objects under a keyfile's name of the same or a higher generation that are still in the vault folder — a concurrent `passwd`, or something planted — are named in every case. And, always, what the command did not do: *"The vault's key is unchanged: changing the passphrase re-encrypts nothing, so whoever holds an old keyfile with its passphrase — or a copy of a device's secrets.json — can still decrypt the vault, including what is uploaded from now on. There is no re-keying yet; see "If a passphrase or a device's key file leaked" in docs/SECURITY.md."*
Two devices running `passwd` concurrently leave two keyfiles of the same generation; both passphrases work until the next `passwd` retires both. A `passwd` that is killed between steps 4 and 5 leaves the old keyfile beside the new one: **`gclone check` warns when the vault folder holds more than one object under a keyfile's name** (§17.29: *"N objects under a keyfile's name are in the vault folder: … Run `gclone passwd` again …"*). No index operation is written. **`passwd` is not a remedy for a leaked key or for a keyfile that was already copied**: there is no re-keying (§14.5, §15); the procedure that works in v1 is a new vault (`docs/SECURITY.md`, "If a passphrase or a device's key file leaked"; §1.3).

**`gclone logout [--revoke] [--forget] [--yes]`**
- Default: delete `<state root>/token.json` and `<state root>/secrets.json` (this device's refresh token and the cached master key) — and, since 0.5.0, `<state root>/secrets.sealed`, the sealed form of the same document (§8.2): "signed in" means that either file exists, both are removed under the secrets lock (§8.3), `secrets.json` first and `secrets.sealed` last, and the temp files of every file of the state root go before them — in this order — a logout that stops between the two is still "signed in" for the next one — together with the temp files `.token.json.tmp-<16 hex>` / `.secrets.json.tmp-<16 hex>` that a write killed before its rename left beside them (`util::remove_atomic_leftovers`, §8.1; a temp copy of `secrets.json` holds the refresh token and the cached key). `config.json` — which also remembers the auth Worker URL (§2.2) — and the vault's state directory stay, so a later plain `gclone login` (no URL needed; for a directory vault no `--vault-dir` needed, §2.6 step 0) re-attaches as the same device (same device id, base rows, rollback marks) after asking for the passphrase again. Output: *"Signed out on this device. The Google token was discarded, not revoked — Google can only revoke the login of all devices at once (`gclone logout --revoke`)."* Not signed in (no `secrets.json`) → exit 0 with a note; a `token.json` or temp copy that is there nevertheless is removed, and the note says so (§17.9).
- `--revoke` ("sign out everywhere"; for a lost or stolen device): after a confirmation (TTY, or `--yes`) — *"This ends the Google login of ALL your gclone devices; each needs `gclone login` again. Continue?"* — `POST GOOGLE_REVOKE_URL`, form-encoded `token=<refresh_token>`, no client credentials. `200` → revoked. `400` (`invalid_token`: already revoked or expired) → treated as done. Network failure → error, and the local secrets are kept so the command can be repeated. Then the default deletion. Everything that can still stop the command comes **before** the request, which cannot be taken back: with `--forget`, the unpublished-changes question below is asked after this confirmation and before the revoke; declining it ends the command with exit 5, nothing revoked and nothing removed (§17.9). *Why this is not the default:* Google documents that revocation "removes all OAuth 2.0 scopes previously granted to a project, invalidating any issued access or refresh tokens for all clients registered under that project" (RESEARCH §6.3) — there is no per-token revoke. Whether files stay visible after revoke + new consent is manual probe 3; in v1 the confirmation text **always** carries that warning (*"It is unverified whether the vault stays visible after a new sign-in — keep a web download of the vault folder first."*). Removing the sentence is an Errata change to this spec once probe 3 has passed; the binary has no way to know.
- `--forget`: additionally delete `config.json` (and with it the remembered auth Worker URL: the next `gclone login` needs `AUTH_URL` again) and this vault's state directory (index replica with plaintext paths, base tables, device id). If `pending`/`outbox` hold unpublished changes this needs `--yes` or a TTY confirmation.
- Directory-backend vaults: `--revoke` is a usage error; the rest applies.
A discarded-but-not-revoked refresh token stays valid at Google until it is unused for six months or falls out of the 100 newest tokens of the account; it existed only on this device.

| `ConfigError::NotLoggedIn` (`config.json` exists but there is no `secrets.json` — after `logout`, **either backend** — or a Drive vault whose secrets hold no refresh token) | "This device is not connected (signed out). Run `gclone login`." — for a directory vault: "… Run `gclone login --vault-dir <config.backend.path>`." | 4 |
| `ConfigError::Locked` (`secrets.json` exists with `keys == []`: signed in, but the vault part of `login` did not finish) | "Run `gclone login` to finish connecting this device (it will ask for the passphrase)." | 4 |
| `ConfigError::KeyStoreUnavailable(text)` (0.5.0: `secrets.sealed` is the device's only copy of the secrets and does not open, §8.2) | the text itself, one of four: the key is dead → "This Mac's Secure Enclave cannot open this device's sealed key (secrets.sealed): … Run `gclone login`; it asks for the passphrase (for a vault on Google Drive it signs in to Google first) and connects this device again. The sealed file is kept until that login has the key again." (0.5.1, §17.30: the sealed store is the default, so this is what a migrated or restored Mac says); the session cannot use the Secure Enclave → "… **Do not sign in again**: the stored key is probably intact. (this one never names `gclone login`; it is also what a session gets in which the Secure Enclave does not answer — "(the Secure Enclave did not answer within 10 s)", after one bounded wait, §8.2 rule 5); the file is damaged or of a newer gclone; this machine or build has no sealer. `login` prints it as a warning and goes on. | 4 |

### 2.9 Day-0 probes (gate the first real use)
`gclone probe` (hidden command) runs the rows marked **A** against a throwaway folder and prints one line per row. Rows marked **M** need a consent at Google, a second device or days of waiting; they are a checklist in `docs/SETUP.md` (written by WP0 into `README.md`; moved, §17.31) to be ticked by hand once.

| # | How | Question | If the answer is bad |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | M | Publish the app (client of type *TVs and Limited Input devices*) with `openid email drive.file`: no verification, no warning screen; the Worker-hosted home and privacy pages are accepted; the `/device/poll` answer has **no** `refresh_token_expires_in` once published (and has it in Testing) | Setup text changes; in the worst case weekly `gclone login` (unacceptable resting state). `login` itself detects the Testing case (§2.4). |
| 2 | M | Two devices, two logins of the same account: both refresh tokens keep working side by side, and device 2 discovers and reads the vault device 1 created | The design depends on it (documented behaviour: up to 100 live tokens per account and client; one app identity because one client). No fallback short of sharing one token. |
| 3 | M | `gclone logout --revoke` on device 2: is device 1 signed out too (documented: yes)? After a new `login`: is the vault listed again? | If a revoke is per token after all: make it the default of `logout`. If files are not visible after re-consent: the lost-device procedure must go through web download + `--vault-dir` (`VaultNotVisible`). |
| 4 | M | A second OAuth client in the same project sees the files the first one created — the device client of 0.2.0 for a vault created through the *Web application* client before it (§17.18): `gclone login` on such a device ends with "Signed in again … Vault unchanged."; and, since 0.4.0, the *Web application* client of the hosted viewer for a vault created through the device client: the viewer finds the vault (§7.5) | `login` reports `VaultNotVisible` with the fresh-login text of §2.8 and changes nothing; the vault is moved while a Worker older than 0.4.0 is still deployed (worker/README.md). The hosted viewer cannot be used with that vault. `WorkerMisconfigured` recovery must use web download. |
| 5 | M | The first real `gclone login`: Google's device-code endpoint accepts the client with `SCOPES` (verified 2026-11-12: `{device_code, user_code, expires_in: 1800, interval: 5, verification_url: "https://www.google.com/device"}`); after the consent, the token answer carries an **ID token** with `email` / `email_verified` (without it `/device/poll` says `403 grant_unusable` and the device ends the login with that sentence) and a refresh token; the `scope` of that answer holds nothing but members of `ALLOWED_SCOPES` (otherwise `/device/poll` says `scope_not_allowed` and names the entry); the error code Google uses for a code that ran out is `expired_token` | No ID token → every login fails closed; the Worker must then ask Google's userinfo endpoint with the access token instead (Errata). A harmless scope spelling outside `ALLOWED_SCOPES` → add it to the set in `worker/src/google.ts` and here (Errata). Another code for an expired device code (e.g. `invalid_grant`) → harmless: the device stops at its own deadline or reports "the code is no longer valid". |
| 6 | A | `409` with a pre-generated ID — at resumable initiation or at completion? multipart? Does `stat` right after the 409 find the object? | all paths are implemented (§6.2 conflict rule). |
| 7 | M | Sustained create rate; does session initiation count? | tune `PACK_MEMBER_MAX`/pacer start. |
| 8 | A (timing printout) | `files.list` lag after a write; `files.get` read-after-write | `GAP_GRACE` tuning; first-device race window (§2.6). |
| 9 | A | `size`, `md5Checksum`, `createdTime` present in the completion body when `fields=` was sent at initiation | the follow-up `stat` fallback (§6.2) carries the load. |
| 10 | A | `generateIds` max `count` | pool falls back to 10. |
| 11 | M | Trashed file downloadable by ID | affects self-heal wording only. |
| 12 | A | Exact multipart size boundary | we stay at ≤ 4 MiB. |
| 13 | A | Is a resumable upload invisible to `files.list` until finalised? | index never references unfinished objects anyway. |
| 14 | M | (0.5.0, §17.26) `gclone passwd` and then `gclone passwd --purge-old`: does `files.list` with `trashed = true` show the keyfile the first run trashed to this `drive.file` login, and is it gone from drive.google.com's trash afterwards? And: does the listing's `md5Checksum` of an index object that was overwritten in place (`files.update` with new content, by hand through the API) change — is the device that had applied it told `Rollback`? | Trash listing not answered: `--purge-old` deletes the listed keyfiles only and says "0 in the Drive trash" — empty the trash by hand, and say so in §2.7. A stale md5 after an overwrite: presence rule (a) of §5.3 cannot see an in-place overwrite on Drive; it then has to read the object (by BLAKE3) on a schedule. |
