Shapes as documented in the Drive v3 reference ([K]: written from the reference, not re-fetched for this revision; the live conformance run of §13 item 10 confirms them). int64 values are JSON **strings**.
```
File (fields=FIELDS)        {"id":"1AbC","name":"s-0a…","mimeType":"application/octet-stream","parents":["1Par"],
                             "size":"16777216","md5Checksum":"9e107d9d372bb6826bd81d3542a419d6",
                             "createdTime":"2026-11-11T09:14:03.123Z","trashed":false}
Folder (fields=FIELDS)      {"id":"1Fld","name":"index","mimeType":"application/vnd.google-apps.folder","parents":["1Par"],
                             "createdTime":"2026-11-11T09:14:03.123Z","trashed":false}                 no size, no md5Checksum
File, no fields= given      {"kind":"drive#file","id":"1AbC","name":"s-0a…","mimeType":"application/octet-stream"}
files.list                  {"nextPageToken":"tok","files":[ <File>, … ]}                               nextPageToken absent on the last page
files.generateIds           {"kind":"drive#generatedIds","space":"drive","ids":["1a…","1b…"]}
about                       {"storageQuota":{"limit":"2199023255552","usage":"442630144000","usageInDrive":"…","usageInDriveTrash":"3328599654"},
                             "user":{"emailAddress":"me@example.com"}}                                  limit absent = unlimited
error envelope              {"error":{"code":403,"message":"User rate limit exceeded.","status":"PERMISSION_DENIED",
                             "errors":[{"domain":"usageLimits","reason":"userRateLimitExceeded","message":"User rate limit exceeded."}]}}
                            `status` and `errors` may be missing; upload/session endpoints and front ends may answer plain text or HTML
resumable                   initiation: 200, empty body, `Location: <session URI>`
                            progress:   308, empty body, `Range: bytes=0-N` (absent = nothing stored), NO `Location`
                            completion: 200 or 201 + File in the projection requested at initiation
```
The device never talks to Google's token endpoint. The shapes of the auth Worker's answers (`/device/start`, `/device/poll`, `/refresh`, the error object) are normative in §2.3 — for the Worker and for `FakeDrive`'s auth routes alike; Google's token-endpoint shapes are used only inside the Worker and are listed in §16.4.
Decoding rules: `size` (string; a JSON number is accepted too) and `md5Checksum` are **optional** — a folder decodes to `size = 0`, `md5 = None`; `parents` missing → `ObjMeta.parent = Handle::top()`; `createdTime` → `util::parse_rfc3339_ms`; unknown fields are ignored; `classify()` never fails on a body that is not JSON (it falls back to the status code).

### 6.5 Pacer and error classification (all inside `DriveBackend`; callers see only terminal errors)
- Two AIMD token buckets: **write** (initiate, multipart create, folder create, trash/untrash, delete) and **read** (list, get, about, generateIds, downloads). Upload part PUTs and status queries are not paced (they still honour throttling responses).
- A 60 s sliding window of quota units keeps usage ≤ `UNITS_PER_MIN_CAP`; `acquire()` waits when the window is full.
- Classification of an HTTP response (`backend/drive/errors.rs`). `reasons` = **all** `error.errors[*].reason` values; `status` = `error.status`; `message` = `error.message`; a non-JSON body has none of them. Rows are tested top to bottom:
| Condition | Class | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `401` | auth | `force_refresh()` once, retry once → `Auth(Expired)` (inside an upload session: §6.2 step 5) |
| `404` | — | `NotFound` |
| `409` | — | conflict rule of §6.2 |
| `403`, reasons ∋ `storageQuotaExceeded` | terminal | `QuotaExceeded(StorageFull)` |
| `403`, a reason or the message contains `uploadLimit`; **or** WRITE_BREAKER tripped | terminal | `QuotaExceeded(DailyUpload)` |
| `403`, a reason or the message contains `downloadQuota` | terminal | `QuotaExceeded(DailyDownload)` |
| `403`, reasons ∋ `dailyLimitExceeded` | terminal | `QuotaExceeded(ProjectApiQuota)` — Google defines it as the Cloud project's API quota, not the 750 GB cap |
| `403`, reasons ∋ `appNotAuthorizedToFile` | terminal | `AppNotAuthorized` (→ `IndexError::VaultNotVisible`, §2.8) |
| `403`, a reason or the message contains `Abusive` (downloads) | — | `AbuseFlag` (§6.3) |
| `429`; `403` with reasons ∋ `rateLimitExceeded` / `userRateLimitExceeded`; `403` with `status == "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED"`; `403` with no recognised reason whose message matches `rate limit` or `quota` (case-insensitive) | throttle | halve the class rate, sleep `max(Retry-After, BACKOFF(n))`, retry (≤ MAX_ATTEMPTS) → then `RateLimited` |
| `500/502/503/504`, connect/read errors, an upload body that stalled or outran its total timeout (§6.4) | transient | sleep `BACKOFF(n)`, retry (≤ MAX_ATTEMPTS) → then `Transient` |
| other `4xx` (including `403 numChildrenInNonRootLimitExceeded`, unreachable below `DATA_FOLDER_MAX`) | terminal | `Fatal{status, reason, message}` |
- The 750 GB/day cap has no documented reason of its own (rclone sees it as `userRateLimitExceeded`): it surfaces as the write breaker, or as `RateLimited`, which `sync::execute` reports as `QuotaExceeded(DailyUpload)` when the upload ledger shows ≥ `LEDGER_WARN` in the trailing 24 h. The backend itself does not read the ledger.
- `QuotaExceeded(_)` / `RateLimited`: the sync engine stops launching transfers, commits what completed (the commit may itself end in `OutboxStuck`; later reads still work, §5.3) and exits 75 with:
  - `StorageFull`: "Drive is full. Files in the trash still count: `gclone gc` then `gclone gc --purge` frees what was deleted more than 30 days ago; `gclone about` shows the numbers."
  - `DailyUpload`: "Google's 750 GB/day upload limit reached; re-run tomorrow — finished work is saved."
  - `DailyDownload`: "Google's download quota for today is used up; re-run tomorrow — finished files are kept."
  - `ProjectApiQuota`: "The API quota of your Google Cloud project is used up (console.cloud.google.com → APIs & Services → Quotas)."

### 6.6 Expected cost (assertable on the fake backends via call counters, §13)
| Operation | API calls |
|---|---|
| no-change `sync` | 1 list (+0 if the token is cached; + one snapshot download the first time another device's snapshot is listed, §5.3) |
| upload of N small files totalling T bytes | ≤ ceil(T / 16 MiB) + 1 blob creates + 1 segment create (+ generateIds) |
| rename of a directory with any number of files, then `sync` | 1 segment create, 0 data bytes |
| `ls` | 1 list + downloads of new segments only |

---

## 7. CLI

Remote paths start with `:` (`:` alone is the vault root). `copy`/`sync` take exactly one local and one remote argument; the direction follows from which one has the `:`.

### 7.1 Commands
```
gclone login  [AUTH_URL] [--no-browser] [--device-name NAME] [--vault-name NAME] [--new-vault] [--vault-id HEX] [--vault-dir DIR]
              [--passphrase-file PATH] [--allow-expiring-login] [--all-keyfiles]
gclone logout [--revoke] [--forget] [--yes]
gclone passwd [--passphrase-file PATH] [--purge-old]
gclone keystore [--json]                      (§8.2: where the secrets are, the choice, the trial's record, the backup exclusion)
gclone keystore check [--new-trial]           (§8.2: can THIS session use the Secure Enclave? exit 0 = yes; stores nothing)
gclone keystore use enclave [--passphrase-file PATH] [--skip-passphrase-check] [--all-keyfiles] [--yes]
gclone keystore use file [--discard-sealed]
gclone status [-q]
gclone about

gclone copy SRC DST   [-n|--dry-run] [--checksum] [--force] [--exclude GLOB]... [--transfers N] [--reset-pair | --keep-pair]
gclone sync SRC DST   [-n|--dry-run] [--checksum] [--force] [--exclude GLOB]... [--transfers N] [--reset-pair | --keep-pair]
                      [--max-delete N] [--yes]
gclone ls    [-l] [-R] [:PATH]
gclone tree  [:PATH]
gclone cat   :PATH [--offset N] [--count N]
gclone web   [--port N] [--no-browser]        (§7.4: the vault in a browser; read-only; runs until Ctrl-C)
gclone serve restic --stdio [--append-only] REPO      (§7.6: restic's REST backend over stdin/stdout; started by restic)
gclone serve restic --port N [--append-only]         (§7.6: the same on 127.0.0.1:N, behind a token; runs until Ctrl-C)
gclone mkdir :PATH
gclone rm    [-r] :PATH...
gclone mv    :SRC :DST [--force]
gclone restore [-r] :PATH... [--list] [--version K]
gclone check [LOCAL :REMOTE | --download [:PATH]]
gclone gc    [-n|--dry-run] [--orphans] [--purge]
gclone repair [--accept-loss]
gclone probe                                  (hidden; the automatable day-0 probes of §2.9)

Global: -v/--verbose (repeatable)   -q/--quiet   --json (copy and sync only: NDJSON events on stdout, one final {"event":"summary",…};
        `gclone keystore --json` prints one JSON object)
Env:    GCLONE_CONFIG_DIR, GCLONE_STATE_DIR (override the two directories of §8.1 — set BOTH for a second device or vault: the login
        and the cached key live under the state root; used by tests)
        GCLONE_AUTH_URL (the auth Worker's URL for `login`, §2.2)
        GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0 (in this process: no Secure Enclave trial and no trial record, no automatic move into the sealed
                                 store, and a login is not sealed unless `keystore use enclave` chose it. A process with it that
                                 is answered from a secrets.json with keys leaves the marker keystore-trial.off, and while that
                                 is there the same holds for EVERY process of the device, §8.2; the test harnesses set it)
Build:  GCLONE_DEFAULT_AUTH_URL (compile-time default for the same; read with option_env!)
```
- `login` is the one command that connects a device — the first or any later one. It signs in through the auth Worker (§2.4) and then creates the vault if this Google login sees none, or attaches to the existing one after asking for the passphrase (§2.6). Run again, it repairs whatever is missing (expired login, interrupted unlock) and changes nothing else. `AUTH_URL` is needed the first time only: it is remembered in `config.json` and survives `logout` (not `logout --forget`). `--vault-name` applies when a vault is created; `--new-vault` creates one although others exist; `--vault-id` picks one of several.
- `login --vault-dir DIR` selects the directory backend (no OAuth, no Worker) and records it in `config.json`; it cannot be combined with `AUTH_URL`. On a device attached to a directory vault a plain `gclone login` means the same directory; switching a device between a Drive vault and a directory vault (or between two directories) needs `logout --forget` first (§2.6 step 0).
- `logout` removes this device's token and cached key; `--revoke` ends the Google login of every device; `--forget` also removes the local vault state (§2.7). `passwd` sets a new passphrase by writing a new keyfile and retiring the old ones — to the trash, or with `--purge-old` for good (§2.7); it changes no key. `login --all-keyfiles` tries the passphrase on every keyfile of the vault instead of the four newest (§2.6 ATTACH).
- `copy` and `sync` take **directories**: the contents of `SRC` go into `DST` (as `rsync SRC/ DST/`; a trailing slash changes nothing; a file as the local argument is `Usage`). `sync` deletes at the destination what this pair synced before and the source no longer has (rows 8/9 of §5.5.1) under guard G4; `copy` never deletes. Entries that exist only at the destination and were never synced are never deleted by either (§5.5.1 precisions). Both skip-and-report instead of overwriting unseen changes; `--force` enables the overrides listed in the table and G2/G3 — nothing else, and the help texts of the flag and of both commands say this in user terms instead of citing section numbers (§17.14). `--max-delete N` is a hard limit (G4).
- `keystore` (0.5.0, §8.2, §17.28) shows and changes where the device's login and key are kept. **Since 0.5.1 (§17.30) the sealed store is a Mac's default and needs no command**: `login` on a device that is not connected seals what it saves, and a device that is on `secrets.json` is moved by the first run after its trial has passed (§8.2, "The automatic move"). The subcommands are for moving at once and for saying no: `keystore use enclave` moves the secrets from `secrets.json` into `secrets.sealed`, sealed by this Mac's Secure Enclave, after it has proven the cached key against the vault and checked that the passphrase opens a keyfile; `keystore use file` moves them back **and is remembered** — no trial, no move and no sealing afterwards, not after a later `login` either, until `keystore use enclave`. Both are refused with the reason where they cannot be done (Linux, a debug build, a session in which no Secure Enclave key can be made, a device that is not connected). **Nothing ever moves secrets into the plain file but `keystore use file`** (and a save that could not seal, §8.2). `keystore check` is made to be run from cron, ssh or a LaunchAgent: it prints the identifiers of the boot and of the session, makes a Secure Enclave key and discards it, opens the trial's test value and, if there is one, the sealed store, and exits 0 when all of that worked. `keystore check --new-trial` discards the trial's record and starts a new key — on a device whose secrets are sealed it only discards the record, there being nothing left to try — and takes the marker of `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` away (§8.2). `keystore use enclave` makes its own move after its own checks, also on a device whose trial has just passed: it never lets the automatic move go first (§17.30).
- `mv` moves into an existing directory, renames otherwise, and replaces nothing without `--force`; `restore` works on files and, with `-r` / `--list`, on directories (§5.5.4).
- Read-only commands (`ls`, `tree`, `cat`, `about`, `status`, `check`, and `web` when it starts) try the lock; if another gclone holds it they use the replica as is and print `note: index not refreshed (another gclone is running)`. `web` lets go of the lock as soon as it has started (§7.4).
- `gc --purge` is the only command that permanently deletes remote **data** objects (§5.9); `passwd --purge-old` permanently deletes retired keyfiles (§2.7). Nothing else deletes. `gc` runs only on a replica that is known to be complete, and only while the store's clock is within a day of the device's (§5.9). `--reset-pair` / `--keep-pair` answer the root-identity guard (§5.5); `--reset-pair` also works when the guard did not fire (the run is then a first sync for that pair: nothing is deleted or overwritten). `--allow-expiring-login` accepts a time-limited Google login (§2.4).
- Secrets never appear in argv or the environment: the passphrase comes from a no-echo prompt or `--passphrase-file`; tokens and keys only ever live in the 0600 files of §8; the one-time link of `gclone web` reaches the browser through a 0600 file, never as an argument of the launcher (§7.4). (`AUTH_URL` is not a secret.)
- Test-only switches, honoured **only by builds with debug assertions** (`cfg!(debug_assertions)`; release builds ignore them): `GCLONE_TEST_FAST_KDF=1` (keyfiles are written with `m_kib = 8192, t = 1`), `GCLONE_TEST_DRIVE_API` / `GCLONE_TEST_DRIVE_UPLOAD` (Drive endpoints), `GCLONE_TEST_REVOKE_URL`, `GCLONE_TEST_BROWSER` (`gclone web`: a file that receives what the browser launcher would have been given — nothing is launched, §17.21), `GCLONE_TEST_FAST_PACER=1` (0.5.0: the Drive backend of the binary runs without pacing and with a 2 ms backoff unit — the settings of the library tests' `fast_pacer`; without it every `restic init` of `tests/restic_e2e.rs` would take a minute). They let `tests/cli_e2e.rs` drive the real binary against `FakeDrive` (§12.1). All of them are read through one function (`cli::context::test_env`); the integrator checked on a release build that `GCLONE_TEST_FAST_KDF=1` is ignored (§17.5). **Key store (0.5.0, §8.2):** `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_SEALER=fake|soft|real` selects the sealer of a debug build, which has none otherwise — `fake`: a stand-in on every platform, a "machine" being the name in `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_MACHINE`; `soft` (macOS): a software P-256 key through the same Security.framework calls; `real` (macOS): the Secure Enclave. `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_FAIL=create|open|open-stored|open-first|open-first-N|hang` makes the stand-in fail (`open-first[-N]`: the first N opens of a stored key fail and later ones work — a transient failure; `hang`: every call into the "hardware" blocks; §17.29; no key at all; nothing opens — a session without access; only keys of other processes fail — a dead blob). `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_STOP=<point>` ends the process with status 137 at a named point of a save, a move or a logout (`save-locked`, `save-plain-temp|done`, `save-sealed-temp|done`, `enclave-sealed-temp|done`, `enclave-choice-temp|done`, `enclave-plain-removed`, `file-choice-temp|done`, `file-plain-temp|done`, `delete-leftovers-done`, `delete-plain-done`; `-temp` leaves the temp file of an unfinished `write_atomic`). `GCLONE_TEST_NOW_MS`, `GCLONE_TEST_BOOT`, `GCLONE_TEST_SESSION` set the trial's clock, boot identifier and session word; `GCLONE_TEST_NOTES=1` stands in for a terminal on stderr for the once-only notes. 0.5.1 (§17.30): `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_STOP` also knows `enclave-note-owed`; `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_WAIT_MS=<n>` replaces the ten seconds one call into the sealer is waited for (`seal::Bounded`), so that a test of `hang` on a sealed device need not wait ten seconds per command; `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_NO_MARKER=1` keeps a run with `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` from leaving `keystore-trial.off` — the harnesses' way to prepare a device and to look at it without deciding its fate (`tests/keystore.rs`: every `Lab::device`; the tests of the variable itself run without it).
- Argument rules enforced by clap (§17.5): `--transfers` is 1..=64; `--vault-dir` conflicts with `AUTH_URL`; `--new-vault` conflicts with `--vault-id`; `restore --list` conflicts with `--version`; `--version` is ≥ 1.
- Ctrl-C (§17.5): during `copy` / `sync` the first Ctrl-C cancels the run — what completed is committed, exit 130 — and a second one exits at once; every other command exits 130 immediately, after restoring the terminal's echo setting (every command tolerates being killed, §5.8). `web` is ended by Ctrl-C: it stops serving and exits **0** (`cli::SERVING`); so is `serve restic --port`. `serve restic --stdio` **ignores SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP** (`cli::DETACHED`, §7.6): it ends when restic closes the pipe.
- `status -q` prints warnings only (it is the keep-alive of §2.4). `--json` is implemented by `copy` / `sync` and, since 0.5.0, by the bare `gclone keystore` (one object, `{"key_store": { "store": "file" | "enclave" | "none" | "unreadable", "path", "usable", "choice": null | "file" | "enclave" | "unreadable", "trial": null | { "running", "days", "restart", "sessions", "failures", "complete", "unavailable", "unavailable_session", "moved", "key_holds_secrets" }, "trial_disabled" (0.5.1: `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` is set for this run), "both_present", "plain_leftovers", "backup_excluded", "cachedir_tag" }}`; `choice` is `null` on a device that was sealed by default — nobody chose; `status` has no JSON output, so this is where a script reads the key store's state). Every other command **refuses it** (`Usage`, exit 2, "--json is supported by copy, sync and `gclone keystore` only", §17.14): `Ui::out` is silent under `--json`, so those commands printed nothing on stdout and exited 0 — `gclone --json ls :` was indistinguishable from an empty vault, and `login --json` dropped the head fingerprint. The flag's help text carries the restriction. A JSON form of the other commands' results stays undone (§14).
- `-q` suppresses plan and skip lines. A run that skipped files still exits 6, so under `-q` (and not `--json`) `copy` / `sync` print the first ten skips with their reasons as `warning: skipped <path>: <reason>` on stderr, plus a count of the rest (§17.14).
- A dry run or a run that only creates directories reports them (`Summary.dirs_created`: "Would create 1 directory.", "… 2 directories created") instead of "Nothing to do" after a `+ mkdir` line.

### 7.2 Exit codes
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | success |
| 1 | other error — including a remote path that does not exist (`ls`, `cat`, `rm`, `mv`, `restore`, a download with `copy` / `sync`, `check`) |
| 2 | usage error: clap's own, and `SyncError::Usage` — a usage error found after argument parsing (mixing backend kinds in `login`, §2.6 step 0; `logout --revoke` on a directory vault) |
| 3 | integrity: crypto failure, index `Gap`/`Rollback`, vault trashed/missing, the vault or one of its index objects needs a newer gclone (`NeedsNewerGclone`, `UnsupportedObject`), `check` found damage, `gc` refused on an incomplete index |
| 4 | fixed by `gclone login`: not connected / signed out / key not unlocked / wrong passphrase / secrets file with unsafe permissions (`ConfigError::{NotConfigured, NotLoggedIn, Locked, WrongPassphrase, InsecurePermissions}`), every `AuthError` (expired or revoked login → "run `gclone login`", Worker problems, expiring login refused), `VaultNotVisible` / `AppNotAuthorized`. An auth Worker that cannot be reached (`AuthError::Network`) is exit 4 for a command that needs the store; a read-only command that can answer from the replica warns and exits 0 (§9.10) |
| 5 | safety guard refused (G2–G4, G6 without confirmation; an explicit `--max-delete` exceeded — never confirmable) |
| 6 | partial: some files were skipped or failed |
| 75 | temporary failure: `QuotaExceeded(_)`, `RateLimited`, `IndexError::OutboxStuck` (a segment could not be published yet) |
| 130 | interrupted |
Precedence when several apply: 3 > 4 > 75 > 5 > 6 > 130 > 2 > 1 (130 and 2 only ever compete with 1 in practice).
`serve restic` (0.5.0, §7.6) has exit codes for its start and end only — 2 for a bad repository name or `--stdio` on a terminal, 4 for a device that is not signed in (or whose secrets file is unsafe; `--port`: signed out while it ran), 1 for a port in use on either loopback address or a stdio connection that broke in a way that is not "closed", 0 when restic closed the connection or Ctrl-C, SIGTERM or SIGHUP ended the listener, 130 for the listener's second Ctrl-C. **What goes wrong while it serves is an HTTP status for restic, not an exit code.**
Cases settled by WP7 (§17.5): a passphrase is needed and there is neither a terminal nor `--passphrase-file` → 2; a passphrase file whose first line is empty or shorter than `PASSPHRASE_MIN_CHARS` when a passphrase is being set → 1; `logout --forget` over unpublished changes without `--yes` and without a confirming terminal → 5; `logout --revoke` without `--yes` off a terminal → 2, declined at the prompt → 1; `gc` refuses with 3 for every refresh outcome other than a complete index (a network error included); a login failure (exit 4) during the refresh of a read-only command or of `gc` is passed on as 4 (§9.10 `RefreshPolicy::Tolerant`) — except `AuthError::Network` / `AuthError::Io`, which say nothing about the login and are treated like any other network error: read-only commands continue on the replica, `gc` refuses with 3 (§17.9).

The `Key store` line (0.5.0, §8.2; 0.5.1, §17.30) is one of:
```
▸ Key store    Secure Enclave of this Mac (secrets.sealed)
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — Secure Enclave trial: 2 of 3 days, no restart seen yet
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — Secure Enclave trial: 3 days, not yet 48 hours apart, a restart survived
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — Secure Enclave trial complete: the next run that can open the test value moves the secrets into the sealed store
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — kept by choice
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — kept: a run with GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0 uses this device (no Secure Enclave trial, nothing is moved; `gclone keystore use enclave` moves the secrets)
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0: no Secure Enclave trial here, nothing is moved
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — kept: nothing is tested or moved while secrets.sealed lies beside it
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — no Secure Enclave on this machine
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600) — no Secure Enclave key could be made in session 0x2 (without graphic access) on 2026-11-20; `gclone keystore check` tries this session
▸ Key store    plain file secrets.json (0600)                                  (Linux, and a debug build)
▸ warning: the Secure Enclave trial failed 2 time(s) in a session without graphic access (last: 2026-11-20). Nothing is moved into the sealed store while a failure is on its record: `gclone keystore` shows the details, `gclone keystore check --new-trial` starts a new trial.
▸ warning: secrets.json and secrets.sealed both exist (an interrupted move, or an older gclone signed in here). gclone uses secrets.json. `gclone keystore use file` or `gclone keystore use enclave` settles it; a move that gclone began by itself is finished by the next run.
▸ warning: secrets.json and secrets.sealed both exist (an interrupted move, or an older gclone signed in here). gclone uses secrets.json. `gclone keystore use file` or `gclone keystore use enclave` settles it. Until then gclone tests and moves nothing by itself here; if an older gclone uses this device (0.4.0 and before read only secrets.json), update it first, or keep the plain file with `gclone keystore use file`.
▸ warning: secrets.json and secrets.sealed both exist (…). gclone uses secrets.json. secrets.sealed is not a copy of it: <why>. `gclone keystore use file --discard-sealed` removes secrets.sealed, `gclone keystore use enclave` replaces it. Until then gclone tests and moves nothing by itself here; …
▸ warning: the secrets are sealed to a key that was made at the move, not to the Secure Enclave trial's key: the trial's record (days, restart, sessions) is evidence for another key. `gclone keystore check` from every session gclone runs in (cron, ssh, a LaunchAgent) shows whether this one opens there; `gclone keystore check --new-trial` forgets the old record.
```
The lines after the first are **why the secrets are not sealed (yet)** on a Mac: every fallback of §8.2 is silent where it happens and shows here and in `gclone keystore`. The "trial complete" line is seen only by a look that takes no step of its own (`gclone keystore`), or where the looking session cannot open the trial's key: any other run has moved the secrets by the time it prints. The line with `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` alone is what a run with the variable prints before any such run has loaded the secrets (`gclone keystore`); from the first one that did, every run prints the "kept: a run with …" line (the marker of §8.2). Of the two "both exist" warnings the first is said only where `secrets.sealed` is sealed to the key of the trial that is running — what an interrupted automatic move leaves; in every other case gclone moves nothing, and the line and the warning say so instead of promising a move that every run then refuses (§17.30). The last warning is shown only when the ended trial had seen more than its first day, or a restart: a record without evidence is not warned about.
`gclone login` on a Mac, where its secrets were not sealed before and are afterwards (stderr, not with `-q`): ▸ *"This device's login and key are sealed by this Mac's Secure Enclave (secrets.sealed): a copy of that file is useless anywhere else. If this Mac is erased or repaired, `gclone login` and the passphrase connect it again. `gclone keystore use file` keeps a plain file instead."*
`--json` events (one JSON object per line): `{"event":"plan","action":"upload","path":…,"size":…}`, `{"event":"done","action":…,"path":…}`, `{"event":"skip","path":…,"reason":…}`, `{"event":"warn","message":…}`, `{"event":"summary","uploaded":…,"downloaded":…,"reused":…,"deleted":…,"skipped":…,"failed":…,"conflicts":…,"bytes_up":…,"bytes_down":…,"exit":…}`.

### 7.4 `gclone web` — the vault in a browser (0.3.0, §17.20)

Everything on Drive is ciphertext, so Google's pages show nothing. `gclone web [--port N] [--no-browser]` serves a file browser for the **decrypted** vault from the gclone process itself: one embedded page (`src/web/assets/{index.html,app.css,app.js,icon.svg}`, `include_str!`; vanilla JS, no build step, no external resource of any kind) and a small HTTP/1.1 API on loopback. It is **read-only**: no route changes the vault or the index; the only things written are gclone's own download ledger (as `cat`) and, during a refresh, the replica (as every read-only command). Both backends.

**Process.** `open_ctx{TryShared, Tolerant, no settle}` — so not connected / signed out / locked / a dead login fail exactly as for `ls`, with its texts and exit codes — then the lock and that vault are dropped and the server keeps: the backend (`Arc<AnyBackend>`; a Drive backend renews its access token on demand for as long as the process lives), the keyring, a `Vault::open_unlocked` over `Db::open_shared` for all queries and downloads (§8.3: a lock-less reader), and a second `open_shared` connection for the ledger. It binds `127.0.0.1:N` (`N` omitted: port 0, a free one) and, if that address is free too, `[::1]:N` — never anything else; there is no flag for another address, and a peer that is not loopback is dropped. It serves until Ctrl-C (exit 0). A port that cannot be bound is exit 1 before anything is printed.

**The link, and the browser.** With `--no-browser` / `want_headless` (§2.4: SSH session, Linux without a display) the link is printed (stdout, also under `-q`). Otherwise gclone opens the default browser itself — and **not with the link**: an argument list is readable by every account of the machine (`ps`, `/proc/*/cmdline`), and on Linux the browser keeps its arguments for as long as it runs. It writes `<state root>/web-open-<port>.html` (`util::write_atomic`, mode `0600`, in the `0700` directory that holds `secrets.json`): `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer"><meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=LINK">` and the link as an anchor, nothing else; hands **that file's path** to `open::that_detached`; and removes the file as soon as the link is used or replaced, and when the viewer ends (`App::delete_when_used`, `App::close`). A launch page older than ten minutes that a killed viewer left behind — its link died with it — is removed by the next one. If the file cannot be written, the link is printed instead; it is never passed as an argument. The terminal shows no link in this mode, only the port. When stdin is a terminal, every line typed there makes a **new link and a new session** (below); the thread that reads it must not stop the process: a background job (`gclone web &`, Ctrl-Z and `bg`) that reads its terminal gets `SIGTTIN`, whose default action stops every thread — so `SIGTTIN` is ignored, the read fails with `EIO`, and the thread tries again each second until the job is in the foreground or the terminal is gone. The texts say "press Enter" only when the process is in the terminal's foreground group at start (`tcgetpgrp(0) == getpgrp()`), otherwise "run `gclone web` again".

**Refresh.** `POST /api/refresh` (and nothing else: there is no timer) does what the start of a read-only command does — the state lock, `Vault::open` on a fresh connection, `refresh()`, both dropped — with two differences that come from the viewer outliving commands: the lock is taken with `state::try_lock_existing`, which creates neither the state directory nor the lock file, and nothing is opened unless the device guard (below) holds, asked once before the lock and once under it (`gclone logout` holds that lock while it removes things, so the second look cannot be overtaken). A busy lock: the answer says that another gclone is running. The state lock is therefore held only for the length of a pull, and a `gclone sync` in another terminal waits for the viewer no longer than for a `gclone ls`. What another process on this device commits is visible at once (same `state.db`). The outcome (`RefreshState { at_ms, ok, applied, note }`) is kept and shown: `Gap` / `Rollback` / an unreachable store → the text of `report_refresh`; a login that ended at Google → the §2.8 text; the server goes on serving the replica in those cases.

**A device that is signed out stops serving** (`cli::web::DeviceGuard`). The viewer holds the keyring, the backend (for Drive: the refresh token) and an open database in memory; `gclone logout` removes files. Without a check, a viewer forgotten in another terminal would go on serving decrypted files after "Signed out on this device", and after `logout --forget` its next refresh would write the state directory — a plaintext index — back. The guard holds while `config.json` names the vault the viewer started with, the key store — `secrets.json` or, since 0.5.0, `secrets.sealed` (§8.2) — holds the same login and keys (a keyed BLAKE3 digest of refresh token, key entries and `min_epoch`, taken at start; the files are read again only when the `stat` of one of them changed; a move between the two by `gclone keystore use` is the same login in another file and no sign-out, neither is a moment in which another gclone holds the secrets lock, nor a load *error* at the moment of the look — §8.3), and `state.db` is the very file the viewer has open (device and inode — a state directory that was removed and made again is another file, which the viewer's open connection would never see). It is asked **for every request**, before the session is looked at — a request after `logout` has returned is answered `403` "The viewer has stopped: …" on every route — **by the refresh**, and **once a second** by the command, which then ends the server, with it every stream, prints the same text and exits **4**. Once tripped it stays tripped: a new login does not revive the viewer. Signing in again to the same vault with the same keys (a directory vault's `gclone login`) is not a change.

**Session.** A session is a random path prefix and a secret: `/s-<128 random bits, base64url>/` and 256 random bits (`util::random`). The secret is the value of the cookie `gclone_web_<port>`, set as `Path=/s-…/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` (a session cookie). **The page, its assets, the API and the files all live under the prefix** — the page's own URLs are relative — and nothing but the link is answered outside it. The prefix is not a credential (it is in the address bar; the cookie is still required, and compared in constant time): it is what keeps the cookie on this server. Cookies are not separated by port, so a cookie with `Path=/` on `127.0.0.1` would be attached to every request the browser makes to **any** server on the loopback host — a development server, another user's listener that a page navigated the browser to — and whoever receives it can read the vault with a plain HTTP client. A cookie scoped to a path that only this server knows is sent to no other (`Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` keeps the path out of requests elsewhere). **Every** route — the page and its assets included — answers `403` with one line of plain text without the session, and so does every path outside the prefix, with or without the cookie. Cookies are read as **bytes** (`Cookie` headers split at `;`, trimmed, split at the first `=`): the browser sends the cookies of every loopback server in one header, and one value that is not ASCII must not hide the session.

The session is handed out for the key of a **one-time link**, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?k=<192 random bits>`: `GET /?k=…` with the current key → the key is used up and the answer carries `Set-Cookie` and leads to the prefix — `303 See Other` when the browser says that no other site began the navigation (`Sec-Fetch-Site: none` or `same-origin`: typed, pasted, opened from a terminal), otherwise (`cross-site` navigation — a terminal in a browser tab, the launch page, which is a `file:` document — or a browser that sends no `Sec-Fetch-Site`) `200` with a page that goes there by `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`: a redirect would stay part of a navigation that another site began, to which `SameSite=Strict` does not send the new cookie. The key is one-time, not absent from history: the browser records the address of the link; what it records is spent. A key that was used is `403` "This link has been used already … If it was not you who opened it, another program on this machine did — press Enter …: that ends every session and gives you a new link" (the last sixteen used keys are remembered for that text); any other key is `403` "not a valid link"; there is no way past the key for a browser that already has a session (its cookie is not sent to `/`), so **every key that reaches the server is spent or refused**. **A new link is a new session** (`App::login_url`): new prefix, new secret, the old session's cookie and path are dead on every route and its file streams are cut (`Session::ended`) — the one action that shuts out whoever redeemed a link first. Comparisons are constant-time (`util::ct_eq`). Neither secret is logged — a request is logged at debug level with its method and its route (the path without the prefix), never its query. A query parameter rather than a fragment, because the fragment never reaches the server, which would have had to serve the page without the secret.

**Checks, in this order, for every request.** (0) The request head — request line and header lines as sent — is at most `HEADER_BYTES_MAX` = 64 KiB, else `431` (enforced by the handler; hyper's read buffer, which grows beyond its nominal size before it gives up, only bounds what is read at all; a request target over hyper's own limit is `414`). (1) `Host` — exactly one, equal (ASCII case-insensitively) to `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>` or `[::1]:<port>`, and the same for the authority of an absolute request target; else `403` (DNS rebinding: a foreign name that resolves to loopback still arrives as that name; an SSH tunnel must use the same port on both ends). (2) `Origin`, if present, is `http://` + one of those; `Sec-Fetch-Site`, if present, is `same-origin` or `none`; else `403` (the link's navigation aside) — although nothing but the refresh is state-changing. Each of `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, `Sec-Fetch-Mode`, `Sec-Fetch-Dest` that is sent **twice**, or holds bytes that are not visible ASCII, is `403` as well: a header the server cannot read must not count as absent. (3) The device guard. (4) The link, or the session and its prefix. (5) The route; an unknown path under the prefix is `404`, a known one with another method `405` with `Allow`. A malformed query (`%` not followed by two hex digits, not UTF-8, a parameter given twice, a path that fails `path::validate`, a number out of range, an `id` this viewer did not give out) is `400`. Remote paths are only ever looked up in the index — no file-system access by a path from the client exists.

**Routes.** `/?k=…` at the root; everything else under the session's prefix (`/s-…/api/info`, …; shown here without it). All `GET`/`HEAD` unless noted; JSON unless noted; errors are `text/plain` with one readable line.

| Route | Parameters | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `/?k=…` (root) | `k` | the link: the cookie, and the way to the prefix (above) |
| `/` | — | the page; `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' blob:; media-src 'self'; frame-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| `/assets/app.css`, `/assets/app.js`, `/assets/icon.svg` | — | the page's style, script, icon |
| `/api/info` | — | `{vault, backend: "drive"\|"dir", device, version, read_only: true, files, bytes, last_change_ms, last_change_by, refresh: RefreshState}` — `Vault::stats`, no call to the store. `last_change_*` is the device last seen alive and when (the greatest `devices.last_ms`): raised by every applied segment of a device, and — since 0.4.0, §17.23 — by the snapshot a replica takes for its base or writes itself (its writer, at its `created_ms`); a snapshot carries only when each device joined |
| `/api/list` | `path` (absent/empty = root), `sort` = `name`\|`size`\|`mtime`, `order` = `asc`\|`desc`, `offset`, `limit` (default `LIST_PAGE` 2000, max `LIST_PAGE_MAX` 5000) | `{path, sort, order, total, offset, entries: [{name, dir, kind, size, mtime_ms}]}`; `404` if there is no such directory. **Order**: directories first, always; `sort=name` by natural order (case-insensitive, digit runs as numbers, ties by bytes), reversed as a whole under `desc`; `sort=size\|mtime`: files by that key (reversed under `desc`), equal keys by name ascending, directories — which have neither — by name ascending. `kind` is `folder` or `image`\|`pdf`\|`audio`\|`video`\|`text`\|`archive`\|`file`; `size` and `mtime_ms` are `null` for directories |
| `/api/stat` | `path` | one entry, with `path`, and for a file with `id`: the path sealed under a key of this process (XChaCha20-Poly1305, the nonce a keyed BLAKE3 hash of the path, base64url — one file, one id; opaque and authenticated; this is the one AEAD call outside `crypto` and outside §4 and its test vectors — it touches no vault key and no vault format — and the id is as long as the path plus 40 bytes, so it shows the path's length to whoever sees the address) — what `/file` takes in place of the path; `404` if absent |
| `/api/search` | `q`, `limit` (default `SEARCH_HITS` 200, max 1000), `sort`, `order` (as `/api/list`) | `{q, sort, order, hits: [entry with path], more}` — `Vault::search`: names (last components, directories with or without a head) that contain `q`, NFC + lower case on both sides; the first `limit` matches in path order, `more` = there are further ones; those are then put in **the order of a listing** (the same function: directories first, natural order of the name, equal names by path), so that the same entries come in the same order in a folder and in a search |
| `POST /api/refresh` | — | the `/api/info` object after the refresh |
| `/file` | `id` **or** `path` (not both), `dl=1` | the file's bytes (not JSON), see below. The page uses `id` only, so that no file name is in an address the browser keeps (a tab opened on a file, the download list); `path` is for other clients |

**File content.** `transfer::read_range` (the reader of `cat`) runs in a task and writes into a bounded channel (16 frames of ≤ 64 KiB) that is the response body: nothing is buffered beyond that, nothing is written to disk, and every chunk is authenticated before a byte of it is sent. The answer waits for the first verified bytes, so a blob that is missing or damaged from the start — or a store that cannot be reached, or a login that ended — is `502` with the text the command line would print ("The file could not be read from the vault: …"); a failure after that cuts the connection (the body ends short of `Content-Length`), so a damaged download never looks complete. A client that goes away closes the channel, which ends the task and with it the request to the store — also while the task is waiting for the store (`Sender::closed`). `Accept-Ranges: bytes`; one byte range (`a-b`, `a-`, `-n`) → `206` with `Content-Range`; a range that selects nothing → `416` with `Content-Range: bytes */<size>`; **several ranges, or a `Range` that is not understood → `200` with the whole file** (RFC 9110 §14.2 allows ignoring the header). `ETag` is the BLAKE3 content hash of the entry in quotes; `If-None-Match` → `304`; `If-Range` with another tag → the whole file. `HEAD` answers from the index alone and **ignores `Range`** (RFC 9110 §14.2: the header is defined for `GET`): always `200` with the whole length. An empty file is `200` with no body. At most `STREAMS_MAX` = 16 file streams run at a time; a request waits 5 s for a free one, then `503` with `Retry-After`. A stream ends with its session (a new link, a device that was signed out). Connections: at most 128, 15 s to send the request head, 64 KiB of head (check 0).

**Vault files are untrusted content** (`src/web/mime.rs`). The `Content-Type` comes from the file name's extension through a built-in table, never from the content, and every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. HTML, XHTML, XML, JavaScript, CSS and every other text format are `text/plain; charset=utf-8`; SVG is `image/svg+xml` (shown through `<img>`, where script does not run); images, audio, video and PDF have their own types; everything else is `application/octet-stream`. `Content-Disposition` is `inline` only for that list (images, PDF, audio, video, `text/plain`) and `attachment` otherwise and whenever `dl=1`. **`inline` is bare: an answer that is shown carries no file name** (§17.23) — a browser takes the `filename` of an inline answer for the title of a tab that shows the file by itself (Chrome for a PDF, Firefox for images, audio and video), and a title goes into the browser's history. An `attachment` carries the name as `filename="<ASCII stand-in>"; filename*=UTF-8''<percent-encoded>` (RFC 6266 / 5987: quotes, non-ASCII, control characters and line breaks cannot end or extend the header); the bidirectional controls (U+061C, U+200E, U+200F, U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069) are `_` in both forms, so that the name a browser saves under does not read differently from what it is (`invoice<U+202E>fdp.exe` would be drawn "invoiceexe.pdf"). `Content-Security-Policy` on file responses: `sandbox; default-src 'none'; …` plus only what the browser's own image, media or text document needs (`img-src 'self'` / `media-src 'self'`, `style-src 'unsafe-inline'`), `frame-ancestors 'none'`; for PDF `default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'` **without** `sandbox`, because browsers do not show a PDF in a sandboxed frame. Everything is `Cache-Control: no-store`.

**The page.** Folder navigation with breadcrumbs (a path that does not fit scrolls, and shows its end); a list with name, size, modification time and a type icon, sortable by the three, directories first; search over the whole vault with a note when the cap cut the result, each match with its folder (cut at its beginning when it does not fit); previews — images and SVG in `<img>` on a light checkerboard of their own (a transparent image with dark content is legible in the dark theme), PDF in an `<iframe>`, audio and video with the browser's controls (seeking uses ranges), text of every kind as text (the first 512 KiB; a byte-order mark decides the encoding, else UTF-8 if valid, else Windows-1252; a character split by the cut is dropped), a card with a download button for everything else and for what the browser cannot show; every preview shows "Loading <name> (<size>)…" until its element has something to show; download — asked of the store first (`Range: bytes=0-0`), so that a file it cannot deliver is the server's message in the page instead of a download that fails silently; the vault summary in the footer and behind the info button, redrawn with the clock and fetched again with every listing; refresh; keyboard (arrows, Home/End/Page keys, Enter, Backspace = up, Esc, `/` = search; ←/→ in the preview). The preview is a modal dialog: while it is open everything behind it is `inert`.

**Nothing of the vault's names where the browser keeps it.** The address is the session's prefix and nothing else, and the title is "gclone", always: the place in the vault (`{dir}`, `{file}`, `{search}`) lives in `history.state` (`pushState(state, '')` without a URL), so reload, back and forward work, and the browser's history — which is on disk, and with history sync on a vendor's servers — records one address and one title. Files are fetched by `id` (above), and a file that is shown in a tab of its own ("Open in a new tab") has no name in its answer (bare `inline`, above): its tab is titled by the browser from the address — the id. What remains is §15.

Lists are drawn as a window of rows over the loaded entries (a directory of 10,000 entries has some thirty rows in the DOM) and loaded in pages. Names reach the DOM as text nodes and attribute values only (`textContent`, `setAttribute`), never as markup; they are shown as they are — `white-space: pre`, control characters as their pictures (U+2400…), the bidirectional controls as U+FFFD (a name is drawn in the order it has; tooltips and labels keep it as it is) — and commands in messages are `<code>` elements built from text. System fonts, light and dark by `prefers-color-scheme`, usable down to phone width, ARIA grid with `aria-activedescendant` (one tab stop, a visible focus ring also without a selected row, the kind of each entry as hidden text). A list of deleted or restorable versions, thumbnails and any write operation are out of scope (§14).

**One page, two providers (0.4.0, §17.22).** The hosted viewer of §7.5 uses this page byte for byte: `app.js`, `app.css`, `icon.svg`, and the markup between `<body>` and `</body>` of `index.html` (which therefore holds no script element, no inline style and no event handler — the hosted viewer's build refuses it otherwise). `app.js` takes everything that differs from a **provider**: `window.gcloneProvider` when a page defines it before the script runs, else the built-in local provider, with which the page behaves exactly as described above. A provider has seven properties: `api(name, params)` (the five calls `info`, `list`, `stat`, `search`, `refresh`, answering the JSON of the table above), `fileUrl(id, download)` (the address of a file by the `id` of its `stat` answer), `unreachable` (the sentence for a provider that does not answer), `privateAddress` (true: `history.state` holds no route — only two numbers, a flag and a tag, `{e, n, depth, began}`, the route staying in the page's memory — so that nothing of the vault's names is in session-restore data either; the local provider keeps `{dir|file|search, depth, began}` as before), `pdfInline` (false: a card with an "Open" button — a tab of its own — instead of an `<iframe>`; the hosted viewer's choice for every browser, §7.5), `openInTab(kind)` (whether a file of this kind is offered "Open in a new tab"; the local provider: always; the hosted one: not for audio and video), and `downloadAttribute` (false: download links are plain navigations without the `download` attribute — Chrome fetches an `<a download>` link past a Service Worker). **The rules that decide what the API answers** — listing order and paging, the search and its order, the JSON shapes, `Range` parsing, `Content-Disposition`, the sentences for "no such folder / file" — are one pure file, `src/web/rules.rs` (no hyper, tokio or rusqlite), used by this server and compiled into the hosted viewer's wasm; the type table `src/web/mime.rs` likewise. `tests/web.rs` is unchanged by the move.
**Shared with `serve restic` (0.5.0, §7.6).** The accept loop (`web::serve`: the connection limit, the loopback-peer check, the HTTP/1 settings, dropping connections at shutdown) takes the handler as a closure, and the `Host` comparison is a function of its own (`web::host_allowed`); `gclone serve restic --port` uses both. `web::bind_v6(port, V6::Required)` is `web::bind` for a server whose client volunteers a secret: a `[::1]:port` that someone else holds is an error instead of "serve on 127.0.0.1 alone". `gclone web` behaves as before (`web::bind`, `CONNECTIONS_MAX`); `tests/web.rs` is unchanged.

### 7.5 The hosted viewer — the vault in any browser (0.4.0, §17.22)

`gclone web` needs a device that is attached to the vault. The hosted viewer needs a browser: `https://<host>/`, served by the auth Worker (§16.8), is the page of §7.4 over another provider. The browser signs in to Google through the Worker (§2.3, `/web/*`), the passphrase is typed (or filled in) on the page, and the browser fetches **ciphertext** from Google Drive directly and decrypts it itself, with gclone's own read path compiled to WebAssembly. Same behaviour and same JSON shapes as §7.4. It is **optional** — without its three secrets and files the Worker is the sign-in helper of §2 and nothing else — and **read-only by its code, not by its token**: `drive.file` has no read-only form. What using it costs is the first row of §1.3: the party that serves the page can take the passphrase. `docs/AUTH.md` has the sign-in as a diagram; `worker/README.md` the setup, the deploy and the first-deployment checklist; `worker/viewer/README.md` and `web-core/README.md` the files.

**In v1**: browse folders, sort, search names in the whole vault, the vault summary, manual refresh; previews of images, SVG (as an image), audio and video with seeking, PDF, text (the first 512 KiB); download of any file, streamed, without holding it in memory; Lock (button; 15 minutes without input; 5 minutes in the background), sign out; the head fingerprint in the info panel, to compare with `gclone status`. **Not in v1** (§14, item 9b): an index cache, any "keep unlocked", passkey unlock, a mode without Service Worker, whole-file BLAKE3 on streamed downloads, rollback detection across visits, conflict losers and deleted versions, thumbnails, any write, offline use, revoking the grant from the page.

**Where things run** — one origin, four contexts besides the Worker. The table is what each context's own scripts do; what holds against *another* script in the page is the seal of the ticket port, below, and §1.3 (the script row) — before 0.5.0 this line read "no key material ever crosses the page", which was the honest page's habit and not a boundary (§17.27):

| Context | Lives | Does | Holds | Never holds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| page (`shell.js`, `provider.js`, `token.js`, and the shared `app.js`) | the tab | sign-in, the unlock screen, Lock by wall clock, sign-out; the UI; creates the two `MessageChannel`s below and transfers their ports | the passphrase while it is typed; an access token; ids and paths; both channels' ports for the moment between making and giving them away | wasm, a master key, a stream key, a ticket it could read, a keyfile |
| KDF worker (`kdf-worker.js`) | one per visit of the unlock screen; ended on success, when the screen is left, on `pagehide`, after two idle minutes | Argon2id and the keyfile candidates (below); hands the **key bundle** to the vault worker over a port the page created | 257 MiB of wasm memory for the derivation | — it does not outlive the unlock (a wasm memory never shrinks, so the 256 MiB must not sit in a long-lived instance; wrong-passphrase retries reuse the one worker and its block) |
| vault worker (`vault-worker.js`, `loader.js`, `drive.js`, `seal.js`) | while the vault is unlocked | lists and fetches index objects from Drive, answers the five API calls, mints per-file tickets and seals them to the Service Worker | the keyring, the decrypted index (1.3 MiB of wasm memory before the index), one key pair per ticket channel | the passphrase |
| Service Worker (`/sw.js`, with `drive.js`, `token.js`, `seal.js`) | the browser's | answers `GET /v/<id>` with decrypted bytes and `Range`, and `GET /seal-key` with its public key | tickets (one stream key and one blob location each), an access token, the seal's key pair (in memory, never stored) | the passphrase, a master key |
| Cloudflare Worker (§16.8) | — | serves the page and its static files, the sign-in | client secrets, `SEAL_KEY` | a file, a name, the passphrase, a vault key |

The **ticket port, and its seal** (0.5.0, §17.27; `worker/viewer/seal.js`). The page creates a `MessageChannel` and transfers one port to the vault worker and the other to the Service Worker; tickets and the access token travel vault worker → Service Worker on it. The page sends only `{id, path}` to the vault worker. **That the page gives both ports away is a habit of its own scripts and binds no other script in the page**: one can keep a port, hand the vault worker a port of its own (the `tickets` call takes the port it is given), or relay between two channels and read along. Until 0.5.0 that yielded the stream key of every file — the audit's L2: 273 tickets in 7 ms, and the vault decrypted from them offline, after Lock, without the passphrase. So what crosses the port is sealed:
- *Keys.* The Service Worker holds one ECDH P-256 key pair per instance — made on first use, private half not extractable, in memory only, dropped with every `forget`. The vault worker makes one pair per ticket channel.
- *Where the vault worker gets the Service Worker's public key*: from its **own** `fetch('/seal-key')` (no cookie, `no-store`). A request of a dedicated worker is answered by the Service Worker that controls it — here out of its memory: `200`, 65 bytes (the uncompressed point), `X-Gclone-Build: <build>` — and no script in the page can answer it, see it or change the answer. This is the whole of the authentication. A key agreement carried over the port itself would be the page's to intercept (it could give each side a key of its own); here the vault worker takes nothing from the port's side at all.
- *The channel key*: HKDF-SHA-256 over the ECDH secret, salt 32 zero bytes, info `"gclone-viewer/ticket-seal/1" ‖ 0x00 ‖ <Service Worker's public key> ‖ <vault worker's public key>` → AES-256-GCM, not extractable.
- *A ticket on the port*: `{type: "ticket", id, build, sealed: {to, from, iv, data}}` — `to`: the public key it is sealed to; `from`: the vault worker's; `iv`: 96 random bits; `data`: AES-256-GCM over the JSON `{ticket, token, exp}` with `"gclone-viewer/ticket-seal/1" ‖ 0x00 ‖ id` as associated data. A refusal is `{type: "ticket-error", id, message, build}`: a sentence, no key.
- *Someone in the middle* sees `id`, `build` and ciphertext. Replacing `from` makes the Service Worker agree a key with the replacement — who can then hand it tickets of their own making, which gets them nothing they could not ask the vault worker for — and opens nothing the vault worker sealed.
- *Nobody answers as the Service Worker* (another status, another length, another build): the vault worker seals nothing. Where no Service Worker controls it, the request reaches the Cloudflare Worker, which has no such address (`404`) and learns nothing; the file's address is answered `502` with a sentence.
- *Lifetime.* `forget` — Lock, sign-out, a page that leaves — drops the tickets **and the key pair**, and the vault worker ends with its page: a sealed ticket that anyone kept opens nothing afterwards. **The Service Worker is the one registered for the whole origin, and only that one** (§17.29): `/sw.js` under any other scope is inert — it imports nothing, has no `fetch` or `message` handler and no key pair, claims no client, and removes its own registration when it is activated. (A script in the unlocked page could register a second instance for `/a/<build>/`; its `clients.claim()` took the running vault worker over, which then sealed real tickets to an instance that no `forget` reached and that answered a window inside its scope with whole files after the Lock — in Chrome and WebKit.) **The lock itself** (`shell.js`, §17.29): the Service Worker is told to forget and the vault worker and the KDF worker are ended *first*, each step in its own `try`, with `ServiceWorker.prototype.postMessage` and `Worker.prototype.terminate` taken when the script loaded; only then the DOM, the history and the reload. Sign out does the same and sends its request whatever the page's DOM does. **Recovery** (`vault-worker.js`, §17.29): a ticket is sealed for, and posted on, the channel that is current when the ticket is ready — when several files are asked for at once after the Service Worker lost its tickets, each `need-ticket` opens a new channel and closes the one before, and tickets that were being sealed for a closed channel were lost (all but the last file answered `410` after 3 s). A Service Worker that the browser restarted has a new pair: it cannot open what was sealed to the old one, drops that page's port and asks for the ticket again (`need-ticket`; the third ticket in a row for one id that it cannot open is answered `502` instead); a new port makes the vault worker ask for the key and agree anew.
- *Engines* (measured, §17.27). The vault worker asks for the key once when it starts, **before the unlock screen**, up to four times within 1.2 s: Firefox lets a new worker's very first request through to the network, and WebKit leaves a worker outside the Service Worker when its script is being loaded for another worker of the same page at that moment. A vault worker that got no key is replaced by the page while it holds nothing — three starts at most, then the viewer stops and says so.

**What the seal does not do** is §1.3, the script row: the page, and so a script in it, still gets the plaintext of what it asks for while the vault is unlocked; and the key bundle's channel (KDF worker → vault worker, the page's to hand out as well) is not sealed, because a script that is in the page at that moment has the passphrase. The keyfile bytes go vault worker → KDF worker on the key port: the page's scripts never hold them either. All ciphertext flows browser ↔ `www.googleapis.com` (`files.list`, `files.get?alt=media` with `Authorization` and `Range`); the Drive host is named in exactly one place, `drive.js`, and is the only foreign host the page's policy allows.

**The core** (`web-core/`, crate `gclone-web-core`, built by `web-core/build.sh` → `web-core/pkg/{core.js, core.wasm, build.json}`). Not a re-implementation: `src/lib.rs`, `src/index.rs` and `src/web.rs` compile the main crate's own source files a second time by `#[path]` — the stream container, the keyfile, index objects, the merge rule, `rules.rs`, `mime.rs` — for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with wasm-bindgen (`--target no-modules`: a classic script that defines the global `wasm_bindgen`, loaded by `importScripts`). It has **its own empty `[workspace]` and its own `Cargo.lock`**, so the CLI's `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and release builds never see it; its lockfile is the CLI's, pruned (`build.sh` fails when a package in both has two versions, and when the `wasm-bindgen` command is not the version of the crate). What the main crate gained for it is additive: 13 `#[cfg(unix)]` / `#[cfg(not(target_family = "wasm"))]` lines in `error.rs`, `types.rs`, `util.rs` (true on every native target); the tickets of §4.1; the two format gates as functions — `VaultDescriptor::readable()` (`min_reader`) and `index::check_snapshot_format()` (`vault_format`) — which the CLI's own loaders now call. No I/O, no clock, no randomness: the module's four imports are wasm-bindgen intrinsics; JavaScript fetches bytes and hands them in. `core.wasm` is 711 KB (219 KB brotli). The API (`web-core/src/api.rs`; shapes in `web-core/README.md`): `parse_descriptor`, `keyfile_candidates`, `keyfile_cost`, `unlock(keyfile, passphrase, vault_id) → key bundle`, `Vault.from_keys(bundle)` (which zero-fills the caller's buffer), `snapshot_candidates` / `load_snapshot` / `needed_segments` / `add_segment` / `finish` / `reset`, `info`, `list`, `stat`, `search`, `ticket(path)`, `FileReader(ticket, start, end)` with `cipher_start` / `cipher_end` / `push` / `resume_at` / `remaining`, `served(name, download)`, `parse_range`. Every failure is an `Error` whose message is `"<code>: <sentence>"`, code ∈ `wrong-passphrase`, `damaged`, `other-vault`, `needs-newer`, `not-found`, `not-a-file`, `corrupt`, `bad-input`; anything else thrown means the instance is dead (out of memory) and is discarded. **The format gates are inside the wasm** (§3.3, "unknown version anywhere → fail closed"): a descriptor with a newer `min_reader`, a snapshot with a newer `vault_format`, a `VaultInit` of a newer format, an unknown codec, body version, suite, flags, chunk size or key epoch all end in `needs-newer`, as in the CLI.

**Loading a vault** (vault worker; everything Drive lists is unauthenticated, so four constants bound what a listing can make the tab do: `SMALL_MAX` = 64 KiB for descriptor and keyfiles, `INDEX_PARALLEL_MAX` = 16 MiB and `INDEX_OBJECT_MAX` = 1 GiB as in §6.1, `INDEX_CONFIRM` = 64 MiB; a body longer than its bound is aborted and counts as corrupt). Listings ask for `pageSize=1000`, `spaces=drive`, `fields=nextPageToken,files(id,name,size,createdTime,mimeType,parents)`, `trashed = false`, and follow `nextPageToken`.
1. **Discover**: list `gclone-vault.json`; a usable vault is one whose descriptor parses and is `readable`; only unreadable ones → "This vault needs a newer viewer"; several usable ones → a chooser (folder, creation date, first 8 hex digits of the vault id). The root's children: exactly one `index` and one `data` folder; the keyfiles are the names `keyfile_candidates` accepts.
2. **Keyfiles** — the CLI's order (§2.6: highest generation first, four names at a time from `keyfile_candidates`), with two differences that keep planted objects from locking the owner out (§17.23). *An object under a keyfile's name that is no keyfile takes no place*: every keyfile-named object — at most `KEYFILE_LOOK_MAX` = 32 fetches of at most 64 KiB; one listed larger is not fetched at all — is costed with `keyfile_cost` **before** the candidates are chosen, and what that refuses (junk, a name whose hash is not the content's, parameters out of bounds) is dropped there; names beyond the 32 are counted and, if no usable keyfile is among those looked at, said. *The candidates are all usable keyfiles, not the first four*: one attempt tries the passphrase on them in order until one opens or four have said `wrong-passphrase` (a candidate that turns out `damaged` / `other-vault` / `needs-newer` is dropped and does not count); when keyfiles remain untried, the unlock screen says so ("That passphrase does not open the 4 newest keyfiles of this vault. N more were not tried.") and offers a tick box to try the others too, one derivation each — never without being asked. A candidate that asks for more than 256 MiB or more than three passes is announced with its cost and can be skipped (a planted keyfile may demand 512 MiB; several are announced together). Opens and names this vault → the key bundle. So both passphrases work after two concurrent `gclone passwd` runs; four junk names of higher generations change nothing; and four well-formed keyfiles of another vault in front of the real one cost the owner one tick and five derivations instead of the vault. (More than 32 keyfile names still hide the real one: the viewer then says that it looked at 32 and names the remedy, `gclone passwd` or removing the strays.)
3. **Index** — the CLI's rule (§5.3): snapshots newest first until one is accepted, **every** listed one is tried; snapshots listed but none readable → the load stops with their names and **no tree is shown** (what the remaining segments describe would be a partial vault presented as the vault); none listed → a young vault, from segments alone. Then `needed_segments` → `add_segment` → `finish`; a `missing` reference with a file id is fetched by that id (at most three rounds), one without is reported as blocked. Before a snapshot is downloaded, and again with the true total before the segments, more than `INDEX_CONFIRM` is asked about ("The index of this vault is N MB…"), with "Skip `<object>`" when one object is more than half of it. Objects above `INDEX_PARALLEL_MAX` are fetched one at a time, the rest six at a time. A `missing` reference's object is bounded like a listed one: its name must have the form of an index object's, its size is asked about like any other, and above `INDEX_OBJECT_MAX` it is not fetched. `refresh.ok` is false whenever there is a note (blocked, damaged, skipped or deferred objects).
4. **Refresh** lists again and fetches only what `needed_segments` names — nothing when nothing changed. **A refresh cannot ask** (the file list is on the screen), so it downloads **at most `INDEX_CONFIRM` in all**: objects beyond that are left where they are and named by count and size in the note ("N new index objects (M MiB) were not loaded: a refresh downloads no more than 64 MiB without asking. Lock the vault and unlock it again to decide." — the next load asks). The same holds for the objects of `missing` references, and for the fresh load a refresh starts when segments stay blocked while a newer snapshot is listed: that load is quiet too, and is not started at all when the newer snapshot alone is above the bound (the loaded state stays, with a note). So a planted index object costs a question or a sentence, at a load and at a refresh, never the tab's memory. Drive errors follow §6.5: `401` → one fresh access token, one retry; `403` rate limit / `429` → backoff; `404` on a blob id → by name, exactly one hit; the abuse flag → one retry with `acknowledgeAbuse=true`. **Patience**: finding the vault and loading its index keep the CLI's schedule (six attempts, pauses of 1–16 s); once the list is shown — a refresh in the vault worker, every read in the Service Worker — one request pauses at most 10 s in all between its attempts and then says why, and a failed request in a browser that reports itself offline (`navigator.onLine === false`) is not repeated at all. The Service Worker remembers for 5 s that the store was out of reach for a file, so that the page's own question after a failed `<img>` or `<video>` ("why?", §7.4) is answered from that instead of a second round.
5. **A listing is also text that someone else chose.** No name out of it reaches the page unless it has the form of a name gclone gives — `[cs]-<16 hex>-<16 hex>-<8 hex>` for index objects, the keyfile names `keyfile_candidates` accepts — which cannot be a sentence; any other object is "an object that is not gclone's (N MiB)". The one free text that is shown, the vault folder's name (unlock screen, vault chooser), is cut to 64 characters on one line, control and bidirectional characters blanked.
A tab the browser killed while deriving or loading says so at the next start (two `sessionStorage` flags), with the keyfile's memory cost or the index size, instead of offering the same step again without comment.

**The unlock screen** is a real credential form (`autocomplete="username"` with the fixed value `gclone vault`, `type="password"` with `autocomplete="current-password"`; the form never submits), so that a password manager fills the passphrase on this origin and on no look-alike — the one control against Phisher (b) of §1.3 — at the price that the browser offers to save it (the password-manager row). It shows the signed-in address and the vault's folder (a habit check, not a control) and two static sentences: that gclone never asks for a code at google.com/device, and where the passphrase may be saved. The sign-in screen carries the same code sentence, the old home page's text, the bookmark advice, and the status line.

**File delivery: one mechanism.** The Service Worker answers same-origin `GET /v/<22 characters>` — and, besides `/seal-key`, touches nothing else — for the page's `<img>`, `<video>`, `<audio>`, `<iframe>`, `fetch()` and download navigations. The id is 128 random bits per path and unlock, which the provider adds to `stat` answers; a ticket for it arrives on the ticket port, sealed (`ticket(path)` of the core: name, size, blob location, the stream's key and header). Without a ticket the Service Worker asks the page (`need-ticket`), which — after making a new channel if the browser had restarted the Service Worker — has the vault worker issue it again; none within 3 s → `410` "This link has expired…", a refusal by the vault worker → `502` with its sentence at once. Per request: `parse_range` (one range → `206`; nothing selected → `416`; several or unreadable → `200`, whole file); upstream ranged `GET`s for exactly the ciphertext chunks that cover the range (`FileReader.cipher_start()..cipher_end()`; the 60-byte header is never requested), **one window of at most `STORE_WINDOW` = 16 MiB at a time**, the next asked for only when the consumer wants more; every network piece goes through `push()` **in slices of at most 1 MiB**, which releases plaintext only after the chunk's tag verified, already cut to the range. Both bounds are the Service Worker's own (§17.23): an engine hands a fast answer over in pieces of any size (WebKit: one piece as large as what has arrived), a piece is copied whole into the wasm memory, and a wasm memory never shrinks — with one unbounded upstream request a 1 GiB download left 942 MiB of it behind. The response is created only after the first verified bytes, so a blob that is missing, damaged from the start or unreachable is `502` with "The file could not be read from the vault: …" (§7.4's rule); a failure after that errors the stream; a broken upstream is re-requested from `resume_at()`, five failures without progress end it. For a media element's ranged request the answer and its upstream are capped at a **window** — 2 MiB after a seek, doubling to 8 MiB in sequential play — because engines rarely cancel abandoned range requests and each window costs one Drive round trip. Headers of every answer come from the file **name** through `served()` — the table of §7.4, `src/web/mime.rs`, compiled into the wasm; content is never sniffed:

| Kind (by extension) | `Content-Type` | Shown with | Response CSP |
|---|---|---|---|
| raster images, SVG | their image type | `<img>` only (script does not run in an image; opened directly, `sandbox` stops it) | `sandbox; default-src 'none'; img-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| HTML, XHTML, XML, JS, CSS, every other text format | `text/plain; charset=utf-8` | the first 512 KiB as `textContent` | `sandbox; default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| PDF | `application/pdf` | a card with "Open": a tab of its own (`target=_blank`, `rel=noopener`), in every browser — never a frame of the viewer's page | `default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'` (no `sandbox`: browsers do not show a PDF in a sandboxed frame) |
| audio, video | their media type | `<audio>`, `<video>` | `sandbox; default-src 'none'; media-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| everything else, and **every download** (`?dl=1`) | `application/octet-stream`, `attachment` | download | `sandbox; default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |

plus `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`, `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, an exact `Content-Length`, and `Content-Disposition` by `rules.rs` (§7.4): a bare `inline` for what is shown, `attachment` with the name for a download. **Why a PDF is never in a frame of the page** (§17.23): it is the one kind of vault content that is shown without `sandbox`, and in Chrome a link annotation in a framed PDF navigates the **top-level** tab — one click in the preview took the unlocked viewer to an address of the file's choosing, a ready pretext for a look-alike "enter your passphrase again" page. In a tab of its own a PDF can only take itself. **"Open in a new tab"** is offered for images, text and (as its card) PDF, not for audio and video: the answer's `sandbox` gives the browser's own media document an opaque origin that the Service Worker does not control, so its player would ask the network for `/v/<id>`. A file in a tab of its own has left the viewer: Lock and sign-out do not reach it (§15), which the card and the button's tooltip say. A download is a **plain navigation** to `/v/<id>?dl=1` that the Service Worker answers as an attachment of type `application/octet-stream` whatever the kind (iOS Safari opens a "download" that carries its real type in the tab, which would replace the unlocked viewer); the link has no `download` attribute (§7.4). There is no `blob:` URL anywhere and no vault byte is ever parsed as markup by the page. When the Service Worker is not in control, a `/v/<id>` request reaches the Cloudflare Worker, which answers `404` and learns nothing but the id. No Service Worker support (some private-browsing modes) → one sentence, and the viewer stops: there is no second delivery path.

**Lock**, by wall clock and never by a timer's own count (a frozen tab's timers do not run): `IDLE_LOCK` = 15 minutes since the last input (`pointerdown`, `keydown`, `touchstart`, `wheel`, and `timeupdate` of a playing media element), `HIDDEN_LOCK` = 5 minutes since the page was hidden (background audio keeps it open; five minutes after it stops, the rule applies), checked on `visibilitychange`, `pageshow`, `focus`, `resume`, on every input event before it counts as input, and every 15 s; **any** restore from the back/forward cache locks, in every state; and the button. **The Lock button and Sign out are for the browser, not for one tab** (§17.23): a `BroadcastChannel('gclone')` carries two words, `lock` and `out`, and nothing of the vault. The button posts `lock` — every other unlocked tab locks ("The vault was locked in another tab."); a lock by the clock is each tab's own. Sign out posts `out` after the Worker's answer (the cookie is gone by then; `lock` if the sign-out did not arrive) — an unlocked tab locks and a tab at the passphrase reloads, and both end at the sign-in screen ("You signed out in another tab."). A tab that leaves (`pagehide`: closed, reloaded, taken to another address) tells the Service Worker `forget` if it was unlocked. **Registrations that are not the viewer's** (0.5.0, §17.27): before it registers `/sw.js` for `/`, the page unregisters every Service Worker registration of this origin that has another script or another scope — the honest deployment has exactly one, and anything else is what someone who served the origin before left behind (a worker for `/callback` alone would take the way back from Google). A page whose Service Worker is gone (the site's data was cleared) locks and says so instead of failing every file; so does a page that is told by the Service Worker that the sign-in is over (`session-ended`: a file could not be read because `/web/refresh` answered `no_session`, `email_not_allowed` or `invalid_grant`) — it ends at the sign-in screen, as it does when the vault worker finds out at a refresh. The shell's listeners are registered in the capture phase before `app.js` exists: when a lock is due, the app root is hidden in the same task and the event that woke the page reaches nothing. **A lock is a reload** — hide the app, tell the Service Worker `forget` (tickets, token, ports, the seal's key pair), end the workers, `history.replaceState(null, '', '/')`, `location.reload()`; the session cookie remains, so the next screen is the passphrase. (A variant that tears down without reloading is specified in the design and not built; it is needed only if a phone cannot derive again after a reload — the device test, `worker/README.md`.) **Sign out** is the same with `POST /web/logout` first, and ends at a static screen that says that the browser is still signed in to Google, with a link to Google's sign-out.
