A fatal error while the list is shown locks and names the reason on the next screen. **After a deployment** the Service Worker answers a ticket of another build with `reload` to the page that sent it — and to no other — naming its own build; a page of that build ignores the message, a page of another build locks ("The viewer was updated."). **A page whose own files did not arrive** shows one screen and nothing to type into: in the markup every screen but the first is `hidden` (the shell keeps the attribute in step, so one screen shows without the style sheet too), the unlock fields sit in a `<fieldset disabled>` that the shell enables, the form is `method="dialog"` (it cannot be sent anywhere, with or without the page's policy), and the first screen says after ten seconds — a CSS animation, no script — that the viewer did not start.

**Nothing of the vault's names where the browser keeps it.** The address is `/`, the title is "gclone", `history.state` holds `{e, n, depth, began}` (§7.4), files are addressed by random ids, and a file in a tab of its own is titled by its id (no name travels with an answer that is shown, §7.4). What a visit leaves behind: the cookie (not after sign-out), `localStorage` `gclone.sort` (not after sign-out), those history entries. Nothing derived from the passphrase, no name, no index object. Outside the viewer's control: a passphrase the owner saved in the browser, the browser's Google session, the download list (a downloaded file is there under its name).

**Headers** — one set, `worker/src/headers.json`, which the Worker puts on `/` and `/callback` and the build writes into `dist/_headers` for `/a/*` and `/sw.js` (a worker script is governed by the policy of its own response):
```
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; media-src 'self';
  frame-src 'self'; worker-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://www.googleapis.com; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types gclone
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer                     X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff              X-Frame-Options: DENY
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin          Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=()
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
```
Against §7.4's page policy: `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (Chrome refuses to compile wasm without it; `eval` still throws), `worker-src`, the Drive host in `connect-src`, Trusted Types, and no `blob:` anywhere. Each context creates one Trusted Types policy named `gclone` whose `createScriptURL` returns its input only for a fixed list of this build's own script URLs; the sinks used are `new Worker()`, `serviceWorker.register()`, `importScripts()` and one `script.src`; no HTML sink is used. No third-party resource of any kind, no COEP, no `SharedArrayBuffer`. No long cache lifetime on the static files (a rule would also apply to the `404` of a file a deployment has not propagated yet): they revalidate with an `ETag`. The per-build directory `/a/<16 hex>/` keeps a loaded page from mixing the files of two deployments.

**The bundle** (`node worker/viewer/build.mjs`, Node built-ins only → `worker/dist/`, what `wrangler deploy` uploads): `index.html` (`viewer/index.html` with the shared body in `<template id="app">` and the build id stamped in), `sw.js` (stamped), `_headers`, and `a/<build>/` with `app.js`, `app.css`, `icon.svg` (from `src/web/assets/`, byte for byte), the hosted-only scripts and styles of `worker/viewer/`, `core.js`, `core.wasm`, and `manifest.json` = `{build, commit, files: {name: sha256}, rustc, tag, version, wasm_bindgen}`. The build id is the first 16 hex digits of a SHA-256 over every input. Deterministic: no time stamps, sorted keys, `\n`; two builds of the same inputs are the same tree. `worker/scripts/check-dist.mjs` is the gate before a `dist/` is packed, unpacked or deployed: exactly `index.html`, `sw.js`, `_headers` and `a/` with one build directory (no `_redirects`, which would act before the Worker); every file of the build directory listed in the manifest with its SHA-256, with an extension of `js`, `css`, `svg`, `wasm`, `json`, at most 25 MiB; `_headers` equal to the text generated from `headers.json`; the page with the status marker exactly once, every loaded resource under `/a/<build>/`, no inline script or style, no event-handler attribute, no `<base>`, no `<meta http-equiv>`; `sw.js` naming the same build; the Drive host named once, in `drive.js`; and for a release (`--release <tag>`) the manifest's `tag`, `version` and a clean `commit`.

**The canonical build, and how it gets deployed** (the supply-chain row of §1.3). The bundle that is deployed is **not** built on the owner's machine: `.github/workflows/release.yml` builds it on the tag, in the job `viewer-bundle`, whose steps are exactly — checkout (pinned by commit, no credentials kept); the tag equals the version in `Cargo.toml` and `web-core/Cargo.toml`; the pinned Rust toolchain with the wasm target; `cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version <the lockfile's> --locked`; `sh web-core/build.sh`; `node worker/viewer/build.mjs`; `node worker/scripts/check-dist.mjs --release <tag>`; pack (`tar --format=ustar --sort=name --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner --mode=… --mtime='UTC 2020-01-01' | gzip -n` → `gclone-viewer-<version>.tar.gz`); `actions/attest-build-provenance` (pinned by commit) on the tarball; upload. **No `npm ci`, no wrangler, no browser, no other action**: no install script of an npm package ever runs in the workspace that produces the viewer's static files. (**That sentence is about the static files and no more** — it used to end "the bytes that will see the passphrase", which says too much (§17.27). The Worker script is not built here, not attested and not compared with anything after the upload: wrangler and esbuild bundle it on the owner's machine after `npm ci`, and it is the Worker that answers `/` — the bundle's `index.html` with one line put in, under headers of the Worker's choosing. §1.3, the supply-chain row.) Its permissions, and only its: `contents: read`, `id-token: write`, `attestations: write`. The job `viewer-test` (macOS) then runs the smoke test and the browser suite against exactly those bytes, and `release` (named `publish` until it stopped publishing: since 0.5.0 it creates a **draft**, and the release is published by `scripts/release-sign-macos.sh` on the owner's Mac, §17.28) — which needs both, and the binaries — adds the tarball to the draft release and to `SHA256SUMS` and names the build id in the notes. `SHA256SUMS` is a convenience; **the trust anchor is the attestation**, which GitHub stores outside the release's files and which names the repository, the workflow file, the ref and the commit. Releases have to be **immutable** (a repository setting, which no file of the repository can turn on — and which the deploy scripts therefore check, below): the attestation follows the tag, and a tag that can be moved can be built and attested again. The binaries are attested the same way since 0.5.0 — each archive in the `build` job that made it, verified once more by the `release` job before the draft is created and by the owner's release script before it is published (`--source-ref`, `--source-digest`) — and `install.sh` verifies that attestation where `gh` is at hand (§1.3, the CLI's supply-chain row; §17.26).
On the owner's machine (never CI, which has no Cloudflare credentials), in `worker/`:
```
node scripts/fetch-viewer.mjs v0.4.0                      download, verify the attestation, unpack to dist/     (before npm ci)
npm ci && npm run deploy                                  check-config; the release check again; wrangler deploy
node scripts/verify-deployed.mjs https://<host> v0.4.0    compare what the host serves with the release
```
All three take their expected bytes from one function, `releaseBundle(tag)` (`scripts/release-bundle.mjs`; Node built-ins and the `gh` command, no npm package): download the tag's tarball into a new temporary directory; `gh attestation verify <tarball> --repo <owner>/<repo> --signer-workflow <owner>/<repo>/.github/workflows/release.yml --source-ref refs/tags/<tag> --deny-self-hosted-runners` — **failing closed**: no `gh`, no attestation, another workflow, another ref → stop; **(0.5.0, §17.26)** with a `commit`, also `--source-digest <commit>`: `fetch-viewer` and `check-release`, the two that deploy, pass the commit their git checkout is at (`git rev-parse HEAD` below `worker/`; none outside a checkout, and they say so) — the Worker's code is deployed from the checkout and the viewer from the release, and both have to be the release's commit; a mismatch is told apart from a failed attestation ("…is attested, but it was not built from commit X, which this checkout is at … `git checkout <tag>` … if this checkout IS at the tag, the tag was moved"); then `gh release verify-asset <tag> <tarball> --repo <owner>/<repo>` — GitHub's own attestation of the release, which exists only for an **immutable** release and binds the tag, its commit and the digests of its files — failing closed as well, except for a release named in `GCLONE_MUTABLE_RELEASE=<tag>` (one that was published before the repository made releases immutable: v0.4.0), for which the scripts go on with a warning; unpack with a reader of its own that takes plain files under a bundle's names and refuses everything else (a link, a path outside the layout, an extended header, a name twice); `check-dist --release`; return `{path, build, files: {path: sha256}}`. `fetch-viewer` replaces `worker/dist/` with that tree and prints the version, the build id, the commit and the tarball's SHA-256 — what a later check is compared with. `npm run deploy` = `check-config`, then `scripts/check-release.mjs` — `releaseBundle(<the tag in dist's manifest>)` once more and a comparison of every file (nothing missing, nothing extra, every hash equal) — and only then `wrangler deploy`: a `dist/` that anything changed after the fetch, one without a tag, and the placeholder do not deploy this way. When `dist/` and the release differ, the message says which side it looks like: the same build and commit on both sides — `./dist` was changed, fetch again; another build or commit in the release than in `dist/` — **the release was changed after it was fetched** (a tag that was moved and built again), and the advice is *not* to fetch again, which would deploy exactly the swapped bytes (before 0.5.0 the message said "Fetch it again" in both cases). `check-release` also lists what in the working tree below `worker/` differs from the commit. `verify-deployed` calls `releaseBundle(tag)` a third time and compares it with the host: `/` and `/callback` (the release's page around one plain-text status line), `/sw.js` and every file of the build directory, each with the header set of the bundle's `_headers`; it never reads `worker/dist/`. **What it proves**: the static files and the page served to these requests are the release's. **What it cannot prove**: that a modified Worker does not answer other requests differently — it asks with its own `User-Agent` and without a browser's headers, and it checks that the release's eight headers are there, not that nothing else is; and **nothing about any browser**: what a hostile serving party left in a browser's profile (a Service Worker, a cached page) is not on the host (§1.3, the Cloudflare row). Development: `npm run viewer:build` builds locally, `npm run deploy:dev` deploys whatever `dist/` holds (the placeholder too) without the release check and says so in one line with the manifest's `rustc` and `tag`; `verify-deployed --dist <dir>` compares against a local build. The viewer's info panel shows version and build — reported by the page about itself: a convenience, not evidence. Reproducibility as known: repeated builds on one Mac, in different directories, give identical wasm bytes (path remapping); Linux against macOS is unknown (CI's `wasm-repro` job reports it), which is why the release's Linux build is the canonical one.

**Tests** (§13 item 8b): the main crate's units for tickets, `rules.rs` and the two gates; `web-core/tests/parity.rs` (the reader against the SQL-backed `Vault`); `web-core/test/run.sh` (the wasm in Node against vaults written by the native release binary); the Worker's `seal` / `web` tests and contract cases; `check-config`, `check-dist` and the release tooling against a stand-in `gh`; `smoke.mjs` under `wrangler dev`; the data layer and the seal (`seal.js`) in Node, the first against a fake Drive; and the browser suite (`worker/test/e2e/`) in the installed Google Chrome and Playwright's WebKit and Firefox **on macOS** — Playwright's Linux WebKit has another media stack than Safari, and every WebKit number in the tests was measured on the macOS build.

**Limits.** Measured to 100,000 files (15 MB of index per visit, about 100 MiB of wasm memory); the index is downloaded on every unlock (no cache in v1). The unlock needs the keyfile's 256 MiB for a moment. A download needs the tab to stay open, on a phone in the foreground; a download in progress continues after Lock. A file opened in a tab of its own stays open after Lock and sign-out. A refresh loads at most 64 MiB of new index. Every visit is a fresh device (§1.3, Malicious Google). **Never deployed**: whether the web client's token sees a vault created through the device client, production asset routing and `_headers`, real Drive from a browser (authenticated ranged reads, CORS), Safari's cookie handling, and everything on a phone are unverified; the list is `worker/README.md`, "First deployment: what to check", and the residual risks are in §15.

### 7.6 `gclone serve restic` — a restic repository on Drive (0.5.0, §17.24)

restic keeps a repository — its own encrypted, deduplicated, content-addressed files — behind a small HTTP protocol (its "REST backend", version 2). `gclone serve restic` speaks that protocol in front of Drive: restic contributes everything about the repository, gclone the sign-in (no OAuth setup), token refresh through the Worker, and the Drive client (resumable uploads, retries, pacing). **The vault is bypassed**: no index, no keys, no passphrase, no `config.json`, no state, no lock; the files live in the tree of §3.4. The store is generic over `B: Backend` and uses `list_strict`, `stat`, `get`, `put`, `trash`, `create_folder` and `new_ids`. `list_strict` is the one addition to the trait (§17.25): `list`, but `NotFound` where the store answers "not found" for the folder itself — `DriveBackend`: a `404` on any page — instead of the empty listing that `list` makes of it; its default is `list`. Nothing else of the Drive client changed.

```
gclone serve restic --stdio [--append-only] REPO      restic -o rclone.program=gclone -r rclone:REPO …
gclone serve restic --port N [--append-only]          restic -r rest:http://127.0.0.1:N/REPO/ …
```
`--b2-hard-delete` is accepted and ignored (hidden), so restic's default arguments (`serve restic --stdio --b2-hard-delete <remote>`) work and `-o rclone.program=gclone` alone is enough. Exactly one of `--stdio` and `--port` (1..=65535); `REPO` is required with `--stdio` and refused with `--port`. `--json` is refused (§7.1). There is no wrapper command: the short form plus `RESTIC_REPOSITORY` and `RESTIC_PACK_SIZE` is short, and tools that drive restic could not use one. Recommended pack size: 64 MiB (`--pack-size 64`): every file costs API calls, and `check` / `prune` list every pack.

**Start-up** (`cli/serve.rs`), in this order: clap (a bad name is exit 2 before anything else); `--stdio` with a terminal as stdin or stdout → `Usage`; `Paths::resolve` → `secret_store().load()` → a refresh token (else `ConfigError::NotLoggedIn` shown as "This device is not signed in to Google. Run `gclone login` first (gclone serve restic needs the sign-in, not the vault passphrase)." → exit 4; unsafe permissions → the `InsecurePermissions` text, exit 4) → `cli::drive_backend(.., TRANSFERS_DEFAULT, cache = true)`. No network request is made before serving. A signed-in device whose vault was never unlocked (`keys: []`), or that has no `config.json` — the state after a `gclone login` stopped at the passphrase question — works. `cli::run` does not offer `gclone login` after a failure of this command (restic is at its stdin, not a person).

**`--stdio`: HTTP/2 over the two pipes.** `restic::stdio::claim()` duplicates descriptors 0 and 1 (`F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`), then points **descriptor 1 at stderr** — a stray `println!` of any code in the process cannot put a byte into the HTTP/2 stream — and descriptor 0 at `/dev/null`. The connection is `tokio::io::join` of two `tokio::fs::File`s over the duplicates (they work on pipes; reads and writes run on the blocking pool), served by `hyper::server::conn::http2` with `max_concurrent_streams(H2_MAX_STREAMS = 1024)` (restic has this one connection and cannot open a second, which is what Go's client does when it runs out of streams), `initial_stream_window_size(H2_STREAM_WINDOW = 1 MiB)` and `initial_connection_window_size(H2_CONN_WINDOW = 64 MiB)`. The windows differ on purpose: hyper's default gives the connection the window of one stream, and an upload that waits for Drive — its body is read only as fast as Drive takes it — would hold the whole connection and stall every other upload and restic's lock refresh. No keep-alive pings; gclone never calls `graceful_shutdown`, so it never sends GOAWAY; a failed response body resets its own stream only. No authentication: the pipe belongs to the restic process that started gclone. restic's readiness probe (`GET /file-<n>`) matches no route and is answered `404` without touching Drive or the token.
- **It ends only when the connection ends** — stdin reached EOF because restic exited, or the pipe broke: exit 0. Everything restic was told with a `200` is durable before the `200` was sent. Uploads that were not answered are **taken back first** (`App::close` → `Repo::close`): every uncommitted attempt is cancelled, and the process waits — at most `EXIT_GRACE` = 10 s — until each has ended the way a cancelled upload ends (aborted, or its object trashed again; a stored index stays — "Uploads", below). With nothing in flight the exit is immediate. **restic does not wait for this**: it exits without waiting for its backend program, on the normal path and after SIGINT / SIGTERM alike (0.19.1, measured: restic gone after 1 ms, the lock trashed 290 ms later), so the take-back runs in a gclone that has outlived its restic — which the stop of a unit does not prevent, because gclone ignores SIGTERM (next item). Two consequences: where the environment kills leftover processes the moment restic exits — restic as PID 1 of a container, the teardown of a CI step — the take-back does not happen, and a lock restic was never answered for stays until `restic unlock`; and a restic started in the same instant can still find that lock and say "already locked" once. The listener does the same after Ctrl-C, SIGTERM and SIGHUP.
- **SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP are ignored** from the moment the pipes are claimed (`cli::DETACHED` for the Ctrl-C loop, `SIG_IGN` for the other two). restic reacts to SIGINT / SIGTERM by removing its lock *through the backend*, and starts the backend in its own process group so that a terminal's Ctrl-C does not reach it — but `systemctl stop`, a shutdown or a `kill` of the unit signal both, and a gclone that died there would leave a lock that blocks exclusive commands on every machine until `restic unlock`.
- **stderr** is shown by restic line by line, prefixed `rclone: `: gclone is silent unless it answers an error. One function writes there, `restic::note`: `gclone: <line>`, write errors ignored (stderr closes when restic exits first), an identical line not repeated within `NOTE_REPEAT` = 60 s. A line is written for an answer of `401`, `403` (layout, an absent repository on a listing, Drive's reasons — not append-only, `Host`, `Origin`, "exists"), `500`, `503`, `507`; nothing for `2xx`, `400`, `404`, `416`. `ui::init_logging` sets `log_internal_errors(false)`: tracing's default reports a failed log write with `eprintln!`, which panics on a closed stderr, and the release profile aborts on panic.

**`--port N`: HTTP/1.1 on loopback** (restic's `rest:http://` transport is Go's plain client, which does not speak HTTP/2 without TLS). `web::bind_v6(N, V6::Required)`: 127.0.0.1 and [::1], and **if `[::1]:N` is in use, start-up fails** (exit 1, `port N is in use on [::1]`); a machine without an IPv6 loopback serves on 127.0.0.1 alone. Reason: restic sends its credentials unasked on the first request, and with `localhost` Go dials `::1` first — another local user holding `[::1]:N` would receive the token. The shared accept loop of §7.4 with `LISTENER_CONNECTIONS` = 64. A connection that has sent no request head holds one of the 64 like restic's own, until the loop's 15 s header time-out: a local process without the token can keep them filled and restic waiting — **the token protects the data, not the availability of the listener** (§15; a web page cannot do it: a browser sends a request head and is answered `401` / `403` with `Connection: close` at once). The repository is the first path segment (`/<repo>/…`, the same name rule); every repository of the signed-in account is served. Checks on every request, in this order: (1) `web::host_allowed` with `127.0.0.1:N`, `localhost:N` and, when bound, `[::1]:N`, else `403`; (2) no `Origin` header at all (restic sends none; browsers do on cross-site writes), else `403`; (3) `Authorization: Basic` — exactly one — whose password equals the token (`util::ct_eq`; any user name), else `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="gclone"`. **A request refused by these is answered at once with `Connection: close`, and its body is never read.** The token is 16 random bytes in hex, new at every start, printed on stdout with the three lines a user needs (only `127.0.0.1` is printed) and never written to disk. A loopback port is reachable by every local user and, through a browser, by any web page (cross-site requests, DNS rebinding): without the token they could read ciphertext, plant a lock, and trash everything. A timer looks once a second whether `secrets.json` still exists: after `gclone logout` the listener says `this device was signed out: stopped` and exits 4. Ctrl-C, **SIGTERM and SIGHUP** — what a service manager, `kill`, `docker stop` and a closing terminal send; `listen` installs handlers for the two (`tokio::signal::unix`; not for one the process was started to ignore, as under `nohup`), whose default action would end the process at once, without the take-back and with the status of a killed process — stop it the same way: `web::serve` returns, `App::close` takes back what was not answered (`EXIT_GRACE`), exit 0. A second Ctrl-C: 130.

**Routes.** The raw request path is matched byte for byte, nothing is percent-decoded (`restic::proto::route`); stdio has the prefix `/`, the listener `/<repo>/`:

| Path after the prefix | Methods |
|---|---|
| (empty) | `POST` — with `create=true` in the query |
| `config` | `HEAD`, `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE` |
| `<type>/`, type ∈ `data keys locks snapshots index` | `GET` |
| `<type>/<name>`, name `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` | `HEAD`, `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE` |

Anything else — the probe, an upper-case name, `..`, `%2e`, an extra segment — is `404` **without a Drive call**; another method on a known path is `405` with `Allow`. No `Server` header is sent (restic changes behaviour on `Server: rclone/…`); nothing is compressed; error answers carry one line of `text/plain`.

**Statuses** (rest-server's behaviour unless noted; `restic::proto::status`):

| Request | Situation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `POST ?create=true` | folders created, or all there already | 200 |
| `POST` (empty path) | without `create=true` | 400 |
| `HEAD` | present | 200 + `Content-Length`, no body |
| `GET` file / config | no `Range` | 200 + `Content-Length` |
| | `bytes=a-` / `bytes=a-b`, `a < size` | 206 + `Content-Range: bytes a-e/size` + exact `Content-Length` (`e = min(b, size-1)`: a range past the end is answered truncated, which restic treats as the error it is; without an exact `Content-Length` restic takes a bounded range for a permanent error) |
| | `a ≥ size` | 416 + `Content-Range: bytes */size` |
| | a file of size 0 | 200, empty, whatever `Range` says |
| `HEAD` / `GET config` | no repository, or one without a config (also while its folders are incomplete — `restic init` then completes them) | 404 |
| `HEAD` / `GET` file | repository or file absent | 404 |
| `GET <type>/` | tree complete (with or without config) | 200, `Content-Type: application/vnd.x.restic.rest.v2`, `[{"name":"…","size":N},…]` sorted by name, `[]` when empty, `Content-Length` set |
| | **repository absent** (differs from rest-server on purpose) | **403** — never 404, which restic reads as an empty folder |
| | a missing, duplicate or trashed folder | 403 |
| | any other failure — also a `404` from Drive for the listing of a folder that is there (R2) | 503 — never an empty or partial list |
| `POST` file / config | stored, verified, confirmed | 200 |
| | an identical file is there already | 200, nothing written |
| | `config` exists with other content; a name exists with another size | 403 |
| | no `Content-Length` | 411 |
| | SHA-256 of the body ≠ name; body not of the announced length | 400 |
| | Drive stored something else (size or md5) — the copy is trashed | 500 |
| | repository absent | 404 |
| | Drive storage full; Drive names the daily upload limit, or the write breaker tripped | 507 |
| `DELETE` | trashed (`index/`, `keys/`: and no longer listed), or nothing of that name | 200 |
| | `--append-only` and not `locks/<name>` | 403 |
| | `config`, right after a `POST config` that was refused: the config is another init's and is kept ("Deletes") | 403 |
| | repository absent | 404 |
| any but `HEAD` / `GET config` | tree incomplete or ambiguous | 403 |
| `HEAD` / `GET config` | duplicate folders, differing configs, a config with folders missing | 403 |
| any | `RateLimited`, `Transient`, `SessionLost`, `Io`, `AuthError::Network` / `AuthError::Io`, a confirming listing that did not arrive, a `404` from Drive for a folder that is there | 503 |
| any | every other `AuthError` (Google no longer accepts the login) | 401 |
| any | `Fatal`, `QuotaExceeded` of the daily download or the project's API quota, `AppNotAuthorized` | 403 |
| any | a task failed | 500 |

Why these classes: restic retries every failure for up to 15 minutes per operation except `401`, `403`, `404`, `416` and `507`, which it treats as permanent (one attempt in `rest:` mode, five over about 15 seconds in stdio mode). A dead login, a full Drive, an append-only refusal, a broken layout and a daily quota cannot clear within a run and must end it within seconds; a throttled or flaky Drive is retried. `403` has no "empty" and no "does not exist" reading on any route.

**The tree** (`restic::layout`; rules in §3.4). `resolve` lists from the top — top level, each candidate root, the repository folder, `data/` — four listings, five with two roots; entries whose own `trashed` flag is set are dropped first. `HEAD config`, which starts every restic command, **always resolves from the top**: there is no shortcut through a remembered folder ID, so a folder that was renamed or moved in the Drive UI while the name was created anew elsewhere stops being served under the name; when any folder ID differs from the stored layout, the caches below are dropped. Other requests resolve only when no layout is stored, or after one was dropped (a folder found trashed, a put that Drive refused, a resolution that found the tree ambiguous). `POST ?create=true` creates what is missing (`CREATE_FANOUT` = 8 at a time) and returns once a resolution **lists** the complete tree (`LIST_CONFIRM_WAIT`, else `503`), because the next restic command is a new process that finds the tree by listing; about a minute at the write pacer's rates, once per repository.

**The ID cache** (`restic::store::Repo`). Per folder — `keys`, `locks`, `snapshots`, `index`, each of the 256 shards, and the repository folder for `config` — what the newest installed listing showed (not trashed, named by the grammar; in shard `xx` only names that begin with `xx`), plus this process's own uploads that no listing has shown yet (kept for `OWN_GRACE` = 10 min, for downloads and deletes only, **never added to a list response**). Sets: every ID this process trashed or tried to, for as long as a listing that shows it can be list lag (*hidden*; R8); uploads not yet committed (*inflight*); own packs no listing has shown (*unlisted*); trashed index and key files a listing may still show (*leaving*); unacknowledged uploads that may still be on Drive — a clean-up that failed, or an index that is not taken back (*orphans*; "Uploads"). *Visible* = not hidden, not inflight. The *canonical* object of a name is the visible one with the smallest `(createdTime, id)`, so every machine picks the same; objects of one name that differ in size or md5 get one stderr line. "A listing started after X" is decided by a counter (`Repo::tick`), not by clock resolution. Rules:
- **R1** Every `GET <type>/` runs its own listing after the request arrived; the answer is that listing's visible entries, one per name, and nothing remembered. No coalescing.
- **R2** An empty listing is checked: `stat(folder)` must show an existing, untrashed folder, else the layout is dropped and the answer is `403` (`list` answers "empty" for a trashed or deleted parent — the rule of §3.3). **A `404` from Drive for a listing is not "empty" either** (`list_strict`, on every path that lists: `GET <type>/`, a miss, a confirmation, the resolution of the tree): the folder is `stat`ed — gone or trashed → `403` as above; still there → `503`, and restic asks again. Drive is only documented to answer `404` there when the parent is gone, but one stray answer must not read as "no snapshots" (on which `prune` trashes every pack) or "no locks"; while the tree is resolved it is `503` too, never "no such repository" (on which `restic init` would make a second one). `data/`: all 256 shards (`LIST_FANOUT` = 8 at a time), **then** one listing of `data/`, which must show exactly those 256 folders — that one call covers every shard that listed nothing. Cost: 257 listings per `check` / `prune`.
- **R3** `HEAD config` resolves from the top. `GET config` uses the entry of the last resolution.
- **R4** `GET` / `HEAD` of a file: a visible cache entry, else a listing of the folder that **started after this request arrived** decides — found, or `404`. Waiters on one folder take turns; one listing serves all that it is new enough for.
- **R5** `NotFound` from Drive for a cached ID (deleted for good): drop the entry, list the folder, try once with what the listing shows, else `404`.
- **R6** `DELETE`: "Deletes", below.
- **R7** Negative results are never cached.
- **R8** Trashed objects are filtered three times: by the query (`trashed = false`), by the `trashed` flag of each returned entry (an index that lags behind the resource), and by *hidden* (this process's own deletes hold without any assumption about Drive). An ID leaves *hidden* when a listing that started after its trash omits it (A2; a listing that shows it afterwards is believed — the file was restored from the Drive trash), or — an ID that a listing still shows `HIDDEN_RECHECK` = 30 s after its trash — when `stat` says that it is not in the trash (asked once per ID and `HIDDEN_RECHECK`; in the trash: hidden on). A hidden orphan stays hidden. A file restored by hand is thereby a file again for a listener that keeps running, as it is for every other machine.
- **R9** An absent repository is never an empty listing: `403` on every attempt, also right after the layout was dropped.

What can go stale: another machine's delete (through its own gclone: `forget`, `prune`, `key remove`, unlock, lock refresh) leaves a cached ID that **still downloads** — Drive serves trashed files by ID — until this process lists the folder again. That is safe: the bytes are the right bytes (the name is their hash), restic decides what *exists* from listings, which are fresh, and the commands that delete hold an exclusive lock. A cached lock can be reported as a conflict for a moment after it was released, never the reverse. The identical-upload shortcut `stat`s first, so a stale entry never turns into a false "stored". There is deliberately no `stat` before every `GET`: one more API call per pack on every restore, to turn "served a file that was deleted seconds ago" into a `404` restic does not need.

**Consistency.** restic's mutual exclusion is: list `locks/`, create a lock, wait 200 ms, list again. `prune` decides what is garbage from the listings of `snapshots/`, `index/` and `data/`; `backup` decides what it need not upload from `index/`. Drive does not document its listings as immediately consistent, and this code base treats list lag as real (§5.3). No acknowledgement therefore relies on timing; each waits for a listing — the first at once, then every `LIST_CONFIRM_POLL` (250 ms, doubling, at most 2 s) for `LIST_CONFIRM_WAIT` = 30 s, any listing of the folder counting, whoever made it — which replaces "visible everywhere within 200 ms" by two weaker assumptions: **A1**, once any listing has shown an object, later listings show it too until it is trashed; **A2**, once a listing that started after an object was trashed has omitted it, later listings omit it too (§15).
- **C1** A new file in `locks/`, `keys/`, `snapshots/`, `index/`, and `config`, is acknowledged only after a listing shows its ID. Of two processes that create conflicting locks, the one whose `POST` returned second finds the other's lock in its second listing.
- **C2** Packs are not confirmed one by one. A `POST` to `index/` or `snapshots/` is acknowledged only after **every pack this process had acknowledged before that request arrived** has been shown by a listing of its shard (only the shards concerned are listed). restic writes an index after its packs and a snapshot after its index, so every command that wrote packs ends with them listed — otherwise a `forget --prune` or `check` started seconds after a backup could list `data/` without the last packs. A pack still unlisted at the time-out is `stat`ed: missing or trashed → `403` ("a pack uploaded in this run is no longer on Drive"), remembered, so that later indexes fail at once; present → `503`. **`--port`: this bookkeeping ends with the restic run it belongs to.** The listener serves one run after another, and a pack that a run left unlisted — it was interrupted before its index — is nobody's to wait for: another machine prunes it, rightly, and holding later indexes to it failed every backup through the listener until it was restarted. A run that writes packs holds a lock from before its first pack until after its snapshot, and restic refreshes a lock by writing the new one before it removes the old one; so *unlisted* and the remembered lost packs are dropped whenever **no lock created through this process is left** — looked at when a lock is removed through it and when a listing of `locks/` is installed (every restic command begins with one); a lock is "left" while it is this process's own upload, shown by the newest listing and not hidden. A pack whose upload was on its way at that moment does not enter the new bookkeeping (`State::run`). The `403` says "through this listener" there. `--stdio` is one run: nothing is dropped, and the `403` holds for the life of the process (restic repeats a `403` five times in that mode).
- **C3** A removed lock is gone for this process at once (*hidden*), and for others as soon as Drive's listing follows: a false conflict for a moment, never a missed one.
- **C4** A `DELETE` of an `index/` or `keys/` file is acknowledged only after a listing that started after the trash no longer shows it (*leaving*; a retried `DELETE` waits again). After `prune` on machine A, a `backup` on machine B that still got the old index would skip blobs that live only in pruned packs — and because trashed files still download, nothing would fail until the trash is emptied. Not confirmed, and why that is safe: `locks/` (C3); `snapshots/` (a forgotten snapshot still listed elsewhere keeps data alive, nothing wanted is lost); `data/` (a pruned pack still listed is an unreferenced pack); `config`.
- **C5** A listed file can be loaded: by the listed ID, also when trashed meanwhile; after a permanent delete, a new listing and `404`.

**Uploads** (`Repo::save`; the HTTP layer hands over body frames through a channel, so restic is read only as fast as Drive takes the bytes). (1) `Content-Length` is required. (2) A name that exists: a visible entry of the same size is `stat`ed; if it is there, untrashed and of that size, the body is read to its end and hashed — SHA-256 = name → **`200` without writing**, else `400`; only entries of another size → `403`; nothing visible → upload without a look at Drive (should the name exist after all, the result is two identical objects, which listings collapse and a delete removes together). `config`: always after a fresh listing; identical (size and md5, or the bytes when Drive has no md5) → `200`, different → `403` — with one stderr line (another init was first, and what to do about the key file this one left: §3.4), and remembered for `CONFIG_REFUSAL` = 60 s for the `DELETE config` that follows ("Deletes"). **Nothing is ever overwritten, in any mode.** (3) One pre-generated ID. `len ≤ SMALL_MAX` (4 MiB): buffered, hashed, one replayable `PutBody::Small`. Larger: `PutBody::Stream` — a pump cuts the body into parts of exactly `PART_SIZE`, hashing as it goes, and takes a channel permit **before** it fills a part, so one upload holds two parts at most. (4) **Before anything exists on Drive**: SHA-256 of the body = name (every type but `config`) and the length is the announced one — in the streamed path **the last part is withheld** until both hold; otherwise the put gets an error in its place, the session is abandoned and no object appears (`400`). (5) After the put: `size` and — when Drive returns one — `md5` equal what was sent (else the object is trashed, `500`), and `trashed == false` (a put into a trashed folder is stored where no listing shows it: `403`, layout dropped). (6) C1 and C2. (7) **Commit**: an upload is an *attempt* from the moment its ID is taken; it is committed — entered in the cache, a pack added to *unlisted* unless listed already — in one step after verification and confirmation, unless it was cancelled. Cancellation — the handler was dropped before the result arrived (restic reset the stream, or went away), or a `DELETE` of the name came in — is observed at two points only: before the last part is released, and after the put returned. **A put is never dropped in mid-flight** (Drive could create the object after a clean-up `trash` answered "not found"): `POST`, `DELETE` and create run in tasks of their own. An attempt that ends uncommitted and may have stored an object trashes its own ID and hides it; if that fails too, the ID is an *orphan*, trashed by the next delete of the name. Uncommitted IDs are never visible. **An index is the exception.** Once Drive has it — the put returned, size and md5 agree, its folder is not in the trash — it is *not* taken back for want of an acknowledgement: cancelled, connection closed, the confirming listing failed or came too late. An index is the one file other machines act on the moment a listing shows it: a backup elsewhere leaves out the blobs it describes and reports "saved", and an index trashed afterwards left that snapshot unrestorable until `restic repair index` (measured, §17.25). The attempt ends with its error; the object stays, a file like any other once a listing shows it, and is remembered as an orphan that is *not* hidden, so that restic's own next step — `DELETE`, then `POST` again — removes it even while no listing shows it (with `--append-only` the repeated `POST` finds it and answers `200` without writing). It is still taken back where it must not be trusted — Drive stored something else, the folder is in the trash, a pack acknowledged before it is gone (C2), the put did not say whether it stored — and when a `DELETE` of the name cancelled it. This is what keeps an interrupted lock upload — its 155 bytes are complete on arrival, restic never learns its name — from leaving a live lock for 30 minutes, and what makes restic's own retry (`DELETE`, then `POST` again) work with `--append-only`. It is also why the process does not exit the moment the pipe closes (`EXIT_GRACE`, above): an interrupted restic is gone within milliseconds, sooner than a put and the trash that takes it back.

**Downloads** (`Repo::open`): resolve the entry (R4), `web::rules::parse_range`, `backend.get` (R5). Headers are written after `get` returned, so a `404` can still be answered; the body is `web::http::Body::Stream` of exactly the announced length, and a stream that fails or ends short is a body error — HTTP/2 resets the stream, HTTP/1 cuts the connection — which restic retries.

**Deletes** (`Repo::remove`): `--append-only` and not a lock → `403` without a Drive call; `config` within `CONFIG_REFUSAL` of a refused `POST config` → `403` without a Drive call, once per refusal — restic removes a file after every upload of it that failed, and here that is the config of the init that was first: carried out, both inits "succeeded" and the first machine could no longer open its repository (§3.4; `upgrade_repo_v2` deletes first and uploads then, and is unaffected); cancel the in-flight attempts of the name (what they stored is not kept, an index included); trash every visible object of the name — from the cache, else from a new listing — and its orphans (`NotFound` is success), hide them; C4 for `index/` and `keys/`; `200`, also when nothing was there. A delete is always the trash (§3.2): recoverable for about 30 days, space freed afterwards. Under `--append-only` everything else is unchanged — `POST` never overwrites in any mode, create and reads work, the server's own clean-up of its unacknowledged uploads is not a client delete — so `backup` and `check` work and `forget`, `prune`, `key remove` fail on their first delete.

**Bodies and errors.** An answer that did not need the request body still reads it to its end first — Go's HTTP/1 client reliably sees a status only then; the same is done over HTTP/2 — except for the listener's refusals above.

**Cost** (Drive calls): start of a restic command 4 listings; `init` 262 folder creations; `GET <type>/` 1 listing (+1 `stat` when empty), `data/` 257; a small file 1 create + 1 listing; an index the same + one listing per shard with unlisted packs; a pack 1 create or 1 session + one `PUT` per 16 MiB; a download 1; a delete 1 per object (+ a shared listing for `index/`, `keys/`). Memory: two parts (32 MiB) plus 1 MiB of window per streamed upload in flight. Every call goes through the backend's pacer; the server adds no limiter of its own.

---

## 8. Local state

### 8.1 Paths (`etcetera::choose_base_strategy()` → XDG on macOS and Linux)
```
<config>     = $GCLONE_CONFIG_DIR or ~/.config/gclone            (0700)
    config.json      0600   non-secret: which vault this device is attached to, and the auth Worker URL
<state root> = $GCLONE_STATE_DIR or ~/.local/state/gclone        (0700; left out of backups, below)
    secrets.json         0600   secret: this device's refresh token (with the auth Worker URL and e-mail) and the cached master key
    secrets.sealed       0600   0.5.0, macOS: the same document, sealed by this Mac's Secure Enclave — in place of secrets.json; a Mac's default since 0.5.1 (§8.2)
    keystore.json        0600   0.5.0: the choice made with `gclone keystore use`; absent = none made: the default (§8.2)
    keystore-trial.json  0600   0.5.0, macOS: the Secure Enclave trial's key, test value and record (§8.2)
    keystore-trial.lock, backup-note.due, keystore-note.due   0600   macOS: the lock of that record; empty markers of a once-only note that is still owed to a terminal (§8.1, §8.2)
    keystore-trial.off   0600   0.5.1, macOS: an empty marker — a run with GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0 uses this device: no trial, no sealing, no move, in any run (§8.2)
    secrets.lock         0600   0.5.0: kernel lock of whoever writes or moves the secrets (§8.3)
    CACHEDIR.TAG         0600   0.5.0: the standard cache-directory tag (below)
    token.json           0600   cached access token (belongs to the login, not to a vault)
<state>      = <state root>/<vault_id hex>                       (0700)
    state.db (+ -wal, -shm)   0600   SQLite (§8.4)
    lock                             kernel lock file (§8.3)
    index-cache/<object name>        raw ciphertext of index objects (feeds `repair`)
```
`gclone logout` deletes `token.json`, `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed` and leftover temp files of any file of the state root (below); `logout --forget` also deletes `config.json` and the vault's `<state>` directory (§2.7). `keystore.json`, `keystore-trial.json`, `keystore-trial.off`, `secrets.lock` and `CACHEDIR.TAG` stay after either: a choice, a record, a marker, a lock file and a tag, no secret; `keystore-note.due` goes with the logout (a note about secrets that are gone is owed to nobody).
`gclone serve restic` (§7.6) reads the device's secrets — `secrets.json` or `secrets.sealed` (the login; the cached key is not looked at, `keys: []` is fine) — and `token.json`, and writes only `token.json` and, on a Mac whose secrets are in the plain file, the trial's record (§8.2: a restic run from a scheduler is the session the trial has to see) — and, like every command that loads the secrets, it makes the automatic move when that trial has passed (0.5.1, §8.2). It reads no `config.json` and no `<state>`.
All files are written via temp file + `fsync` + `rename` in the same directory (`util::write_atomic`): the temp file is opened `O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW` with its final mode, never chmod-ed afterwards. The temp file is named `.<name>.tmp-<16 lowercase hex digits>`; a process killed between its creation and the rename leaves it behind as a full copy of what was being written, so whatever deletes a secret file also removes these (`util::remove_atomic_leftovers(path)`: `SecretStore::delete` — `logout` — for `token.json`, `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed`, `keystore.json` and `keystore-trial.json`, §2.7; every save of a `login`, `gclone keystore use` and the automatic move, under the secrets lock, for `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed` and `keystore.json`). Nothing sweeps them at other times — a concurrent writer's temp file must not be taken away. Directories are created with mode 0700 at creation (`util::create_dir_private` = `DirBuilder::new().recursive(true).mode(0o700)`), not created and then tightened.

**Why the secrets are not in `<config>`.** `~/.config` is what dotfile repositories, synced home folders and selective backups pick up; the master key cannot be rotated in v1 (re-keying is deferred), so one leaked copy is permanent. The state root is machine-local state. `secrets.json` must never be copied to another machine — a new device gets its own login and unlocks with the passphrase. gclone itself never syncs `<config>`, `<state root>` or a directory vault's directory, even when the sync root contains them, and refuses a sync root inside one of them (§5.5.3).

**Strict loading** (like ssh `StrictModes`; `config::read_private`, used for `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed` and `keystore.json` alike): before reading `secrets.json`, `lstat` the state root and `fstat` the file opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`; each must be owned by the effective uid and have no group or other permission bits (`mode & 0o077 == 0`), else `ConfigError::InsecurePermissions(path)` (exit 4 with the chmod hint of §2.8) — nothing is read and nothing is repaired silently. An absent file is simply "no secrets" (`Ok(None)`). `token.json` gets the same check; a failure there only discards the cache.

**Backups (0.5.0, §17.28).** The plain `secrets.json` in a backup is the vault key for good — the key cannot be rotated in v1 — so the state root is kept out of backups as far as a tool can be told:
- **macOS**: the directory carries the extended attribute `com.apple.metadata:com_apple_backup_excludeItem` (the 61-byte binary property list of the string `com.apple.backupd` that `tmutil addexclusion` writes; set with `setxattr`, `keystore::macos::exclude_from_backups`). On the **directory**, because the files in it are replaced by rename and an attribute on a file is lost with the first one; measured: it covers the files in the directory and below, and survives a rename inside. It is set, when missing, by every `save` (`login`), by every move and by the first load of the secrets in a process — so a Mac that only ever runs `sync` gets it with the first run of this version. This also covers `state.db` (plaintext paths) and `token.json`.
- **Every platform**: `CACHEDIR.TAG` with the standard signature line. restic, borg and GNU tar leave such a directory out when asked to (`--exclude-caches`); nothing honours it unasked. **Linux has no attribute that backup tools honour by default**: the documentation names the flags (`--exclude-caches`, `--exclude-if-present CACHEDIR.TAG`; `chattr +d` with `--exclude-nodump`).
- **One note, once, on a terminal** when the attribute is set on a state root that already held a login (when it becomes due in a run without a terminal it is owed — the empty marker file `backup-note.due` in the state root, created with `O_EXCL` — and shown by the next run on a terminal, which removes the marker first: whoever removes it shows the note, once, whatever runs beside it; §17.29). **It does not depend on the trial** (§17.30): `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` used to switch it off too, so a Mac whose scheduler sets that — and whose first run of 0.5.0 was the scheduler's — was never told: *"note: gclone's state folder is now left out of Time Machine backups. Backups made before today still contain secrets.json with the vault key in plain; delete it from them if they leave your hands. A restored Mac signs in again with `gclone login` and the passphrase."*
- Both are best effort (a failure is logged at debug level; `gclone keystore` shows the state) and neither changes what gclone 0.4.0 does in the same directory (§17.28). Limits: other backup tools need not honour the Time Machine attribute; APFS local snapshots contain the directory anyway, on the same encrypted disk; `CACHEDIR.TAG` also keeps unpublished work (`pending`, the outbox in `state.db`) out of a backup made with `--exclude-caches` — intended; older backups keep what they have (§15).

### 8.2 File formats
`config.json`:
```json
{ "version": 1, "vault_id": "<32 hex>", "vault_name": "gclone",
  "backend": { "kind": "drive" } | { "kind": "dir", "path": "/abs/path" },
  "auth_url": "https://gclone-auth.example.workers.dev",
  "root_id": "…", "index_id": "…", "data_id": "…" }
```
`auth_url` (Drive vaults only; the key is absent for directory vaults) is a copy of the Worker URL the device was attached through. It is not a secret; it is here so that `gclone login` after a `logout` needs no URL (§2.2). It is validated when used, like every stored URL.

`secrets.json`:
```json
{ "version": 1, "auth_url": "https://gclone-auth.example.workers.dev", "refresh_token": "1//…", "email": "me@example.com",
  "consent_ms": 1794400000000, "refresh_expires_at_ms": null, "client": "device",
  "keys": [ { "epoch": 1, "key": "<base64url-nopad 32 bytes>" } ], "min_epoch": 1 }
```
There is no OAuth client ID or secret in it — those exist only in the Worker. `client` names which of the Worker's OAuth clients issued `refresh_token` and is sent with every `/refresh` (§2.3): `"device"` for every login made by 0.2.0 or later. **A file without the field is read as a login of the legacy client** (`AuthClient::Legacy`; every `secrets.json` written before 0.2.0) and is written back without it; any other value is a load error. `version` stays 1: an older gclone ignores the field. `keys` is `[]` between a successful sign-in and the end of the vault part of `login` (commands then fail with `ConfigError::Locked`, or `NotConfigured` while no `config.json` exists, §2.8); once filled it is the cached master key, so the passphrase is never asked again on this device. For `--vault-dir` vaults the login fields `auth_url`, `refresh_token`, `email` (and `consent_ms`) are **absent** — they are `Option`s in `config::Secrets`, never empty strings. `refresh_expires_at_ms` is `null` unless Google time-limited the grant (§2.4). **Loading never validates `auth_url`**: `FileSecretStore::load` checks permissions (§8.1), JSON and `version` only. The URL is validated where it is used — `Secrets::endpoints()` (§9.10), which is called only when `has_login()` is true — so a directory vault's secrets load without any URL.
`token.json`: `{ "access_token": "…", "expires_at_ms": …, "refreshed_at_ms": … }`. It stays a plain file in both key stores: an access token of at most an hour.

#### The key store (0.5.0, §17.28; the sealed store as a Mac's default: 0.5.1, §17.30): `secrets.json` or `secrets.sealed`

A device's secrets are ONE document — the `secrets.json` document above — kept in one of two stores:

| store | where the secrets are | platforms |
|---|---|---|
| `file` | `secrets.json`, plain JSON, 0600: the version-1 format above, unchanged | all; the only store on Linux |
| `enclave` | `secrets.sealed`: that document encrypted to a Secure Enclave key of this Mac, whose blob is in the same file | macOS with a Secure Enclave — **there it is the default** |

**Which store, without anybody choosing (0.5.1, §17.30).** The owner's decision: *"test the Secure Enclave, and then that is just the default for all users"* — no command, no question.
- **A login on a Mac that is not connected seals from the start** (the save table): the key is made or picked, a value is sealed and opened again in the same process, and the secrets are written to `secrets.sealed`; a `secrets.json` never exists. Where that cannot be done — no Secure Enclave, a virtual machine, a session without access, a build without a sealer, any error — the login goes to `secrets.json` **without a word**, and one line of `gclone status` / `gclone keystore` says why (§7.3). **A login does not seal where the bar below applies**: on a device that is working from a keyed `secrets.json`, on a signed-out device whose trial is running and has not passed (a `logout` and a `login` in the middle of it), and where the trial's record holds a failure ("The bar").
- **A device that is on `secrets.json`** — every Mac that ran 0.5.0, and a login that fell back — **is tested and then moved**: the trial below is the test, and the first run after it has passed moves the secrets ("The automatic move").
- **The opt-outs**: `gclone keystore use file` (remembered in `keystore.json`: no trial, no move, no sealing, also after a later login) and `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` in a run's environment — that run takes no trial step, moves nothing and seals no login, **and a run with it that uses a keyed `secrets.json` leaves the marker `keystore-trial.off`, which holds the same for every run of the device** ("`GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0`" below). `gclone keystore use enclave` moves at once and opts back in.
- **Linux is untouched**: no sealer, so none of this happens; the plain file stays as it was.

What each buys. The plain file: anyone who obtains a copy — a backup, a synced folder, a disk image, a file-read bug in another program — has the vault key for good and the login until it is revoked. The sealed file: **a copy is useless anywhere but on this Mac**; to use it one has to run code as this user on this Mac after the first login since boot. Any program that can do that can ask the enclave exactly as gclone does — or simply run `gclone copy : /somewhere`, or `gclone passwd` and read the new keyfile — so the sealed store closes every "copy of the file" path and **nothing else**. Its cost: if the Mac is erased, its logic board replaced, the files brought to another Mac (a migration, a restore from a backup) or the blob otherwise lost, **the passphrase is the only way back for this device** — `gclone login`, as on a new device (for a Drive vault with the Google sign-in first). The plain file would have survived three of those — a new logic board with the disk kept, a migration, a restore of a backup that included the state root — and the erasure not. `gclone keystore use enclave` checks the passphrase before it moves; **the automatic move and the sealing login do not** (no question is the point): a login has just been given the passphrase or has just set it, and a device moved after its trial is told once, in the note. What nobody can check is that the passphrase is still known a year later: `gclone passwd` on a connected device sets a new one without the old (§15).

Rules that never change:
1. **Reading finds the secrets wherever they are** (the load table).
2. **Four things create, replace or remove `secrets.json` or `secrets.sealed`, each under the exclusive secrets lock (§8.3)**: `login` (`save`, and the move at its end), `logout` (`delete`), `gclone keystore use` (the two moves) and — since 0.5.1, replacing "no automatic step" of 0.5.0 — the automatic move towards `secrets.sealed`. **Nothing moves secrets into the plain file** but `gclone keystore use file` and a save that could not seal.
3. **`secrets.sealed` is never written unless it was opened in the same process, or is made from the exact bytes of a `secrets.json` that holds keys and is read back, through the enclave, to those bytes before that file is removed; and it is never removed unless `secrets.json` holds the keys** — or the user is logging out. (0.5.0 required the keys of that `secrets.json` to be proven against the vault first; the command still does that, the moves that nobody asked for do not — they seal the bytes the device was working with, change nothing about them, and `keystore use file` gives back those bytes.) **Sealed keys are never replaced by a document without keys** (§17.29): a login that has no key (yet) is saved to `secrets.json`, beside the sealed file. A move that nobody asked for never writes over a `secrets.sealed` it cannot open or that holds other keys.
4. **gclone never shows a dialog.** There is no Keychain call at all (`SecItem*`, `SecKeychain*`, `SecCode*` do not occur in the binary's own code; a test reads `src/keystore/macos.rs` for it), and the enclave key has no user-presence, biometry or password condition.
5. **Neither the trial nor the automatic move influences what `load` returns, and neither holds a command up without a bound.** The trial's errors are recorded, not raised; its step runs on a thread of its own that the command waits for at most `trial::STEP_WAIT`, two seconds (§17.29); a move that the command started is waited for at most `keystore::AUTO_MOVE_WAIT`, ten seconds, and a login's first call into the enclave (making or picking its key) at most two. **No call into the Secure Enclave is waited for without a bound, whoever makes it** (0.5.1, §17.30): every sealer of a gclone process is wrapped in `seal::Bounded` (`keystore::sealer`), which runs `create` and `open` on a thread of their own and answers "the Secure Enclave did not answer within 10 s" (`seal::CALL_WAIT`) when one does not come back — and at once, without a second wait, for every later call of that process. That is what a **sealed** device depends on: its every command opens the store, `status` and `keystore` included, and `login`, `logout`, `keystore use` and the saves open it under the secrets lock.
6. **The automatic move never happens from a process that did not open the trial's test value itself**, with the very key it then seals to (§17.30).

`secrets.sealed` (JSON, written with `util::write_atomic`, read as strictly as `secrets.json`: owner, mode, `O_NOFOLLOW`, private directory, size limit):
```json
{ "version": 1,
  "store": "enclave",
  "alg": "ecies-p256-x963-sha256-aesgcm",
  "public": "<base64url, 65 bytes: the key's public half, X9.63>",
  "key": "<base64url, some 300 bytes: the Secure Enclave key blob>",
  "sealed": "<base64url: ECIES(public, the exact bytes of a secrets.json document)>",
  "vault_id": "<32 hex: the vault the sealed keys belong to; absent while the document holds no keys>",
  "sealed_ms": 1794400000000 }
```
- What is sealed is a complete `secrets.json` document, parsed after opening by the same code. There is no second secrets format, and `keystore use file` gives back the bytes that `keystore use enclave` took.
- The key: P-256 in the Secure Enclave, **not permanent** (no Keychain item), access control "after first unlock, this device only" with `privateKeyUsage` and nothing else. `key` is the opaque blob the framework hands out for it (the attribute `toid` of `SecKeyCopyAttributes`; the same bytes as CryptoKit's `dataRepresentation`), which only the enclave that made it can use. Sealing is Apple's ECIES, `kSecKeyAlgorithmECIESEncryptionCofactorVariableIVX963SHA256AESGCM` (overhead 81 bytes): one platform call each way, no cipher composition of gclone's own.
- `public` lets a save seal without an enclave call and lets every open detect a reloaded key that is not the one sealed to: **after every reload of a key from its blob its public half is compared with `public`; different → the open fails and nothing is decrypted.** (The framework returns a new, different key without an error when the blob is passed only as the data argument of `SecKeyCreateWithData`; it has to be in the attributes.)
- `vault_id` is not secret. It is copied from `config.json` at the save that stores keys (`login` writes `config.json` first) and guards the merged view below.
- An unknown `version`, `store` or `alg`, a member that is not base64url, a sealed document that is not a secrets document → a load error that names the file ("damaged or written by a newer gclone"), never a guess. No error text quotes the file.

`keystore.json`: `{ "version": 1, "store": "file" | "enclave" }`, written only by `gclone keystore use`, under the exclusive lock. **It records what the owner said, never what gclone did**: a login that sealed by default and the automatic move leave it alone.

| `store` | meaning |
|---|---|
| absent (no file) | no choice made: **the default** — a login seals where it can, a device on `secrets.json` runs the trial and is moved when it has passed |
| `file` | the owner keeps the plain file: no trial, no move, no sealing login, no hint |
| `enclave` | the owner chose the sealed store: as the default, and also where the default would hold back — a login seals although the trial's record holds a failure, and with `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` set; if the device is on `secrets.json` all the same, `status` and `login` say so |

An unreadable, insecure or unknown `keystore.json` never blocks a read. It counts as "no choice made" **with the trial, the move and the sealing login suspended**, and `status` and `gclone keystore` warn about it.

`keystore-trial.json` (every member but `version` optional; it never holds vault key material or a token; a file that does not parse is replaced by a new trial). **Every change is a read-change-write under the kernel lock of `keystore-trial.lock`** (`trial::update`, §17.29; waited for at most 1.5 s, else the step is skipped; never held across a call into the enclave): each process used to write back the copy it had loaded before its enclave call, and of several commands starting together the later writer undid the earlier one's entry — a failure, a note.
```json
{ "version": 1,
  "public": "…", "key": "…",
  "canary": "<base64url: ECIES(public, 32 random bytes)>", "canary_hash": "<BLAKE3 of the 32 bytes, hex>",
  "created_ms": 1794400000000, "created_boot": "<kern.bootsessionuuid>", "os": "27.2",
  "last_ok_ms": 1794572800000,
  "ok": [ { "day": 20770, "boot": "<uuid>", "session": "0x2030" } ],
  "failures": [ { "ms": 1794400000000, "boot": "<uuid>", "session": "0x2", "fresh_key_ok": true, "error": "…", "timed_out": true } ],
  "failure_count": 0,
  "unavailable": { "ms": 1794400000000, "boot": "<uuid>", "os": "27.2", "session": "0x2", "error": "…" },
  "moved_ms": 1794400000000,
  "notes": { "ready_ms": 1794400000000 } }
```
`ok` has one entry per (UTC day number, boot, session), the newest 64; `last_ok_ms` (0.5.1; absent in a record of 0.5.0, whose first step of this version writes it) is the moment of the newest success that was written down — with a new `ok` entry, and one time more when a success is the first that lies 48 hours after `created_ms` (most runs still write nothing): `created_ms` and `last_ok_ms` are the trial's age ("Complete"); `failures` keeps the last 5 and `failure_count` all of them. `boot` is `kern.bootsessionuuid` (it names the boot without depending on the clock); `session` is the attribute word of `SessionGetInfo` for the caller's session (`0x10` = graphic access), `"none"` where there is no session. `timed_out` (absent = false) marks a call that did not return in time (a step: two seconds; a move that was started: ten); `unavailable.session` is the session that could not make a key — recorded by the trial's first step, and since 0.5.1 also by a login that could not seal (the reason `status` shows). `notes.ready_ms` is what 0.5.0 wrote when it had shown "the trial is complete: `gclone keystore use enclave`"; nothing writes it any more and nothing reads it. `moved_ms`: the secrets went into the sealed store — by the automatic move, at a login or by the command — and the trial ended. After `moved_ms` the record keeps `public`: whether the trial's key is the key the secrets are sealed to is read off the two files — `public` here against `public` of `secrets.sealed` — never claimed by a flag (§17.29). **Every moment in the record comes from one clock** (`trial::clock_ms`), so that "after the move" can be told from "before it". **A record whose trial ended at one sealing is forgotten at the next sealing to another key** (0.5.1, §17.30; `trial::note_sealed`): a login after a `logout`, a login on a Mac whose sealed key had died, `keystore use enclave` after `keystore use file`. Forgotten means: the file is removed — or, where it holds `notes` of 0.5.0, rewritten with nothing but `version` and `notes`, which is "no trial" to everything that reports. (Removed rather than left empty because gclone 0.5.0 on the same Mac shows an empty record as "the test value opened on 0 day(s)".) `backup-note.due` is an empty marker beside these files: the once-only note about older backups (§8.1) became due in a run without a terminal and is still owed; it is created with `O_EXCL` and consumed by its removal, so that concurrent first runs cannot lose it (it was a member of `notes` before §17.29, and was lost in about half of the rounds with eight processes at once). `keystore-note.due` (0.5.1) is the same kind of marker for the note about the automatic move (below). `keystore-trial.off` (0.5.1) is the marker of `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` (below): created once with `O_EXCL`, empty, removed only by `gclone keystore use enclave` and `gclone keystore check --new-trial`.

**Load** (`keystore::LayeredStore::resolve`, behind `config::secret_store`; no lock on the normal path, §8.3):
1. Read `secrets.json` strictly, as before. An error (insecure permissions, bad JSON) is that error, whatever `secrets.sealed` is.
2. It holds keys (`keys` not empty) → it is the answer. `secrets.sealed` is not opened. If that file exists too, `status` reports it.
3. It is absent or keyless → read `secrets.sealed` strictly.

| `secrets.json` | `secrets.sealed` | answer |
|---|---|---|
| absent | absent | look at `secrets.json` again; still absent → once more at both under the shared lock (§8.3); nothing → not signed in |
| absent | opens | the sealed document |
| absent | does not open | `ConfigError::KeyStoreUnavailable(text)`, exit 4 (texts below) |
| keyless | absent | look at `secrets.json` again and answer with it |
| keyless, has a login | opens, holds keys, and its `vault_id` equals the one in `config.json` | **merged**: the login fields of `secrets.json`, `keys` and `min_epoch` of the sealed document — what a re-login does. In memory only. |
| keyless | opens, any other case | `secrets.json` (the command reports `Locked` or "not connected" as before) |
| keyless | does not open | `secrets.json`, with the cause as a note at `-v` and in `status` |

The keyless rows exist for one sequence: the device is sealed, an older gclone says "not signed in", the owner runs its `login`, signs in, and the passphrase prompt is abandoned — gclone 0.4.0 has then written `secrets.json` with the login and `keys: []`. The key stays where it is and the device keeps working with the login just made. The next `gclone login` of this version (or `keystore use file`) writes the two as one `secrets.json`.

**`KeyStoreUnavailable`: which text.** Before choosing, the same process makes a fresh key, seals a few bytes and opens them (`seal::probe`, about 12 ms):

| stored key | fresh key | text, in short |
|---|---|---|
| fails, **and fails again 300 ms later** (§17.29: one failed call is not a dead key — `open_sealed_patiently`; a second try that works is the answer, with a warning in the log) | works | "This device's key was sealed for another Mac, or this Mac's Secure Enclave was reset: the stored key cannot be used any more (…; tried twice, and a new key works). Run `gclone login`; it asks for the passphrase. The sealed file is kept until that login has the key again." |
| fails | fails | "The Secure Enclave cannot be used in this session (…). Run gclone from a terminal or a LaunchAgent of the logged-in user; `gclone keystore check` shows what this session can do. **Do not sign in again**: the stored key is probably intact. If gclone has to run in this session, `gclone keystore use file` — from a session where it works — moves the secrets back to the plain file, which every session reads." — this text never names `gclone login` |
| **does not answer** within ten seconds (`seal::Bounded`, rule 5) | not asked: the process's later calls fail at once | the same text, with "(the Secure Enclave did not answer within 10 s)" — exit 4 after one bounded wait, for `status` and `keystore` too, instead of a command that stands still (0.5.1, §17.30) |
| the file does not parse, or names an unknown version, store or algorithm | — | "secrets.sealed … is damaged or was written by a newer gclone (…). Use that gclone, or run `gclone login`." |
| no sealer in this process (Linux; a debug build) | — | on Linux: the file was sealed by a Mac, `gclone login`; a debug build: use a release build, nothing was changed |

**`login`** treats `KeyStoreUnavailable` as "no usable secrets", prints the text and goes on (§2.6); every other load error stays fatal. It never writes to a sealed file it could not open — **and never puts a keyless document in the place of sealed keys, whether or not the file opens by then** (the save table; §17.29).

**Save** (only `login` saves; `LayeredStore::save_with`). A Drive login saves twice — the grant without a key before the passphrase is asked, then with the keys; a directory vault's login once. Each save takes the exclusive lock, removes the temp copies that killed writes left of `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed` and `keystore.json` (§17.29: every writer of these files holds this lock, so whatever lies there belongs to nobody — a plain `.secrets.json.tmp-…` used to stay beside a sealed store until a `logout` or a move), looks at the files as they are **now**, writes, releases. The lock is never held across a sign-in or a passphrase prompt.

| `secrets.json` | `secrets.sealed` | the save goes to |
|---|---|---|
| exists | any | **`secrets.json`**, as before |
| absent | opens (in this process), and the save does not replace keys by none: the document to save holds keys, or the sealed one holds none | **`secrets.sealed`**: seal to its `public`; open the new ciphertext in memory, it must equal the document; `write_atomic`; read the file back and compare the bytes. On any failure the save goes to `secrets.json` instead and says so (a warning). |
| absent | opens and holds keys; the document to save holds **none** | **`secrets.json`** (§17.29). The sealed file is not touched: beside it the keyless login is the merged view of the load table, and the device keeps working. `login` saves the grant without a key before it asks for the passphrase, and it gets here also when its own look at the sealed file failed a moment before (a transient error of the enclave) — re-sealing that document over the file destroyed the only device copy of the vault key before the passphrase was asked, and a wrong or abandoned passphrase left the device locked. The one exception names the keys it gives up: `SecretStore::save_dropping_keys(new, dropped)`, used where `login` lost a creation race (§2.6) and drops the lost vault's keys — it replaces a sealed file that holds exactly the keys of `dropped`. |
| absent | exists, does not open | **`secrets.json`**. The sealed file is not touched. |
| absent | absent | **`secrets.sealed`, with a key picked now** (0.5.1: by default; 0.5.0 only where the choice was `enclave`) — unless one of these holds, and then **`secrets.json`**: the choice is `file` or cannot be read; `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` is set and the choice is not `enclave`; the marker `keystore-trial.off` is there and the choice is not `enclave`; this process has no sealer (Linux, a debug build); the trial's record of this Mac holds a failure or a session that could not make a key, and the choice is not `enclave` (evidence that some session of this Mac cannot use the enclave is not sealed over; `gclone keystore check --new-trial` clears it); **a trial is running on this device and has not passed, and the choice is not `enclave`** (0.5.1, §17.30: a `logout` and a `login` do not jump the bar — "The bar"); the trial has passed and its test value does not open in this process; no key can be picked (below); or the sealing fails — the checks of the row above. **Picking the key** (`LayeredStore::key_for_login`, `keystore::pick_key`): the trial's own key if the trial has passed and its test value opens right now — the record then ends, and says whose key took the secrets — and where there is no record, or one that ended with a move, a new key that sealed 16 random bytes and opened them in this process; on a thread of its own, awaited two seconds. A save on a signed-out device also removes the marker of an owed note about a move (`keystore-note.due`): nothing of an earlier login is left for it to be about, and an older gclone's `logout` leaves that marker behind. **A fallback of the default is silent** (a debug-level log line) and writes its reason into the trial's record as `unavailable` (or as a failure of the trial's key): that is the line `status` shows. A fallback of the *choice* `enclave` is a warning, as in 0.5.0. |

After a save to `secrets.json` that stored keys, a `secrets.sealed` beside it is removed when one of these holds, and otherwise stays: the keys came from a keyfile in this run (`SecretStore::save_proven`, called by `Session::save_connected`: the passphrase was just proven); or the sealed file opens and its keyring equals the one just saved. So a sealed file that does not open survives a login whose passphrase prompt failed or was interrupted, and is removed by the login that has the key again. A connected device whose view is the merged one: a `login` that renews nothing still saves once, which writes the merged document to `secrets.json` and removes the sealed copy of the same keys.

**The end of a login** (0.5.1; `cli::login::settle_key_store`, `keystore::seal_after_login`). The first rows of the table send some logins to `secrets.json` on a Mac whose default is the sealed store: the login found a sealed file that did not open (the files came from another Mac; the passphrase has now put the key back), or an older gclone's keyless login beside the sealed keys. **Those secrets are moved at the end of the same login** — a key picked as above, then the move sequence of `keystore use enclave` (below) with `MoveBy::Login`: it waits for the lock, records no choice and owes no note. So a login on a Mac ends sealed whenever sealing is possible, and a plain file with keys exists at most between two steps of one command. **Not on a device that was working from a `secrets.json` with keys when the login began**: there a store that stops opening could break what runs unattended, and the trial decides — a re-login does not jump that queue. **Nor where a trial was running and had not passed when the login began** (looked at before the login loads anything: `keystore::trial_undecided`; a trial that the login's own loads start does not count, and lends its key). The move at the end of a login removes the marker of an owed note about an earlier move, like the command: the login says itself where the secrets are. Where the secrets were not sealed before the login and are after it, `login` says so in one line (§7.3); where a login ends on `secrets.json` although the *choice* is `enclave`, it warns and names `gclone keystore use enclave`, as before; a fallback of the default says nothing.

**Delete** (`logout`, and `login`'s own `delete`): under the exclusive lock, remove `token.json`, then the temp leftovers of `token.json`, `secrets.json`, `secrets.sealed`, `keystore-trial.json` and `keystore.json`, then `secrets.json`, then `secrets.sealed` — in this order, so that a `logout` killed half-way still finds the device signed in and the next one finishes — and last the marker of an owed note about a move (`keystore-note.due`). "Signed in" for `logout` = `secrets.json` or `secrets.sealed` exists. `logout --forget` treats these files the same.

**The trial: a test value, not the secrets** (`keystore::trial`) — **the test that the automatic move waits for** (0.5.1). It runs in release builds on macOS (in a debug build only with a test sealer), from `SecretStore::load` after the answer is determined — on a thread of its own, awaited for at most two seconds (rule 5; §17.29) — once per process, when `secrets.json` is the store that answered, the choice is not `file`, the choice file is readable, `GCLONE_KEYSTORE_TRIAL=0` is not set and has left no marker — `serve restic` included. **With a `secrets.sealed` beside the plain file the step runs only if that file is sealed to the key of the trial that is running** (0.5.1, §17.30; `LayeredStore::sealed_beside_is_foreign`, read off the two files): that is what an interrupted automatic move leaves, and the next run finishes it. Any other sealed file beside a `secrets.json` — the store of an earlier sealing with an older gclone's login beside it, an interrupted `keystore use`, a file of another Mac — stops the trial and the move until the owner's command settles it ("Older binaries"). The step itself writes `keystore-trial.json` and nothing else. A device whose secrets are sealed has no trial.
1. No record, or a record without a key → make a key (reload its blob, compare the public half), seal 32 random bytes, open them, write the record with the first `ok` entry.
