6. A pack found gone at the C2 time-out is remembered (`lost_packs`), so that restic's further attempts for that index fail at once instead of after 30 seconds each.
7. A resolution that fails with a layout error marks the stored layout as not to be used; otherwise a listing after a refused `HEAD config` would still have been served from the folders known before.
8. "No such repository" is written to stderr only for listings. On `HEAD config` it is restic's question at the start of `init`, and a line there would be shown to the user as `rclone: gclone: …` on every `init`.
9. The identical-upload shortcut answers `403` when the body hashes to the name but the object on Drive has another md5 (the existing object is not what its name says); the design had only "a mismatching body → 400".
10. The request body is read to its end before an error is answered in HTTP/2 mode too, not only for the listener; the pipe is local, and it keeps one code path.
11. When the identical-upload shortcut finds its cached pack gone or trashed, the pack also leaves *unlisted*: the upload that follows takes its place.
12. Tests: E2 (the vault is untouched) is part of the workflow test E1. E5's "re-listing after the 404 from Drive" cannot be reached through restic's command line — a new restic process has no cached ID, its miss is answered by a listing — so E5 asserts the failure and the listing, and the cached-ID path (R5) is tested end to end with the test client on the binary's pipes (`stdio_after_a_permanent_delete`) and in the unit tests. The fault tests run restic with `-o rclone.connections=1`, so that ten failures in a row meet one upload. `Stale` exists in the unit tests; `tests/restic_http.rs` has a smaller wrapper of its own (`Gated`: a put held at a gate), because integration tests cannot see the library's test code.
13. `tokio::fs::File` over the pipes held up in every test, with multi-MiB transfers in both directions; the fallback of two copying threads was not needed.
14. **The process does not exit the moment the connection ends** (the design: "returns 0 at once"). It first cancels every uncommitted upload and waits, at most `EXIT_GRACE` = 10 s, until each has taken back what it stored (`Repo::close`); with nothing in flight the exit is as immediate as before. Without it the cancel path of the design could not do what it is there for: a restic that is interrupted while it creates its lock is gone within milliseconds, the pipe closes, and a process that exits there leaves the lock it had just put — live, and unknown to restic — for 30 minutes. A test on the binary's pipes shows exactly that when the wait is taken out. (This item said that restic waits for its backend program to exit. It does not — §17.25 item 7; the take-back runs after restic is gone.) The connection's end cancels the attempts itself and does not rely on hyper dropping the handlers.
15. `GCLONE_TEST_RESTIC` names the one binary to test with; `PATH` is searched only without it (a named binary that is missing or too old is "no restic", not a reason to pick another).
16. E8's failing upload needs a pack above 4 MiB to exist: restic 0.19 spreads the blobs of a run over two packers, so 6 MiB of new data sometimes ended as two packs below the limit and the injected faults were never met (one run in seven). The test writes 10 MiB — more than two packers can hold below the pack size.

**Results.** Unit tests of `src/restic/`: 37; two more in `web` (`host_allowed`, `bind_v6`), and the three clap tables of `cli` extended. `tests/restic_http.rs`: 10. `tests/restic_e2e.rs`: 20 — seven with the test client on the binary, twelve with restic 0.19.1 (nixpkgs' build, and the release binary the CI script installs) against `FakeDrive`, one for the version check. Without restic on `PATH` the twelve print their note and pass; with `GCLONE_REQUIRE_RESTIC=1` they fail there. The flow-control test was also run with the connection window at 1 MiB: it fails there, as it must.

**Not verified.** Nothing ran against real Google Drive: assumptions A1 and A2, downloads of trashed files, `trashed` on a put into a trashed folder, two logins of one account seeing each other's files, Drive's signal at the daily upload limit, and the real pacing (a minute for `init`, 257 listings for `check`) are untested there; the first live run is the owner's. The release binary cannot be pointed at the fake Drive (it ignores the test switches), so with it only the command line, the start-up errors and restic's handling of them (`error talking HTTP to rclone: exit status 4`, at once) were run by hand; everything else is the debug binary's. Linux: the code paths are the same and the tests run there in CI, not on a Linux machine by hand. restic older than 0.19.1 (0.17 and 0.18 are accepted) was not run. The listener's interplay with restic's 5-minute watchdog on a slow uplink is reasoned, not measured. Open for the owner: whether a sign-in-only form of `gclone login` is wanted instead of Ctrl-C at the passphrase question.

### 17.25 Review of 0.5.0 — `gclone serve restic`: fourteen reports, thirteen issues (2026-11-13)

Reviewers of §17.24 — adversarial runs of the real restic against the fake Drive, the listener as a process, the Drive client's answers, the documents — filed fourteen reports; one is a reviewer's disclosure and no defect (item 14). Each of the other thirteen was reproduced or re-derived from the code and is real. Seven are faults of the code, each fixed at its cause with tests that fail when the fix is taken out (run that way once: every test named below failed); six are faults of the documents or left-over code. Edited in place: §3.4, §7.2, §7.6, §9.5, §10, §13 item 8c, §15, §17.24 item 14; `README.md`, `worker/README.md`.

**The store.**
1. *An index that other machines could already list was trashed when its uploader went away before the acknowledgement* (high). The clean-up of unacknowledged uploads applied to every file type; it was built for locks. Reproduced with restic 0.19.1: machine B deduplicated against machine A's index, was told "snapshot saved", A's restic was killed, the index went to the trash, and B's snapshot could not be restored until `restic repair index`. **An index that Drive has, verified, is not taken back for want of an acknowledgement** — cancelled, connection closed, a confirming listing that failed or came too late (§7.6, Uploads). It is still taken back where it must not be trusted (md5, a trashed folder, a lost pack, a put that did not say whether it stored) and when a `DELETE` of the name cancelled it (`Attempt::deleted`). Beyond the reviewer's proposal: a failed confirming listing (`Backend`) keeps the index like a late one does, and the kept ID is remembered as an orphan that is not hidden, so that restic's `DELETE`-then-`POST` removes it without needing a listing to show it. `Repo::upload` reports what a failed attempt left as `Left::{Nothing, Unknown, Stored}` in place of a flag.
2. *Two `restic init` runs seconds apart both reported success, and the first one's config ended in the trash.* The second `POST config` was refused correctly (`403`); restic then removes the file it failed to upload — `DELETE config` — and that trashed the winner's, after which the retried `POST` went through. The delete that follows a refused `POST config` is not carried out: `403` (`Error::ConfigKept`), without a Drive call, once per refusal and within `CONFIG_REFUSAL` = 60 s, so that a refusal whose delete never came does not swallow a delete that is meant (§7.6, Deletes; `403` rather than the `200` the reviewer also allowed: nothing was deleted, and restic ignores the status of that clean-up). The refused upload writes one stderr line that names what is left to do — the loser's key file stays in `keys/`, which gclone can neither prevent nor recognise (§3.4, §15). §3.4 said that concurrent inits end in duplicate folders only; it now has the three outcomes.
3. *In `--port` mode, an interrupted backup followed by a prune on another machine failed every later backup through the listener* (`403` after 30 s, then at once, until restart): the packs of the interrupted run stayed in *unlisted* for the life of the process, and C2 held every later index to them. **The pack bookkeeping ends with the run it belongs to**, and the run is told by restic's own locks: it is dropped when no lock created through the process is left (§7.6, C2). Not taken from the proposals: a timer (a backup right after the prune would still fail until it ran out), and "the next `HEAD config` with no request in flight" (it would drop the packs of a second run that is between two requests). `--stdio` keeps the sticky `403`. The message says "through this listener" there.
4. *In `--port` mode, files restored from the Drive trash stayed invisible until the listener was restarted*: *hidden* was never emptied. An ID leaves it when a listing that started after the trash omits it, as proposed — and, because that alone leaves a file hidden for good when it was restored before any listing omitted it (packs after a `prune`, which lists nothing afterwards: exactly the recovery the README describes), an ID that a listing still shows 30 s after its trash is `stat`ed (§7.6, R8; `HIDDEN_RECHECK`). A hidden orphan stays hidden.
5. *A `404` from Drive's `files.list` for a folder that exists was answered to restic as `200 []`* — for `snapshots/` the listing on which `prune` trashes every pack. The Drive client maps a `404` on a listing to "empty" (right for the vault, whose callers handle a vanished folder), and the store's check of an empty listing found the folder alive. `Backend::list_strict` (§9.5) keeps the two apart; the store and the resolution of the tree use nothing else, `stat` the folder on `NotFound`, and answer `403` (gone) or `503` (there). `FakeDrive` already answered `404` for an absent parent; it was not changed.

**The process.**
6. *`serve restic --port` died of SIGTERM and SIGHUP* — at once, without the take-back, with the status of a killed process — although a listener is what runs under a service manager. Both now stop it like the first Ctrl-C (exit 0). A SIGHUP the process was started to ignore (`nohup`) stays ignored.
7. *§7.6 said that restic waits for its backend program to exit.* It does not (measured by the reviewer: restic gone after 1 ms, the lock trashed 290 ms later). §7.6 and the README say what happens, and what follows where leftover processes are killed (a container with restic as PID 1, CI teardown): the lock restic was creating can stay until `restic unlock`. §17.24 item 14 carried the same sentence and points here.
8. *Connections without a request share the listener's 64 slots with restic's.* A local process without the token can keep restic waiting; it cannot read or write. **Documented, not changed in code** (§7.6, §15, README): a larger cap for waiting connections exceeds the default descriptor limit of a macOS process (256) and would turn a stall into failing Drive calls; a head time-out of its own and separate caps raise the bar from 64 idle sockets to an active flood and no further; a unix socket closes it, is a second transport with its own tests and documents, and stays on the "not built" list of §17.24.
9. *At the daily upload limit a restic command hangs for about twelve minutes, four of them silent*, where the README said it fails. The README says so; the first line — a throttled `POST locks/…` — now names the daily limit as a possible cause and `--no-lock` (`Error::note` takes `Asked::{Listing, Lock, Other}` in place of a flag).

**Documents and left-overs.**
10. README: "only need the two settings" was not true for the default install — units and cron do not have `~/.local/bin` on their `PATH`. It says to name the program in full and to run restic as the user who signed in.
11. `worker/README.md` named 0.4.0 in the seven places of the viewer's deployment steps; they name 0.5.0, like the main README's example. (The scripts' own examples of a tag's form are examples.)
12. §10 had no flow for `serve` and showed the old call of `web::serve`. Both are there.
13. `restic::layout::Tree::folder` was used by no code but tests (the store's tests as well as the one assertion the report names). Removed; the tests have a helper of their own, and the layout test asserts the order of `Tree::small` by the folders' names.
14. *Disclosure*: a reviewer's private debug build was once started without isolated directories, read this user's `secrets.json` and exited on its closed stdin; no request left the machine and nothing was written (checked by the reviewer). Nothing to change in the repository. The debug build was not given a refusal for that case: `serve restic` needs no test switch to be useful by hand, and the release build is what a user runs.

**Tests.** Unit (`src/restic/store/tests.rs`, U33–U36, and additions to U27 and U4/the stderr table): 41 in `src/restic/` (37 before). `tests/drive_http.rs`: `list_strict`. `tests/restic_http.rs`: the config row. `tests/restic_e2e.rs`: 25 (20 before) — B8 with an index, B9, B5 with SIGTERM, SIGHUP and an ignored SIGHUP, E14–E17 with restic 0.19.1; §13 item 8c has the list. One existing test was wrong in the way item 7 describes: E13 asserted that no lock is left the moment restic has exited, and failed when the signal met restic while it was still creating its lock (seen once, under the load of the new tests); it now waits for gclone to end first.

**Results** (macOS, Apple silicon). `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --locked` with restic 0.19.1 and `GCLONE_REQUIRE_RESTIC=1` — 786 passed, 3 ignored (lib 349; `tests/drive_http.rs` 43, `tests/restic_http.rs` 10, `tests/restic_e2e.rs` 25: nine without restic, sixteen with it — four runs in a row; with no restic the sixteen print their note and pass); `cargo build --release --locked`; `actionlint` (the workflows did not change).

**Not verified.** Everything §17.24 lists. In addition: SIGTERM from a real systemd or launchd unit (the test sends the signal itself); the twelve minutes of item 9 were measured by the reviewer and not run again — the test asserts the text of the line, not the timing; E17 depends on stopping machine A's gclone between the put of its index and the acknowledgement — if the acknowledgement won that race the test would pass without having tested anything, and a passing run does not show which it was (asserted: A's backup is still running, and machine B's "Added to the repository: 0 B"; with the fix taken out the test failed in the run made that way); restic older than 0.19.1 is still untested; how the real Drive answers a listing of a folder that was just deleted is as documented (`404`), not observed.

### 17.26 The cryptography audit of 0.4.0 — the CLI and core part (2026-11-13)

An independent audit of v0.4.0 (six reviews — construction, implementation, index authenticity, keyfile and KDF, hosted viewer, dependencies — each finding of "low" or above then handed to a second reviewer whose job was to refute it) found the cryptographic core sound: no way to read, forge, swap, truncate or reorder file content or index data without the keys. All 21 findings that went through the refutation survived it; none is rated above low. What it found is around the core: written claims that were false, one destructive command that failed open, an alarm that could be silenced, and nothing that watched the dependencies or signed the binaries. This entry is the part that concerns the CLI, the core, the release tooling and the documents. Each finding was confirmed in the code first; each code change has a regression test, named below. **Not in this entry**: the hosted viewer's ticket boundary and what a hostile host leaves in a browser (the audit's L2, L6) — now §17.27 — and keeping the master key out of a plaintext file (I6), a separate change. On-disk and on-Drive formats are unchanged; no state is migrated; 0.4.0 and 0.5.0 devices work on one vault (the two places where they differ in behaviour are named in items 3 and 5).

Edited in place: the title line, §1.1, §1.2, §1.3, §2.2, §2.6, §2.7, §2.8, §2.9 (row 14), §3.2, §4, §4.7, §5.2.2, §5.3, §5.9, §5.10, §6.1, §7.1, §7.3, §7.4, §7.5, §9.1, §9.4, §9.5, §9.7, §9.9, §10, §12.1, §13, §14, §15, and notes at §17.2 and §17.23 item 12; `README.md`, `worker/README.md`; `install.sh`; `.github/`.

**Code.**
1. *`gclone gc` ran on a replica that had just ignored an index object* (audit L3). `gc` refused on a refresh error and on a blocked segment, and on nothing else: a refresh that returned `Ok` after ignoring a listed index object that failed verification, or with a newer snapshot it could not use, let `gc` run — on a view the device itself knew to be incomplete. Reproduced by the audit at the command line: `gc --orphans` exit 0, "Trashed 0 dead blobs (0 B), 1 orphans (293.1 KiB)" — the blob of a file that was live on another device; and with `--purge` a restored version's blob deleted for good. **`gc` refuses in all three steps, `--dry-run` included, and names the object** (§5.9). `RefreshReport` gains `unused_snapshot` and `incomplete()`; the CLI's check is `cli::gc::refusal`; and the refusal is also in the library — `Vault::index_incomplete()`, set by every refresh of the process, and `sync::gc` returning `IndexError::Incomplete` (exit 3) — so that no caller can forget it. The "newer snapshot left unused" state had no test anywhere and has one now.
2. *An index object overwritten or re-created under its own name silenced the rollback alarm* (L4). Presence rule (a), the base-on-offer test and `repair`'s republish condition looked at listed **names**. Whoever can write to the folder without the key could overwrite an applied object in place, or delete it and create another under its name: every device that had applied it then refreshed cleanly — the same rollback as a deletion, without `Rollback`, without a hint to run `repair` — while devices that had not applied it were held on the older state. **Presence is the object the replica accepted**: the listed size and md5 against the cached copy (whose BLAKE3 must be the applied hash; without a cached copy the listed object is read once and compared by hash) in rule (a), the recorded size and md5 of the base in the base-on-offer test, the same comparison for `stat` by id (an object overwritten in place keeps its id), and in `repair` (§5.3, §5.10). `repair` moves an impostor under a cached object's name to the trash and puts the cached object back — beyond the audit's proposal, and needed for it to work on a directory vault, which holds one object per name. No schema change: the cache already holds what is compared. Two existing tests asserted the old behaviour in so many words ("the writer's replica is complete … `a.refresh().await.unwrap()`", "names suffice for presence") and assert the new one. Not taken from the audit's proposal: failing *mutating* commands on any ignored object of a well-formed name — it would let one planted object stop every device, which §4.6 accepts only for objects that claim a newer format; the device warns on every command and `gc` refuses (item 1).
3. *The restore window and the gc grace ran on a timestamp the folder-writer chooses* (L5). `removed_ms` was the listed creation time of the segment object; Drive takes a creation time from whoever creates a file. An authentic segment deleted and re-created forty days in the past made every device that had not applied the original record its removals as forty days old: `restore` no longer offered the versions, `gc` trashed their blobs at once. **`removed_ms = max(listed creation time, SegmentV1.created_ms)`** (`index::removal_time`, used by the replica and by the viewer's reader alike, §5.2.2): the store can only lengthen the windows. `gc` additionally refuses (`SyncError::ClockSkew`, exit 5) while the offset the `Date` header gives is more than a day (`Backend::clock_offset_ms`, §5.9). *Mixed versions*: 0.4.0 keeps using the listed time alone, so the two may record different `removed_ms` when a writer's clock is ahead of Drive's; nothing compares them. In the tests the fake store's clock stands still while the machine's runs, so the writer's clock is "ahead" by milliseconds: `tests/index_props.rs` now starts its store an hour ahead, which is what the exact times it asserts always assumed.
4. *Four planted keyfiles made the CLI say "Wrong passphrase" to the right passphrase* (L10). ATTACH took the four highest generations **by name**, junk included. Four well-formed keyfiles — the keyfile of any other vault under a higher generation; no secret is needed — filled the four places: the real keyfile was never tried and the answer was "Wrong passphrase." (exit 4), with no hint at any verbosity that more keyfiles existed. With no connected device left, the owner would have concluded that the passphrase was lost while the vault was recoverable. **The CLI follows the hosted viewer's rule** (§2.6 ATTACH): objects that are no keyfile are refused before any derivation and take no place (`format::check_keyfile`, shared with the viewer's `keyfile_cost`); one attempt still costs at most four derivations unasked; while well-formed keyfiles remain untried the message says how many and the passphrase is never called wrong; a question at the terminal, or `gclone login --all-keyfiles`, tries them. The bounds on unauthenticated work stay: 32 objects of 64 KiB looked at (1024 on request), four derivations per attempt, three attempts. The acceptance test that covered only the junk case — and asserted exit 3 for it — is rewritten (§12.1).
5. *The generated passphrase has 26 symbols, 130 bits* (was 20 and 100; raised after the audit — not a finding of it, which rated 100 bits out of reach: the keyfile can be attacked offline for as long as Google keeps it, and the margin costs six characters, once). Shown as `XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXXX`. The normalisation recognises both shapes (§2.6). **Existing passphrases are the same passphrases**: the 20-symbol rule is untouched, and for the one input the new rule reads differently from 0.4.0 — a *typed* passphrase that happens to have the 26-symbol shape, which 0.4.0 used as typed — `open_keyfile` tries the older reading second (`Passphrase::legacy`). Proven against keyfiles sealed by the v0.4.0 source and frozen in `tests/vectors/passphrase_v0_4_0.json`. The hosted viewer compiles the same file (`#[path]`) and has the same behaviour; its export test replays the shapes through the wasm module. *Mixed versions*: gclone 0.4.0, and the hosted viewer deployed from 0.4.0, accept a **generated** 26-symbol passphrase only in its canonical spelling — which is how it is shown and stored — and a **typed** passphrase of that shape exactly as it was typed when it was set, which is what 0.5.0 seals it under (§17.29, item 1; this entry first had every input of the shape sealed under the canonical form, which locked 0.4.0 out of a typed one).
6. *`passwd` could not remove an old keyfile for good, and hid its caveat under `-q`* (I5, L8). `passwd --purge-old` — and a question on a terminal — deletes the retired keyfiles instead of trashing them, including those in the Drive trash (`Backend::list_trashed`, new: `files.list` with `trashed = true`, which `drive.file` answers for the app's own files). The new keyfile is now read back from the store and compared before anything is retired. Trashing stays the default: the trashed keyfile is the way back when a new passphrase is lost with the last connected device. The caveat — what remains of the old keyfiles, and that the key is unchanged — is printed with `ui.warn` (§2.7).
7. *Key wiping* (I7): `sha2` is built with `zeroize` (SHA-256 states, hence HMAC and HKDF states), `poly1305` and `cipher` likewise (direct dependencies for the feature only; no new package, no version change in either lockfile); `KeyfileKey` wipes its base64 key text on drop; the viewer's `Ticket` no longer derives `Debug`. **Not done**: wiping the key bundle that `unlock` returns across the wasm boundary — wasm-bindgen frees the returned buffer itself, so it needs another interface between `core.js` and the KDF worker (or a wiping allocator), which belongs with the viewer change above; the worker is terminated right after the unlock. §4 now says what wiping covers and what it does not, in place of "all secret byte arrays live in `Zeroizing`".
8. *A parse error of `secrets.json` could quote a secret* (a single reviewer's note): serde_json's message names the value it did not expect, and the comment in `config.rs` said it never does. Only the kind of failure and its position are reported.

**Release, installer, dependencies.**
9. *Nothing watched the dependencies* (L7, I9). `.github/workflows/audit.yml`: `cargo audit` (a pinned version, built from source; no new action) over `Cargo.lock` and `web-core/Cargo.lock`, weekly, on every push to main and on pull requests that touch a manifest or lockfile; a vulnerability, an unsound or a yanked crate fails it. `.github/dependabot.yml` gains `cargo` (both manifests) and `npm` (the Worker and the pinned Playwright driver), with a 14-day cooldown for version updates. **Two repository settings no file can turn on** — Dependabot alerts and Dependabot security updates — are named in both files and in the README.
10. *The binaries were authenticated by a checksum from the same release* (I4). `release.yml` attests each archive in the job that built it and verifies every attestation again in the publish job (`--source-ref`, `--source-digest`) before anything is published. `install.sh` runs `gh attestation verify` (repository, signer workflow, `refs/tags/<tag>`, no self-hosted runner) **when the GitHub CLI is installed, knows the command and is signed in** — `gh attestation verify` needs a login even for a public repository (checked against gh 2.103.3) — and then refuses an archive that does not verify; "no attestation" is never taken for "nothing to check", because that is exactly what a replaced archive looks like. Otherwise it checks `SHA256SUMS` and says in one line what that is worth. `--require-attestation`, `--no-attestation` (releases before 0.5.0 carry none for the binaries). §1.3 has a row for the CLI's supply chain.
11. *The release checks followed the tag* (L9). `releaseBundle` also runs `gh release verify-asset` — which passes only for a file of an **immutable** release — and fails closed; `fetch-viewer` and `check-release` pass `--source-digest` with the commit of the checkout they deploy from; the mismatch messages say whether the copy or **the release** changed, and no longer advise fetching again when it was the release (§7.5). Both `gh` subcommands and the flag exist in gh 2.103.3. Found while doing it: **release v0.4.0 of this repository is not immutable** (`isImmutable: false`; `gh release verify-asset` answers "no attestations found for tag v0.4.0") — the setting has to be turned on before 0.5.0 is published, and v0.4.0 is used by the scripts only when named, `GCLONE_MUTABLE_RELEASE=v0.4.0`.

**Documents: sentences that were false or said too much.**
12. *File sizes are not hidden* (L1): §1.2, §1.3 and §15 and the README said "files ≥ 1 MiB to within 0.03 %; smaller files hidden in packs". Every file's exact size and the number of files are visible to whoever holds the ciphertext — large files because the container length is invertible, small ones because each pack member carries its own cleartext header — as are the order within an upload, device ids in data-folder names, commit counters and the keyfile generation, and the growth of index objects with path lengths. Said where it was denied.
13. *What the head fingerprint proves* (I2, and a single reviewer's note): 40 bits, unkeyed, computable by the store; agreement between two devices, not currency; the reference is the device that wrote last. §2.6, §15, the README, and the line `login` prints.
14. *"Every modification is detected … by every device that has seen newer state"*: true for applied objects since item 2; the residual — withholding of the newest objects, a fork of views — is stated in §1.3, §15 and the README where it was a subordinate clause.
15. *No re-keying* (L8): the README said a leak "is permanent for the data that existed then" — for a party that keeps receiving ciphertext it covers everything uploaded later. README and §15 have the procedure that works in v1 (a new vault) and what it does not undo; §2.8 has the row.
16. *The passphrase rules*: that the shape rule also folds a typed passphrase (`hello hello hello hello` → `HE110-…`), that nothing is trimmed and a byte-order mark in a passphrase file is part of the passphrase, and that length is the only rule enforced, are stated (§2.6, §15). The short-passphrase warning says that a later `passwd` does not take a weak passphrase back.
17. *"No module other than `crypto` calls an AEAD"* (`src/crypto/mod.rs`): the local viewer's file ids do, outside §4; the sentence says so.

**Tests.** `src/cli/gc.rs` (the refusal table), `src/cli/login.rs` (`unlock` with a limit; planted well-formed keyfiles), `src/format/keyfile.rs` (`check_keyfile`; the older reading costs a second derivation only where it differs), `src/config.rs` (no secret in a parse error). `tests/index_adversary.rs`: a segment replaced under its name, deleted-and-re-created and overwritten in place; presence without a cached copy; the whole index replaced; `gc` on an ignored object and with an unused newer snapshot; a re-planted segment with an old creation time. `tests/sync_e2e.rs`: the `--purge` scenario of the audit. `tests/index_props.rs`: `retire_keyfiles` with and without `purge`. `tests/crypto_format.rs`: both generated shapes; the frozen keyfiles of 0.4.0. `tests/drive_http.rs`: the clock offset. `tests/cli_e2e.rs`: the overwritten index object, the `gc` refusal, the clock guard against the fake Drive, planted keyfiles (also on a pseudo-terminal that is the binary's controlling terminal — a passphrase prompt reads `/dev/tty`), `passwd --purge-old`. The backend conformance suite: `list_trashed`, on every backend (memory, directory, the two behind `Flaky`, `AnyBackend`, and the Drive client against `FakeDrive`). `web-core/tests/parity.rs` and the wasm replay: the passphrase shapes and the 0.4.0 keyfiles. `tests/install/test.sh`: 19 cases for the attestation, among them the audit's swap of archive and checksum list. `worker/scripts/release-bundle.selftest.mjs`: the commit, the immutable release, the moved tag.

**Results** (macOS, Apple silicon; cargo and rustc 1.99.0 from nix). `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --locked` with restic and `GCLONE_REQUIRE_RESTIC=1` — 807 passed, 3 ignored (786 before: lib 354, `tests/cli_e2e.rs` 34, `tests/index_adversary.rs` 21, `tests/index_props.rs` 64, `tests/sync_e2e.rs` 54, `tests/crypto_format.rs` 40, `tests/drive_http.rs` 44, the others as they were); `cargo build --release --locked`. `web-core/`: `cargo fmt --check`, clippy for the host and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `tests/parity.rs` 19; the wasm module built with that toolchain and wasm-bindgen 0.2.130 (four imports, all wasm-bindgen's own, as before), `web-core/test/run.sh` against the release binary (19 keyfile cases replayed through the module, 7 before). `worker/`: `npm run typecheck`; `npm test` — 56 script tests (53 before), 237 Worker tests. The viewer bundle built from that module passes `check-dist` and the browser suite (`worker/test/e2e/run.mjs`) in Chrome 157, Playwright's WebKit 27.2 and Firefox 159, without the large media fixture. `tests/install/test.sh`: 82 cases (63 before; 78 where `wget` is missing) under `sh`, `dash` and `bash`; `shellcheck`; `actionlint`. Each new regression test was also run once against a copy of the tree with its fix taken out: every one of them failed there.

**Not verified.** Everything ran against the fakes and directory vaults. On **real Drive**: that `files.list` with `trashed = true` shows the trashed keyfiles to a `drive.file` login, and that deleting them works (`passwd --purge-old`); that a same-name re-creation or an in-place overwrite shows the md5 it should (item 2 rests on Drive's listed `md5Checksum`); that `files.create` accepts a caller's `createdTime` at all (item 3 closes it either way). On **GitHub**: the release workflow with the new attestation steps and the `attestations: read` permission of the publish job has not run; `gh release verify-asset` was seen to *fail* for the mutable v0.4.0 and has not been seen to pass, because the repository has no immutable release yet; `gh attestation verify` and `--source-digest` were exercised against the real attestation of the v0.4.0 viewer bundle (pass with the tag's commit, fail with another); the advisories workflow has not run on GitHub (the `cargo audit` command lines were run locally against a copy of the advisory database: no finding in either lockfile), and Dependabot's `cooldown` key is from its documentation. `install.sh`'s attestation path was tested against a stand-in for `gh`, not against a release with attested binaries — there is none before 0.5.0. Linux: nothing here ran on Linux.

### 17.27 The cryptography audit of 0.4.0 — the hosted viewer part (2026-11-13)

The second part of the audit of §17.26: its findings L2 (a script in the viewer's page could take the stream key of every file), L6 (a Service Worker planted while the host was hostile survives the clean redeploy) and I3 (the Worker script is outside the attestation). L2 is a change of code — a boundary the documents claimed and nothing enforced; L6 is a procedure that was missing, with two aids in code; I3 is wording. Each was reproduced first. On-disk and on-Drive formats are untouched; nothing of the CLI changed; a viewer of 0.4.0 and one of 0.5.0 never talk to each other (a page of one build that meets the Service Worker of another is told to reload, as before).

Edited in place: the title line, §1.3 (the Cloudflare row, the script row, the viewer's supply-chain row), §2.3, §4.1, §7.5, §13 (item 8b), §15, §16.8; `README.md`, `docs/AUTH.md`, `worker/README.md`, `worker/viewer/README.md`.

**1. Tickets are sealed to the Service Worker (L2).**

*What was wrong.* §1.3 said "no stream key crosses the page — so what [a script in the page] keeps afterwards is at most one hour of access token", §7.5 "no key material ever crosses the page", and the header comments of `vault-worker.js`, `sw.js` and `provider.js` the same. What existed was a convention of the honest page: it creates the ticket channel and gives both ports away. The vault worker's `tickets` call adopted **any** port the page handed it and `issue` posted the ticket of any path to it — in the clear: the 32-byte stream key, the header, the blob's location, and the access token. A script that starts in the page after the unlock (an extension with access to the page; an injection, of which the audit found no way) learned the vault worker object from the page's next message to it, handed over a port of its own and asked for every path: 273 tickets in 7 ms, 94 kB, and all 273 files decrypted from them offline, after Lock, without the passphrase. Reproduced here against the tree as it was, by the test of item 5: "what the script collected holds a stream key or a blob's name".

*The two designs that enforce the boundary, and the choice.* (a) Keep the read path and make what crosses the port unreadable to the page. (b) Keep stream keys in the vault worker altogether: it decrypts, and hands verified plaintext to the Service Worker. **(a) is built.** (b) has no protocol to get wrong and would make Lock end every read — but it moves the whole delivery path (the store windows, the retry and resume rules, the memory bounds of §17.23) into the worker that also answers the list, puts every byte of a video through a second hop behind that worker's one thread, and ends the two behaviours the viewer has on purpose — a download in progress outlives Lock, and a long download in a background tab survives the five-minute rule — unless the lock rules are changed as well. (a) is additive: one small module, one request, the read path and every Lock rule as they were, the throughput step unchanged. What (a) costs is an assumption about browsers (below), which (b) would not need.

*Why a key agreement over the port would not do, and what authenticates this one.* The page brokers the port. An ECDH exchange carried on it is the textbook case for someone in the middle: the page gives each side a public key of its own and reads everything. Neither side has a secret the page lacks — all three run the same public scripts — so no signature or pre-shared key can fix that. What the two workers do have is a way to each other that does not lead through the page: **a dedicated worker's own `fetch()` is answered by the Service Worker that controls it** (or, when none does, by the host), and a script in the page can neither answer that request, see it, nor change the answer. So the vault worker fetches the Service Worker's public key itself — `GET /seal-key` — and takes nothing else from anyone. The vault worker's public key travels with each sealed ticket, unauthenticated, and need not be: replacing it yields a channel between the Service Worker and the replacer, over which the replacer can hand the Service Worker tickets of their own making — which was never worth protecting, since a ticket only tells the Service Worker how to decrypt something for whoever asks. The construction is §7.5, "The ticket port, and its seal"; the code is `worker/viewer/seal.js` (WebCrypto only: ECDH P-256, HKDF-SHA-256 bound to both public keys by role, AES-256-GCM with the file's id as associated data and a random 96-bit nonce; no key extractable), used by `vault-worker.js` and `sw.js`.

*Could a script in the page put a Service Worker or a worker of its own in the way?* A Service Worker's script has to be a same-origin URL that the host serves as JavaScript, and Service Worker script requests bypass Service Workers; the origin serves the build's files and nothing else (vault content at `/v/<id>` is `text/plain` or an attachment, `nosniff`, and comes from the Service Worker, which a Service Worker script request never reaches). So every Service Worker that can exist on the honest origin runs the build's code. Registering one of the build's scripts for another scope changes nothing about keys: it is honest code, it has another key pair than the instance that holds the page's port, and the result is a file that does not open (and a registration that the page now removes, item 3). A worker of the script's own making — which the page's policy does not allow either — would hold no vault key and get only the public key. Whoever can change what the origin *serves* is another adversary: the Cloudflare row.

*What a `forget` does now.* It drops the key pair with the tickets. Without that, a script that kept sealed tickets could hand them to the Service Worker again after Lock, from a page of the origin, and read through it; with it they open nothing — the vault worker's half of the agreement ended with its page, the Service Worker's with the `forget`. A ticket whose unsealing is still under way when a `forget` arrives is discarded (a counter of `forget`s; the unsealing is asynchronous, which the plain hand-over was not).

*What browsers actually do with a worker's request* — measured, because the seal depends on it (Chrome 157, Playwright's WebKit 27.2 and Firefox 159, macOS; real Safari and phones: not tested). Chrome: every request of a worker created under a controlled page is the Service Worker's, also after a forced reload and a claim. Firefox: the **first** request a new worker makes goes to the network; from the second on, or after a few hundred milliseconds, the Service Worker answers. WebKit decides a worker's controller when its script is loaded — and a worker whose script is at that moment being loaded for another worker of the same process is left **without a controller for good** (reproduced with two `new Worker()` of one URL in a row; never with distinct URLs; never in the viewer's own flows, which were tried with four same-opener popups started together). The consequences in the code: the vault worker asks for the key up to four times within 1.2 s; it asks once when it starts, **before the unlock screen**, and reports whether it got one; a vault worker that did not is ended and replaced by the page while it holds nothing, three starts at most, after which the viewer stops with "The viewer's Service Worker does not answer the worker that holds the vault's keys…". After the unlock the outcome of a missing key is a file that is answered `502` with a sentence, never an unsealed ticket and never a key on the network: the question that can reach the host is a `GET` for a public key, without a cookie. In the browser suite as run (below) no such request reached the host in any engine, and two tabs that reloaded at the same moment started one vault worker each.

*The statement that now holds.* **After the unlock, nothing that reaches the page, or any port, worker object or address a script in the page can get hold of, contains a master key, a stream key, or data from which one can be computed.** A script in the page obtains: sealed tickets (ciphertext to it), ids, names and sizes, the access token, and — through the Service Worker, for as long as the vault is unlocked — the plaintext of any file it asks for. After a Lock that took place — the Service Worker of the origin forgot, the vault worker ended — it holds nothing that opens anything. *What remains true and is said in §1.3* (restated in §17.29, which found the earlier wording too kind): such a script reads every file's plaintext while the vault is unlocked, by the same addresses the page uses; one that is in the page when the passphrase is typed or filled in has the passphrase (and could take the key bundle's port, which is not sealed, for that reason) — also one that arrived after the unlock and is still there at the next entry; one that is in the unlocked page can keep that tab from locking or signing out and then reads on for as long as the tab lives, not merely until the browser stops the Service Worker; and the boundary is the browser's — it does not hold against the party that serves the scripts, nor against an extension that rewrites responses or attaches a debugger. The gain is the audit's delta, reversed: what such a script carries away is what it read, not 350 bytes per file that open the vault later.

**2. A Service Worker left behind by a hostile host (L6).**

*What was wrong.* The recovery text ended at "redeploy, rotate every secret". A page served while someone else controlled the Worker or the domain can register a Service Worker for the origin, which then answers `/` from inside the browser: the release that is deployed again never loads in that browser, `verify-deployed` (no browser profile) reports the host clean, and the page that asks for the passphrase is the other party's. Reproduced here in Chrome with the real Worker code (`signin.mjs`).

*The procedure* — `docs/AUTH.md` ("If something is lost or stolen", with the menu paths per browser), `README.md` ("After a change of hands (the hosted viewer)"; "What you trust"), `worker/README.md` ("Operating it"), §1.3: take the host back and rotate; deploy from a clean checkout and compare; **clear the site's data in every browser that had the viewer open in that time, before the passphrase is typed there again**; if the passphrase was typed in that time, it and the key are known. `verify-deployed` cannot see a browser, and the documents say so where they describe it.

*The Worker-side switch the audit proposed — built, and what it is worth.* `handle()` adds `Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "storage"` to its answer when the request is for the script of a Service Worker (`Service-Worker: script`; `Sec-Fetch-Dest` absent or `serviceworker`) at any path but `/sw.js` (§16.8). It is sound in the sense that it cannot fire for the honest viewer: the viewer's one Service Worker is `/sw.js`, which the asset layer serves; the scripts it imports are requested with `Sec-Fetch-Dest: script` (and in Chrome and WebKit without `Service-Worker` at all — Firefox does send it for imports, which is why the second header is checked); no other site can make a browser send the header. **It is not what the audit's one-browser test suggested.** Measured in three engines: Chrome drops the registration, the storage and the cache — at the registration's next update check, so one more visit shows the other party's page; **Firefox does not act on `Clear-Site-Data` in the answer to a Service Worker's script** (it does in the answer to a page's own request); **WebKit clears the storage and keeps the registration**, on every kind of request tried. And the Worker only sees paths that run it: under `wrangler dev` a miss under `/a/` is the asset layer's, so a script planted there with `Service-Worker-Allowed: /` — which is what someone who has read this would do — never asks the Worker anything. (A foreign script at `/sw.js` itself is replaced by the release's at its update check, with or without the switch.) So: an aid for the commonest browser against the plain case, including a Service Worker that an earlier use of the domain left; **the manual step is the remedy**, and the documents put it first.

*The page's own part.* `shell.js` unregisters, before it registers `/sw.js` for `/`, every Service Worker registration of the origin that has another script or another scope. In every engine, whenever the viewer's page runs at all — which a foreign worker for the whole origin prevents, and a foreign worker for a part of it (the way back from Google, `/callback`, say) does not.

**3. The Worker script is outside the attestation (I3) — wording.** §7.5 said of the release job that "no install script of an npm package ever runs in the workspace that produces the bytes that will see the passphrase", and the README that the deploy scripts verify the attestation "before they upload anything". Both are true of the static files and read as more. The Worker's script answers `/` and `/callback` — the bundle's `index.html` with the status line put in, under headers the Worker sets — and it is bundled by wrangler and esbuild on the owner's machine, after `npm ci` (186 packages in `worker/package-lock.json`, three with install scripts: esbuild, workerd, fsevents), from the working tree. Since §17.26 the deploy scripts refuse a checkout that is not at the release's commit, and `check-release` lists local changes without refusing them; nothing builds the Worker script in the release workflow, attests it, or compares what Cloudflare runs with the tag, and `verify-deployed` identifies itself and checks for the presence of the release's headers, not for the absence of others. Said in §1.3 (the supply-chain row's "Left:"), §7.5, §15, the README ("What you trust") and `worker/README.md`. **Not done** (the audit's hardening, a change of the release and deploy path): building and attesting the Worker script in the release workflow and deploying it with `--no-bundle`; a `verify-deployed` that asks like a browser and reports unexpected headers.

**4. Other changes that came with these.** The header comments of `vault-worker.js`, `sw.js`, `provider.js`, `shell.js` and `kdf-worker.js` say what holds: the ports are the page's to hand out; tickets are sealed; the key bundle's channel is not, and why that loses nothing. The bundle has one more file (`a/<build>/seal.js`; `build.mjs`'s list, each worker's Trusted Types list). `worker/test/e2e/server.mjs`, the fake of the Worker in the browser suite, answers as the Worker does. `worker/README.md`'s first-deployment list has two rows: the seal in Safari and on a phone (13), and the Worker's answer to a foreign Service Worker with three `curl` lines (17).

**5. Tests.** *The audit's attack, in three engines* (`worker/test/e2e/run.mjs`, step `seal`). The test computes the vault's real tickets itself — in Node, from the passphrase, with the core and the loader of the bundle under test — so it knows every stream key. A script in the unlocked page then does what the audit's did: takes the vault worker from the page's next message, hands it a port, asks for the ticket of every path (275 in the full run; two are empty files, which have no key). Asserted: it is answered (275 messages, in about 20 ms); none of the 273 real stream keys — as bytes, base64url, base64 or hex — no blob name and no access token occurs anywhere in what it collected, nor in anything the page was told; every message is `{type, id, build, sealed: {to, from, iv, data}}`; none opens under any key the script can derive from the Service Worker's public key (which it may fetch too), the vault worker's and a key pair of its own; **while unlocked the script does read files** — it hands its sealed tickets to the Service Worker and fetches three addresses, byte-identical to the fixture (the test states what remains true as well as what does not); after Lock the same sealed tickets, handed to the Service Worker again, are answered `410` and the Service Worker holds no ticket. Second, a script that is in the page from the start and relays the ticket channel: files open as ever, and what crossed it is sealed tickets only. Third, a vault worker that reports no key: replaced twice, the third works; three in a row, the viewer stops with its sentence. **Run against the bundle as it was before this change, the step fails at its first assertion** (the stream keys are in what the script collected). *The seal by itself* (`worker/test/viewer/seal.node.mjs`, Node's WebCrypto): what one side closes the other opens; not under another id, with a flipped bit in the nonce or the data, cut short; not with a third party's key pair in any of the four combinations, with the vault worker's public key replaced, with the roles swapped, or by another Service Worker instance; private halves and channel keys are not extractable; 65 bytes that are no point are refused. *The Worker's switch*: `worker/test/refresh.test.ts` (the header for a foreign Service Worker's script on unknown and known paths and without `Sec-Fetch-Dest`; never for `/sw.js`, for an imported script as Firefox requests it, for any other `Sec-Fetch-Dest`, another header value, an ordinary request, or any JSON route; sign-out keeps its own value), `scripts/smoke.mjs` under `wrangler dev` (the Worker's paths with it, `/sw.js` and a miss under `/a/` without), and `worker/test/e2e/signin.mjs` in Chrome through the Worker's real `handle()`: a planted Service Worker keeps answering `/` after the release is back, the Worker answers its update check `404` with the header, Chrome drops it, the next visit is the viewer. *The page's part* (`run.mjs`, step `planted`, three engines): a registration for `/callback` is gone after the next load.

**Results** (macOS, Apple silicon; cargo and rustc 1.99.0 from nix; Node 24.21). The main crate and `web-core/` are untouched by this entry and were run again on the final tree: `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --locked` with restic and `GCLONE_REQUIRE_RESTIC=1` — 807 passed, 3 ignored, as in §17.26; `cargo build --release --locked`; in `web-core/` `cargo fmt --check`, clippy for the host and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `tests/parity.rs` 19, the module built again (the same bytes as §17.26's: four imports, all wasm-bindgen's), and `web-core/test/run.sh` with its browser smoke test in the three engines. `worker/`: `npm run typecheck`; `npm test` — 56 script tests, 239 Worker tests (237 before); `npm run test:viewer` — 45 (39 before); `npm run smoke` — 362 checks under `wrangler dev`. The bundle built from this tree and that module (a development build, 19 files) passes `check-dist`, and against exactly that bundle, **with** the large media fixture (48.8 MiB, 20 Mbit/s): `worker/test/e2e/run.mjs` — Chrome 157.0.8103.51, Playwright's WebKit 27.2 and Firefox 159.0 all pass (148 s, 156 s, 149 s), the streaming, memory and throughput steps as before the change (the recording plays without waiting after its first second; the Service Worker's wasm memory after the 48.8 MiB download is 3.8 / 3.6 / 1.7 MiB); `signin.mjs` (Chrome) and `local.mjs` (three engines) pass. The steps `seal` and `planted` were also run against the bundle built before this change and fail there, each at its first assertion about the fix.

**Not verified.** Nothing ran on a deployment, in Safari itself, in release Firefox, or on a phone: that a vault worker's request reaches the Service Worker there is `worker/README.md`'s first-deployment row 13, and a browser where it does not shows a sentence before the passphrase screen instead of opening files. The three engines' handling of `Clear-Site-Data` was measured over `http://127.0.0.1` with the builds named above, not over `https` and not in Safari; whether a miss under `/a/` runs the Worker in production is known from `wrangler dev` only (row 17). That a dedicated worker's request can be answered by nobody but its Service Worker and the host is how the three engines behave and what the Service Worker specification describes; no specification states it as a security boundary against the worker's own page. The WebKit behaviour above (a worker left uncontrolled when its script is being loaded twice at once) was reproduced on a test page, not provoked in the viewer, and its cause in WebKit not established. Linux: nothing here ran on Linux.

### 17.28 Where a device keeps its secrets: the Secure Enclave key store; draft releases signed on the owner's Mac (2026-11-13)

Finding I6 of the audit of §17.26 — `secrets.json` holds the vault key in plain, the key cannot be rotated, so every copy of the file (a backup, a synced folder, a disk image) is permanent — and its L8 (no rotation) are what this entry is about. It adds a second place for the same document, **sealed by the Secure Enclave of the Mac**, keeps the state root out of backups on both platforms, and changes how a release is published. It followed a design in two revisions with feasibility experiments on the owner's Mac (macOS 27.2, Apple silicon, FileVault on) and two reviews of the first revision ("lock-out and unattended operation", "macOS platform and signing"). **No version-1 format changed**: `secrets.json`, `token.json`, `config.json`, `state.db` and everything on Drive are byte for byte what they were; a device that does nothing stays on `secrets.json`; gclone 0.4.0 keeps working beside the new files (measured, and a test); old and new binaries interoperate while the device is on the plain file.

Edited in place: the title line, §2.5, §7.1, §7.3, §8.1–§8.3, §9.1, §9.2, §9.10, §11, §13 (item 8d), §14 (item 4), §15; `README.md`, `docs/AUTH.md`, `worker/README.md`.

**What was built.**
- **The sealed store** (`src/keystore/`): §8.2 is the specification — the envelope `secrets.sealed`, the load and save tables behind the unchanged `SecretStore` trait (one new method, `save_proven`), `delete`, the secrets lock, the choice file, the two moves and their crash points, the trial with a test value. `src/keystore/macos.rs` is its only unsafe code: the foreign surface is `SecKeyCreateRandomKey`, `SecKeyCopyAttributes`, `SecKeyCreateWithData`, `SecKeyCopyPublicKey`, `SecKeyCopyExternalRepresentation`, `SecKeyCreateEncryptedData`, `SecKeyCreateDecryptedData`, `SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags` (declared by `security-framework-sys`), `SessionGetInfo` (declared in the module itself), and `sysctlbyname`, `getxattr`, `setxattr` from libc; CoreFoundation objects are owned through `core-foundation`. No `SecItem*`, no `SecKeychain*`, no `SecCode*`: a test reads the source for it. The release binary already linked Security and CoreFoundation (TLS): no new library, no new package in `Cargo.lock`.
- **The backup exclusion** (§8.1): the Time Machine attribute on the state root, `CACHEDIR.TAG` on both platforms, one note about older backups.
- **The command** `gclone keystore` (§7.1), the `Key store` line of `status` (§7.3), `ConfigError::{KeyStoreUnavailable, KeyStoreBusy}` (§9.10), the watchers of `web` and `serve restic --port` (§8.3), `login` that is tolerant of a sealed store it cannot open and never writes to it, `logout` that removes both files.
- **Releases**: `release.yml` stops at a **draft**; `scripts/release-sign-macos.sh` signs and publishes; `install.sh` installs the signed macOS build (below).

**What was cut from the first revision, and why.**

| cut | reason |
|---|---|
| a `keychain` mode (the key's handle in the login Keychain) | Locked in cron (measured). Its access list is "identifier and team" only: one binary ever signed with that identifier and a loose entitlement reads every user's item (measured by the reviewer). Void on the Mac that holds the signing key. gclone's own commands walk around it. A foreign `SecItemUpdate` or a login-password reset locks the owner out. Built on calls Apple is retiring. §14 item 4 says what bringing it back needs. |
| automatic removal of `secrets.json` after a trial | It is the one step that can lock a device out, and it cannot be made safe without a list of gates one of which — seeing an older gclone on a scheduler's `PATH` — needs a change to `token.json`, a frozen format. An unattended run could remove the last portable copy with nobody reading the note. The move is one explicit command instead. |
| a sealed copy of the secrets on trial beside the plain file | Replaced by a test value: the same evidence without a second copy of the secrets, without rules for two copies that disagree, and without an older `logout` leaving a usable sealed copy behind. |
| `auto`, `GCLONE_KEYSTORE`, re-keying a sealed store through a `.prev` file | Nothing automatic is left for them to steer; a new key comes with `use file` followed by `use enclave`. |

**Review findings and how they are met** (the first revision's): F1 — `login` failed on a sealed store it could not open, and made tolerant it would have overwritten the key before the passphrase was proven → `login` maps `KeyStoreUnavailable` to "no usable secrets" and saves go to `secrets.json`; the sealed file is removed only by the save that has the keys from a keyfile. F2 — "differs → remove the sealed copy" let a keyless or stale `secrets.json` delete the only key (gclone 0.4.0 writes `keys: []` before its passphrase prompt) → the rule is gone; a keyless `secrets.json` beside a sealed file that opens gives the merged view, guarded by the vault id; nothing is deleted. F3 — crash points of the moves → the new file exists before the old one is removed, the choice is written first on the way back, no step is finished automatically (§8.2's table; a test for every point). F4 — the trial proved less than claimed → it decides nothing; it records days, a later boot (by `kern.bootsessionuuid`, not by the clock), the session of each success and every failure. F5 — an older binary is invisible → no automatic removal; the command says what happens to older binaries and lists other `gclone` files; a writer field in `token.json` is rejected (frozen). F6 — readers rewrote the file that holds the opt-out → two files: `keystore.json` (written only by `keystore use`, under the lock) and `keystore-trial.json` (any reader). F7 — notes nobody reads; the recovery path unchecked → the plain file is removed only by a command a person runs, which lists the keyfiles **and checks the passphrase against one**. F8 — "are there secrets" was two stats → three looks, then one under the shared lock (§8.3). F9 — lock scope → `login` holds the lock around each save only, never across a prompt.

**Measurements** (the experiments' logs are not in the repository).
- *Secure Enclave from Rust.* A non-permanent enclave key can be exported and reloaded: the blob (284–324 bytes) is the attribute `toid` of `SecKeyCopyAttributes`; reload with `SecKeyCreateWithData` and `{type EC, class private, token id Secure Enclave, "toid": blob}`. **Pitfall**: with the blob only as the data argument the framework returns a new, different key without an error — hence the public-half comparison after every reload. The blob has CryptoKit's format (`SecureEnclave.P256.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey(dataRepresentation:)` loads it and shows the same public key). ECIES overhead 81 bytes; 4–6 ms per open; 24 processes opening at once in 0.11 s. **No signature is needed**: an ad hoc binary opens a blob made by a Developer ID signed one and the reverse — the blob is usable by any program of this user on this Mac. A flipped byte in the blob: `CryptoTokenKit error -3` at decrypt; a truncated blob: an error at load; a flipped ciphertext byte: an AES-GCM failure — never a wrong plaintext. A **permanent** enclave key is out of reach for a bare executable (`-34018`: the data-protection keychain needs an entitlement and a provisioning profile). One key seals a test value and later a 1.6 kB document; both open in separate processes. "The stored key fails while a fresh key works" tells a dead blob from a session without access.
- *Sessions.* Terminal and LaunchAgent: the login Keychain unlocked, the enclave opens and creates. **cron: the login Keychain is locked** (`-25300`) while unlocked in the same user's desktop session at the same moment; the enclave opens and creates there. Not measured: ssh, the per-user background launchd domain, a locked screen, after the user's logout, before the first login without FileVault.
- *Time Machine.* The attribute on a directory excludes the directory, the files in it and two levels below, and survives a file inside being replaced by rename; on a file only, it is lost at the first rename.
- *gclone 0.4.0 beside the new files* (the released binary, an isolated home): with `secrets.sealed`, `keystore.json`, `keystore-trial.json`, `secrets.lock`, `CACHEDIR.TAG` and the backup attribute in the state root, its `ls`, `status` and `copy` work unchanged; with only `secrets.sealed` it says "not connected (signed out)", exit 4, and its `logout` says "nothing to do" and leaves the file; its `login` there writes `secrets.json`; its `logout` and `logout --forget` with both present remove `secrets.json` and leave `secrets.sealed`.
- *Finding neither file during a move* (one writer moving a file between two names under a lock, six readers, three runs): two looks (first name, second name) found neither 6, 21 and 3 times in 2 to 4 million looks; three looks 0 times; two looks and one under the shared lock 0 times.
- *Signing.* `codesign --force --sign <Developer ID> --identifier <id> --options runtime --timestamp` runs without any dialog, also from a process without a terminal: **any program of the user can sign as the owner while the identity is in the login keychain**. The CI-built binary signed that way with no entitlements works. **Equality apart from the signature**: `codesign --remove-signature` on a copy of each, then `codesign -f -s - -i <one fixed name>` on each: byte-identical; one changed code byte makes them differ. **The proof is blind to flags and entitlements**: the 0.4.0 binary signed with the runtime flag and three entitlements normalises to the same bytes as the CI binary — hence the separate checks of the flags field and of `codesign -d --entitlements - --xml`. The nix-built local binary links a libiconv from the nix store and does not start under the hardened runtime: only the CI-built binary can be the signed release.

**Releases** (replaces "the publish job publishes" of §17.17; needs the owner's decision to sign at all — the key store does not depend on it).
- `release.yml`, job `release`: `gh release create "$TAG" --draft --verify-tag …` and stop. The draft's notes start with a paragraph "DRAFT until signed …".
- Repository setting: **immutable releases on, before the tag is pushed.**
- `scripts/release-sign-macos.sh <tag>`, on the owner's Apple-silicon Mac; everything that can fail comes before publishing, and until then it can be run again — **also after an upload of step 13 that was cut off** (§17.29: `gh release upload --clobber` deletes the old asset before it uploads; the draft may then lack `SHA256SUMS`, or the signed archive its `SHA256SUMS` lists, or both — `SHA256SUMS` is *derived* from the four attested archives in step 4, never an input that must exist). The script puts `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin` first on `PATH` (the system's `tar`, `file`, `otool`, `lipo`, `codesign`; inside the project's nix shell GNU tar and another `file` made step 5 refuse an attested binary). **Order on a release day** (§17.29): push the tag *alone* (`git push origin v<version>`), wait for the workflow, run this script, deploy the viewer — and push `main` only after the release is published: the README's one-liner pipes `install.sh` from `main`, the new `install.sh` refuses a release without attested binaries, and until the draft is published the latest release is the previous one. Steps: (1) preconditions — `gh` with write access, immutable releases enabled, the tag at the same commit locally and on GitHub, exactly one identity of type *Developer ID Application* in the (optionally separate, `GCLONE_SIGN_KEYCHAIN`, unlocked by the script and locked again on every way out) keychain, or `GCLONE_SIGN_IDENTITY`; (2) the release is a draft with exactly the workflow's files; (3) download; (4) every archive's attestation (`--signer-workflow …/release.yml --source-ref refs/tags/<tag> --source-digest <commit> --deny-self-hosted-runners`), every line of `SHA256SUMS`, and the digests GitHub reports; (5) the macOS archive has one member, the regular file `gclone`: a thin arm64 Mach-O, ad hoc signed, linking only system libraries; (6) sign a copy — identifier `io.github.dwahdany.gclone`, `--options runtime --timestamp`, no entitlements; (7) the signature: `codesign --verify --strict`, flags **exactly** `0x10000(runtime)`, no entitlements — by codesign's **exit status and** empty output: a codesign that cannot answer (one that does not know `--xml`) is a refusal, here and in `install.sh` (§17.29) —, a timestamp, an Apple-issued Developer ID (`anchor apple generic and certificate 1[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.6] exists and certificate leaf[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.1.13] exists` — no team in the script), the designated requirement of the expected shape; (8) continuity — the designated requirement's text **equals** that of the previous signed release, and the new binary satisfies it; the first signed release prints it and asks for a typed confirmation — and "first" is something GitHub **answered**: a `gh release list` or a `gh release view` that fails stops the script (§17.29; both failed open, and a typed confirmation then published a release that nobody had compared with the previous signer); (9) equality apart from the signature; (10) the signed binary runs in a temp home: `--version` (the tag's version, this target), a directory-vault `login`, `copy`, `cat`, `gclone keystore check`; (11) notarization if `GCLONE_NOTARY_PROFILE` is set (a bare executable cannot be stapled); (12) pack `gclone-aarch64-apple-darwin-signed.tar.gz` without owner or extended attributes; (13) `SHA256SUMS` = the workflow's lines plus the signed archive's, sorted; upload both; (14) download the whole draft again: the file set, every checksum, every attestation, and keep these files and their hashes (`L`); (15) publish after a typed confirmation — immediately before, the draft's digests must equal `L` — with `gh release edit --draft=false --latest` and notes without the draft paragraph (the team is not named); (16) the published digests equal `L`, `gh release verify`, `gh release verify-asset` for each file of `L`, and `install.sh --require-attestation` from the release — **each question asked up to four times, five seconds apart, with gh's own error text kept** (§17.29). Two outcomes are told apart: published digests that differ from `L` — "THE PUBLISHED RELEASE DOES NOT VERIFY … cannot be repaired in place", exit 1; and a question that was not answered or was answered with an error — "THE PUBLISHED RELEASE COULD NOT BE VERIFIED YET", exit 3, with what failed and the instruction to run **`scripts/release-sign-macos.sh --verify-published <tag>`**, a mode that needs no draft, no state of the run and no signing identity and changes nothing: it downloads every file, checks `SHA256SUMS`, the four attestations, the signed binary (step 7's checks and the equality with the attested one), `gh release verify`, `verify-asset` per file and `install.sh`. (One transient error of gh after publishing used to produce the "cannot be repaired … publish a new patch release" verdict, with no way to look again: a second run stops at step 2, the work directory is gone.) A mismatch in (16) cannot be repaired in place: a new patch release and a notice.
- `install.sh` on macOS: where `SHA256SUMS` lists the signed archive it is installed (`--unsigned`: the attested build) after `codesign --verify --strict`, the Developer ID requirement, flags exactly `0x10000(runtime)`, no entitlements, and the equality proof against the unsigned archive of the same release; with `gh` also the unsigned archive's attestation and `gh release verify-asset <tag>` on the signed one. **What gh must be able to do is probed, not assumed** (§17.29): `gh attestation verify` without `--source-ref` (gh 2.49 to 2.67) counts as "too old to verify attestations: it needs gh 2.68.0 or newer" — the checksum note, or a refusal under `--require-attestation` — and a gh without `release verify-asset` (before 2.75.0) verifies the attestation and says that the signed archive's place in the published release was not checked (a refusal under `--require-attestation`). Both used to end in "unknown flag" / "unknown command", reported as a release without attestations and as a signed archive that is not in the release. **Continuity for whatever is about to be installed**: if the gclone in place is Developer ID signed, the new binary must satisfy its designated requirement — a release without a signed archive and `--unsigned` included ("the installed gclone is signed; this one is not") — unless `--allow-signer-change`. The first signed install trusts the signer it finds. An older `install.sh` ignores the extra line of `SHA256SUMS` and installs the attested build. What the continuity check is worth: the README pipes `install.sh` from `main` into `sh`, and whoever can publish a release can normally change that script; the check holds for someone who runs a saved copy.
- Tests have no Developer ID: `install.sh` (away from the real GitHub only, `GCLONE_TEST_ACCEPT_ADHOC_SIGNATURE=1`) and the release script (`--selftest`, which runs against `tests/release/fake-gh.sh` only and refuses any other `gh`) accept an ad hoc signature with the hardened runtime in its place.

**Deviations from the design** (revision 2), each on purpose:
1. **The backup exclusion is also applied by the first load of the secrets in a process**, not only "when the state root is created, and on every later save or `keystore use`": with the design's wording a Mac that never signs in again would never get it, which contradicts the design's own "a Mac whose owner does nothing stays on the plain file, with the backup exclusion".
2. **`status` has no JSON output** (§7.1 refuses `--json` there), so the design's `key_store` object is what `gclone keystore --json` prints.
3. **`keystore use enclave` makes or picks the key first** and opens the vault second (the design's steps 1 and 3 swapped): a session that cannot use the enclave is told so before the network is asked.
4. **`keystore use enclave` has `--all-keyfiles`** (as `login` has): its passphrase check uses `login`'s unlock, whose messages name the flag.
5. **A `login` that renews nothing on a device whose view is the merged one saves once**, writing the two files as one `secrets.json`: the design said "a later `login` settles it", and without the save a login that is still valid would settle nothing.
6. **`keystore use file` with a keyless `secrets.json` and a sealed file that does not open is refused even with `--discard-sealed`** (rule 3: the sealed file may be the only copy of the key).
7. **A debug build has no sealer and reads no sealed file** unless `GCLONE_TEST_KEYSTORE_SEALER` names one; it says so instead of touching hardware.
8. **The clock hook the design calls "existing" did not exist**: `GCLONE_TEST_NOW_MS` was added, for the trial only.
9. **The old-binary test takes the 0.4.0 binary from `GCLONE_TEST_OLD_GCLONE`** and prints SKIPPED without it: no CI job downloads a release today.
10. **`install.sh` runs the equality proof also without `gh`** (both archives are at hand): it then shows "the signed archive is the unsigned one of this release", not provenance, and the one-line note says which.
11. **The release script's self-test covers steps 1 to 16**, not 5 to 13, by way of a fake `gh`; with an ad hoc signature it cannot exercise the timestamp, the Developer ID requirement and the shape of a real designated requirement.

**Results** (macOS 27.2, Apple silicon; cargo and rustc from nix; restic on `PATH` and `GCLONE_REQUIRE_RESTIC=1`; `GCLONE_DEFAULT_AUTH_URL` unset.) `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --locked` — **873 passed, 3 ignored** (807 before this entry) — also with `GCLONE_REQUIRE_ENCLAVE=1` and `GCLONE_TEST_OLD_GCLONE` naming the released 0.4.0 binary, so that both hardware tests ran against the real Secure Enclave and the old-binary test ran; `cargo build --release --locked`, without a warning. **Linux** (a container on the Mac, `rust:1.99.1` — the pinned toolchain — aarch64, glibc, an unprivileged user): `cargo fmt --check`, clippy with `-D warnings`, `cargo test --locked` — 867 passed, 3 ignored (the six macOS-only unit tests are not compiled; no restic there) — and the release build without a warning. `tests/install/test.sh`: 108 cases under `sh`, `bash` and `dash` on macOS with wget (83 on Linux, where the cases of the signed build are skipped with a note); `tests/release/selftest.sh`: 40 cases, with `GCLONE_REQUIRE_ENCLAVE=1`; shellcheck clean on `install.sh`, both test scripts, the release script and the fake `gh`. `web-core/` compiles `src/error.rs`, which gained two variants, and its lockfile gained the main crate's two new dependency names: `cargo fmt --check`, clippy for the host and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `tests/parity.rs` 19 passed, `web-core/test/run.sh` OK — and **the wasm module is byte for byte what it was before this entry** (same SHA-256, 688,216 bytes), so the viewer bundle does not change. The Worker is untouched (typecheck and its 239 tests run again). **By hand, with the release binary and the real Secure Enclave**, in an isolated home under a temp directory: `login` (directory vault), `keystore check` (a key made and used in 9 ms), the trial's first step, `keystore use enclave` (a 324-byte blob, a 65-byte public key), reads by the binary and by a copy of it with another ad hoc signature and another identifier, 16 processes at once, the backup attribute on the state root, `keystore use file`, `logout`; the login keychain held the same number of items before and after — the keys are not permanent and nothing is stored outside the directory, which was removed.

**Not verified.** **The sealed store on real machines over time**: a sealed file across a restart or a macOS update; ssh, a LaunchDaemon, `user/<uid>` agents, a locked screen, after the user's logout, before the first login without FileVault; gclone's own binary from cron and from a LaunchAgent (the experiments measured a probe binary there, not gclone); a reset of the login password; a Mac without a Secure Enclave (only the stand-in's "no key can be made" path ran — on such a Mac and on a hosted CI runner the framework is expected to return an error; that it does not hang there was not seen). The trial ran over days, boots and sessions only with the test clock and test identifiers; the two once-only notes were shown only through the test switch, never on a real terminal. That Time Machine skips the directory was measured in the experiments with `tmutil`'s own attribute; the test compares gclone's bytes with it and does not run a backup. **Releases**: nothing ran against GitHub. `release.yml`'s draft step; every `gh` call of the release script against a real draft (finding a draft by its tag, downloading from it, `--clobber`, publishing with `--latest`), the immutable-releases query, `gh release verify` and `verify-asset`; signing with a Developer ID — the secure timestamp, the Developer ID requirement, the shape of a real designated requirement for this identifier (the pattern was compared with the text `codesign` prints for a third party's Developer ID application, not with a signature of this identifier), a separate signing keychain (unlock, `codesign --keychain`, `find-identity` on a keychain file, the lock on the way out), notarization; `install.sh` with a real Developer ID signed archive (its tests and the self-test use an ad hoc signature with the hardened runtime in its place). The steps added to `ci.yml` (the installer's and the release script's tests on the macOS runner) have not run on GitHub. **Older binaries**: gclone 0.4.0 for macOS was run beside the new files; the Linux build of 0.4.0 was not, and neither was a long-running 0.4.0 `gclone web` across a move. **Linux**: the run above was a container (aarch64, glibc) — not musl, not x86_64, not a Linux machine of its own. To be done by hand on the owner's Mac before `gclone keystore use enclave` is recommended in the README without reservation: `gclone keystore check` from cron, from a LaunchAgent and over ssh; a restart, then `gclone status` (the trial shows "a restart survived"); a restic run through `serve restic` from the scheduler actually in use, then `gclone keystore` (that session is in the record); and, if releases are signed, a scheduled job that needs a privacy grant, before and after the first signed build.

### 17.29 Review of §17.26–§17.28 before the release: twenty-four reports (2026-11-13)

The work of §17.26 (the audit's fixes in the CLI and core), §17.27 (the hosted viewer's key boundary) and §17.28 (the key store, the signed release) was reviewed before anything of it was committed: with a gclone 0.4.0 built from its tag beside the new binary, in the three browser engines, with the stand-in sealer and with the real Secure Enclave, and with gh's own source at the versions in question. Twenty-four reports; two pairs name one cause, so twenty-two causes. **All were real**; each was confirmed again here (most by its regression test failing on the code before the fix), fixed at its cause, and has a test. Nothing of the key store was switched off: the one finding that could lock a device out (item 10) is a rule of the save table now, and the unasked trial is bounded in time (item 13) — the sealed store itself was opt-in already. The sections named were edited in place.

**The passphrase (§2.6).**

1. *A typed passphrase of the 26-symbol shape, set by 0.5.0, was "Wrong passphrase" on gclone 0.4.0 and in a hosted viewer still on 0.4.0* (two reports). §17.26 item 5 canonicalised every input of that shape when a passphrase was **set**; 0.4.0 uses such an input as typed. Five ordinary words without a `u` and with 26 letters are enough (`the new victim passphrase long`), and the user never learns the canonical spelling `THENE-WV1CT-…`.
